docs.title: Textual
docs.text:
Textual is the closest alternative in the same language, and the most complete: it has a large widget library with data tables, trees, tabs, select menus, checkboxes and progress bars, text selection, visible scrollbars, an inline mode, Windows support, and a way to serve apps in a browser.

The difference is how you describe a UI. In Textual, a UI is a tree of widget objects that live across renders. You change it by setting reactive attributes, by querying for widgets and calling methods on them, and by handling messages that bubble up the tree. What the screen shows at any moment depends on the history of those changes.

In Counterweight, a UI is a function of state. Components are functions that return elements, and every change to state renders the tree again from those functions, so what the screen shows depends only on the current state. A component's props are its function arguments, so a type checker checks every place a component is used.

Styling differs in the same direction. Textual's TCSS stylesheets match widgets by type, ID and class from a separate file or class variable, with a cascade deciding which rule wins. Counterweight's styles are values written on the element they style, so you can see what an element looks like without looking anywhere else.

Layout differs too. Textual's grid has its own rules, and it has no flexbox. Counterweight's layout is the web's flexbox and grid, so what you know from CSS carries over (see Layout).

Choose Textual when you need its widgets, Windows, inline mode or the browser, or a framework that many apps already depend on.

docs.title: Ink
docs.text:
Ink is React itself, rendering to the terminal. Its README lists Claude Code, Gemini CLI and GitHub Copilot CLI among the tools built with it. If you know Ink, you know most of Counterweight: components, use_state, use_effect, use_ref, use_memo, keys and memo all follow React's rules (see Components). Both render only the components whose state changed and the components they return, skipping memo components whose arguments are unchanged.

The main reason to choose Counterweight over Ink is Python. A Counterweight app runs in the same process as the Python libraries it presents, such as a model client, a data pipeline or a test runner, with no separate service between them.

Beyond the language:

  • Effects are async functions. Where a React effect returns a cleanup function, a Counterweight effect is cancelled when its dependencies change or its component unmounts, so cleanup goes in a try/finally block (see use_effect).
  • Counterweight lays out with grid as well as flexbox.
  • Counterweight has mouse input, through on_input handlers and the use_mouse and use_hovered hooks. Ink has none.

Ink renders inline by default, below the shell prompt, and its <Static> component writes output that stays in the terminal's scrollback. Counterweight always takes over the whole screen. Choose Ink for a command-line tool whose output should stay in the scrollback, or when your code is already in JavaScript.

docs.title: Ratatui
docs.text:
Ratatui is an immediate-mode library: it keeps no tree of your UI between frames. Each frame, your code draws widgets into a screen-sized buffer, and Ratatui writes the cells that differ from the previous frame's buffer. Your code owns the event loop, the input handling and all of the state.

Counterweight owns all three. It keeps the component tree and its state between renders, reads input, calls your handlers, and renders again when state changes. Its output stage works like Ratatui's: every render paints a full buffer, diffs it against the last one, and writes only the changes.

Their layout models differ. Ratatui splits an area by constraints on the parent, while Counterweight uses flexbox and grid, where content can size its container. Coming from Ratatui? shows the equivalents of Ratatui's constraints, and where they behave differently.

Choose Ratatui for a single compiled binary, for full control over when and what you draw, or when frame time is the constraint: Counterweight renders in Python, and Ratatui in Rust.

docs.title: What Counterweight doesn't do
docs.text:
These are the gaps you're most likely to hit, with what to do instead:

  • Text selection, and scrolling a long line. use_text_input and use_text_area have no selection, and a single-line value wider than its box doesn't scroll to keep the cursor in view. Tracked in #420 (scrolling a long line).
  • Inline rendering. Counterweight always uses the terminal's alternate screen, so nothing it draws remains in the scrollback when the app exits. Tracked in #393.
  • Windows. Counterweight reads input through POSIX terminal APIs, and is tested on Linux and macOS.
  • A widget library. Counterweight's widgets are a text input and a text area, and its rich text renders Markdown and highlighted code. Tables, trees, menus, tabs and the rest you build from elements, layout, styles and hooks.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: This page is for an app that feels slow. It covers finding where a frame's time goes, which components a frame runs, and how to skip the ones whose output can't have changed. It quotes no frame times, since they depend on the app, the machine and the terminal: measure your own.

docs.title: Where does my frame's time go?
docs.text: When an event changes state, Counterweight runs a frame: it re-runs the components that need it, lays out the elements, paints the screen, compares the paint with the previous frame's, and writes the difference to the terminal.

docs.title: The devlog
docs.text:
Every app writes a log of each frame to a file. Run counterweight devlog in another terminal to follow it as the app writes it. It holds counterweight's records and your app's at every level, and other loggers' from INFO up; pass app a log_levels mapping to change that by logger name, such as {"some_library": logging.DEBUG} to include a library's debug records. Each frame logs one line per stage, with microsecond timestamps, so the gaps between lines show where a slow frame went. Here is the process table below handling one key press:

03:36:29.273368 DEBUG    counterweight.app Updated shadow tree components_run=3
03:36:29.273499 DEBUG    counterweight.app Calculated layout
03:36:29.273592 DEBUG    counterweight.app Generated new paint
03:36:29.273606 DEBUG    counterweight.app Healed borders in new paint hint_cells=0 diff_cells=0
03:36:29.273638 DEBUG    counterweight.app Diffed new paint from current paint diff_runs=2 diff_cells=50
03:36:29.273655 DEBUG    counterweight.app Generated instructions from paint diff
03:36:29.273667 DEBUG    counterweight.app Reconciled effects
03:36:29.273675 DEBUG    counterweight.app Completed render cycle

components_run counts the components the frame called, which is the number the rest of this page is about.

docs.title: Profiling
docs.text:
Python's sampling profiler, profiling.sampling, shows which functions the time went to. Run the app under it (-m my_package profiles a module), use the app until it feels slow, quit, and open the flamegraph:

python -m profiling.sampling run --flamegraph -o profile.html my_app.py

Below render_loop, each stage of a frame is one function:

  • update_shadow calls your components, so your component functions appear under it.
  • layout_changes and LayoutTree.compute lay out the elements.
  • paint_layout, heal_borders, diff_paint and paint_to_instructions draw the screen.
  • handle_effects starts and stops effects.

If most of the time is under update_shadow, in your own functions, the rest of this page is for you. Layout and paint grow with how many elements are on screen and how many of them changed; if they dominate a profile, please open an issue with the flamegraph.

docs.title: Which components run in a frame?
docs.text:
In each frame, every component has one of three outcomes:

  • Re-run: its function is called again. A component re-runs when its own state changed, or when the component that returned it re-ran and so built it again: calling metric_card(...) makes a new Component every time.
  • Pass through: it isn't called, but a component below it re-runs, so its previous output is kept and searched for the component that changed.
  • Reuse: neither it nor anything below it changed, so its previous output is kept whole, and layout doesn't reconcile it again.

A component that calls use_rects also re-runs when its rectangles move, and one that calls use_clock when its next tick starts. The first frame, and the frames after a resize or a resume from a suspend, re-run every component.

Here's a dashboard whose root holds a note you type into:

def note_line(field: TextInput) -> tuple[Text, Div]:
    return (
        Text(content="Note: "),
        Div(
            style=row | overflow_x_scroll | stick_to_end_x,
            on_input=field.on_press,
            children=(
                Text(content=field.before_cursor, style=text_wrap_none),
                Text(content=field.at_cursor, style=text_wrap_none | CURSOR, handle=field.cursor_cell),
                Text(content=field.after_cursor, style=text_wrap_none),
            ),
        ),
    )


@component
def metric_card(label: str, value: str) -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=fill(1) | col | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
        children=(
            Text(content=label, style=text_color("slate", 400)),
            Text(content=value),
        ),
    )


@component
def dashboard() -> Div:
    note, set_note = use_state("")
    field = use_text_input(note, set_note, auto_focus=True)

    return Div(
        style=col,
        on_input=field.on_input,
        children=(
            Div(style=row, children=note_line(field)),
            Div(style=row, children=tuple(metric_card(label, value) for label, value in METRICS)),
        ),
    )

Each key press changes dashboard's state, so it re-runs, builds a new metric_card for each metric, and every card re-runs too, though none of them shows anything that changed:

flowchart TB
    dashboard["dashboard"]:::rerun --> column["Div"]:::rerun
    column --> note_row["Div: Note: d"]:::rerun
    column --> cards_row["Div"]:::rerun
    cards_row --> cards["metric_card ×4"]:::rerun

    classDef rerun fill:#f59e0b,stroke:#b45309,color:#000

Move the state down into the component that shows it:

@component
def note() -> Div:
    text, set_text = use_state("")
    field = use_text_input(text, set_text, auto_focus=True)
    return Div(style=row, on_input=field.on_input, children=note_line(field))


@component
def dashboard() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            note(),
            Div(style=row, children=tuple(metric_card(label, value) for label, value in METRICS)),
        ),
    )

Now each key press re-runs note alone. dashboard passes through to it, and the cards are reused:

flowchart TB
    dashboard["dashboard"]:::through --> column["Div"]:::through
    column --> note["note"]:::rerun
    column --> cards_row["Div"]:::reuse
    cards_row --> cards["metric_card ×4"]:::reuse

    classDef rerun fill:#f59e0b,stroke:#b45309,color:#000
    classDef through fill:#93c5fd,stroke:#1d4ed8,color:#000
    classDef reuse fill:#d1d5db,stroke:#6b7280,color:#000

Orange re-runs, blue passes through, and grey is reused. Elements are drawn too, since a frame passes through or reuses them the same way. Holding state in the component that uses it is the first thing to try, and it needs no new API. The same goes for use_clock: call it in the component that shows the time, and each tick re-runs that component alone.

docs.title: How do I skip a component whose arguments didn't change?
docs.text:
State can't always move down. A process table re-runs whenever the processes or the selection change, and so builds every row again, though most rows show the same process with the same selection as before. Declare the row memo, and it's reused when its arguments equal the previous frame's:

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Process:
    pid: int
    name: str
    cpu: float


@component(memo=True)
def process_row(process: Process, is_selected: bool, select: Setter[int]) -> Text:
    return Text(
        content=f"{process.pid:>6}  {process.name:<10} {process.cpu:>5.1f}%",
        style=text_bg("slate", 700) if is_selected else text_color("slate", 300),
        on_input=on_click(lambda: select(process.pid)),
    )


@component
def process_table(processes: tuple[Process, ...]) -> Div:
    use_focus(auto_focus=True)
    by_cpu = use_memo(lambda: sorted(processes, key=lambda process: process.cpu, reverse=True), deps=(processes,))
    selected_pid, set_selected_pid = use_state(by_cpu[0].pid)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        pids = [process.pid for process in by_cpu]
        index = pids.index(selected_pid) if selected_pid in pids else 0
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Up):
                set_selected_pid(pids[max(index - 1, 0)])
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Down):
                set_selected_pid(pids[min(index + 1, len(pids) - 1)])
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col,
        on_input=on_input,
        children=tuple(
            process_row(process, process.pid == selected_pid, set_selected_pid).with_key(str(process.pid))
            for process in by_cpu
        ),
    )

Moving the selection re-runs process_table and the two rows whose is_selected changed, and reuses the rest. A new sample in which one process's CPU changed re-runs that process's row alone, wherever the new order moved it. Three choices make that work:

  • The rows are keyed by pid. An unkeyed memo component compares its arguments with whatever item was at its index last frame, so when a sort reorders the list, most rows get a different process and re-run. A key compares each row with its own previous arguments.
  • Selection is passed as is_selected, computed from the pid. Passing the selected index instead would change every row's arguments whenever it moved.
  • select is the setter itself. A setter is the same object on every render, so it compares equal. A handler built while rendering, such as lambda pid: set_selected_pid(pid), is a new object every time, so it never does.

docs.title: How do I cache a value?
docs.text:
use_memo keeps a value from one render to the next, computing it again only when its dependencies change. Use it for:

  • A value derived from arguments or state. process_table sorts the processes only when they change, not when the selection moves.
  • An unchanging part of a component's output. A component that returns the same element object as last render keeps the components inside it from re-running, as a reused component does.
  • A handler passed to a memo component that has to do more than call a setter: use_memo(lambda: handler, deps) keeps it the same object until deps change.

Caching per item goes in the item's own component, as process_row does with memo=True. A parent can't call use_memo once per item, because hooks are matched up by the order they're called in, so the number of calls can't change from one render to the next. See use_memo or functools.lru_cache? for when a module-level cache fits better.

docs.title: What goes wrong?
docs.text: Each mistake below either makes a cache miss every time, which is correct but slow, or makes it hit when it shouldn't, which shows stale output.

docs.title: With memo=True
docs.text:
A callback argument built while rendering never equals the previous one:

process_row(process, process.pid == selected_pid, lambda pid: set_selected_pid(pid))

Every row re-runs whenever the table does, as if it weren't memo. Pass the setter itself, or a handler kept with use_memo.

An argument mutated in place equals itself, since it's the same object:

@component(memo=True)
def key_list(keys: list[str]) -> Text:
    return Text(content=" ".join(keys))


@component
def key_log() -> Div:
    use_focus(auto_focus=True)
    keys = use_ref(list[str]())
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        if not isinstance(event, KeyPressed):
            return None
        keys.current.append(event.key)
        set_count(lambda count: count + 1)
        return ()

    return Div(on_input=on_input, children=(key_list(keys.current),))

key_list keeps showing the keys from when it last ran. Replace the value instead of changing it: hold a tuple in state, and set a new one with set_keys(lambda keys: (*keys, event.key)).

A hidden input, such as a module-level setting, isn't one of the arguments:

SETTINGS = {"accent": "amber"}


@component(memo=True)
def title(text: str) -> Text:
    return Text(content=f"[{SETTINGS['accent']}] {text}")

Changing SETTINGS doesn't show until text changes. Pass the setting as an argument: title(text, accent=SETTINGS["accent"]).

An unkeyed list that reorders pairs each row with a different item:

process_row(process, process.pid == selected_pid, set_selected_pid)

Rows re-run wherever the order changed. Key each row by its item, as .with_key(str(process.pid)) does above.

A large argument rebuilt every render still hits, but slowly:

line_list(tuple(line.upper() for line in lines))

The new tuple is never the same object as last render's, so every hit compares it item by item with the previous one. Keep it with use_memo(lambda: tuple(line.upper() for line in lines), deps=(lines,)), so a hit is one identity check.

docs.title: With use_memo
docs.text:
A dependency missing from deps keeps the cached value from following it:

busy = use_memo(lambda: [process for process in processes if process.cpu > threshold], deps=(processes,))

Changing threshold keeps showing the old count. List every value compute reads: deps=(processes, threshold).

A cached handler that captured state keeps acting on the value it captured:

count, set_count = use_state(0)
on_input = use_memo(lambda: lambda event, _: set_count(count + 1), deps=())

Every key press sets count to 1. Pass a function to the setter, which receives the latest value, so the handler captures nothing that changes: set_count(lambda count: count + 1).

A dependency that's new every render never equals the previous one:

def submit(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> None:
    if isinstance(event, KeyPressed):
        on_submit(event.key)


on_input = use_memo(lambda: submit, deps=(on_submit,))

When the parent passes on_submit=lambda text: set_query(text), compute runs on every render. Pass something that stays the same object, such as the setter, or keep the parent's handler with use_memo.

use_memo in a loop calls a different number of hooks when the loop's length changes:

labels = [use_memo(lambda: f"{process.name} ({process.pid})", deps=(process,)) for process in processes]

When the number of processes changes, the render raises InconsistentHookExecution. Render a component per item and cache inside it.

Caching something cheap costs more than it saves: every render still compares deps and keeps a hook, which costs more than an f-string or a dictionary lookup. Nothing looks wrong; it only shows in a profile.

docs.title: Which mistakes check_purity catches
docs.text:
Mistake Symptom check_purity memo: callback argument built while rendering Always re-runs Not caught memo: argument mutated in place Stale Raises ImpureComponent memo: hidden input Stale Raises ImpureComponent memo: unkeyed list that reorders Re-runs wherever the order changed Not caught memo: large argument rebuilt every render Slow hits Not caught use_memo: dependency missing from deps Stale Raises StaleMemo use_memo: cached handler that captured state Stale Raises StaleMemo use_memo: dependency that's new every render Always recomputes Not caught use_memo in a loop Raises InconsistentHookExecution Not needed use_memo on something cheap Slower than not caching Not caught

The ones it doesn't catch produce correct output, only slowly, so find them with the devlog's components_run or a profile.

docs.title: How do I catch stale output?
docs.text:
Pass check_purity=True to app in tests, and drive the app with an autopilot:

async def test_process_table_is_pure() -> None:
    await app(
        root(),
        headless=True,
        dimensions=(32, 7),
        autopilot=[KeyPressed(key=Key.Down), KeyPressed(key=Key.Down), KeyPressed(key=Key.Up), Quit()],
        check_purity=True,
    )

After each frame, every component is run again with the same arguments and hooks, and if that builds a different tree from the one the frame built, the app raises ImpureComponent, naming the first component whose output differs. That catches output a frame kept from a component that should have re-run, and a component that returns something different each time it's called. Every use_memo whose deps didn't change computes its value again, and raises StaleMemo if the result differs from the cached one. Elements are compared with ==, and where that fails, piece by piece, with handlers compared by their code and the values they captured, since a re-run builds new ones that never == the old ones.

The second run costs about as much as re-running everything, so leave it off outside tests. It only checks the frames a test drives, so drive the interactions that change what a component might read without being told, such as a setting changed from another screen. use_ref covers what it catches for refs.

docs.title: counterweight.utils.clamp
docs.text: clamp(min_: C, val: C, max_: C) -> C

docs.title: Components
docs.text: A component is a function decorated with @component that returns an element and holds state through hooks. This page covers how a component's state survives from one render to the next, how to use keys to control that, and how to skip re-running a component whose arguments didn't change. The rules are the same as React's; React's Preserving and Resetting State covers the same ground with interactive examples.

docs.title: How a component keeps its state
docs.text:
A render calls a component function again when that component's state changed, or when the component that returned it was called again (unless it's a memo component whose arguments didn't change), and builds a new tree, keeping the previous render's output for every component it didn't call. Counterweight then pairs each component in the new tree with one from the previous render. A component that finds a partner continues it: it keeps its hooks, so use_state returns the stored value and its effects keep running. A component that finds no partner mounts with fresh hooks, and a previous component that nobody paired with unmounts: its effects are cancelled, its state is discarded, and calling one of its use_state setters does nothing.

Pairing happens among siblings (the children of one parent), and a partner must be the same component function. Among those:

  • An unkeyed component continues the unkeyed sibling at the same index.
  • A keyed component continues the sibling that had the same key, wherever that sibling was.

So without keys, a component's position is its identity. That is the right default for most of a UI, where the same component sits in the same place every render, and it is why an ordinary unkeyed component keeps its state across renders.

docs.title: When position isn't identity
docs.text:
Position stops being identity when the children come from data that changes shape. Here each row of a to-do list holds its own checkmark:

from counterweight.components import component
from counterweight.elements import Div, Text
from counterweight.handlers import on_click
from counterweight.hooks import use_state


@component
def todo_row(title: str) -> Text:
    done, set_done = use_state(False)

    return Text(content=f"[{'x' if done else ' '}] {title}", on_input=on_click(lambda: set_done(not done)))


@component
def todo_list(titles: list[str]) -> Div:
    return Div(children=tuple(todo_row(title) for title in titles))

Check off a, then remove it from titles:

before: [x] a    after: [x] b
        [ ] b           [ ] c
        [ ] c

Row b is now checked. The component at index 0 continued the old index-0 row, a's state included, and was only told its title is now b. The old index-2 row is the one that unmounted. State stays with the position, while the data moved.

Key each row by the item it shows, and the state follows the item instead:

@component
def todo_list(titles: list[str]) -> Div:
    return Div(children=tuple(todo_row(title).with_key(title) for title in titles))

before: [x] a    after: [ ] b
        [ ] b           [ ] c
        [ ] c

Now a's row is the one that unmounts, and b and c keep their own state. The same holds when keyed rows are reordered or a row is inserted at the front: each existing row keeps its state and effects, and only a new key mounts.

The same shift happens without any list, when a child conditionally appears in front of a component:

Div(children=(Text(content="Saved!"), editor()) if saved else (editor(),))

When saved becomes true, editor moves from index 0 to index 1, finds no unkeyed sibling there, and remounts with empty state. Either key it (editor().with_key("editor")), or keep its position fixed by always rendering the slot in front of it:

Div(children=(Text(content="Saved!" if saved else ""), editor()))

docs.title: Choosing a key
docs.text:
• Use whatever identifies the item in your data: a database id, a file path, a title if titles are unique.
  • Keys are strings, so convert a numeric id with with_key(str(item.id)).
  • Don't use the item's index in the list. with_key(str(i)) behaves the same as no key at all, because the key follows the position, not the item.
  • A key only has to be unique among siblings, so two separate lists can reuse the same keys. Keyed siblings that share a key raise DuplicateKey; any number of unkeyed siblings is fine.

docs.title: Resetting state with a key
docs.text:
Since a different key means a different component, changing a component's key is how you throw away its state on purpose. The Wordle example keys its game board by the solution word:

play(solution=solution, stop_playing=stop_playing).with_key(solution)

Starting a new game picks a new solution, so a fresh play mounts with an empty board, and play doesn't need to reset each of its own state variables. Adding a key to a component or removing one counts as a change too.

docs.title: Keys go on components
docs.text: Only components take a key; elements like Div and Text are always paired by position. A component inside an element moves only as far as that element does, so to move a subtree along with its state, make the root of that subtree a component and key it.

docs.title: Skipping a component whose arguments didn't change
docs.text:
A component that re-runs calls every component it returns again, even when it passes them the same arguments as last render. Declare a component memo to skip it in that case:

@component(memo=True)
def todo_row(title: str) -> Text: ...

When its parent re-runs and passes it arguments equal (==) to last render's, with the same key, a memo component keeps its previous output instead of re-running, along with every component below it. It still re-runs when its own state changes, and on the renders that re-run everything: the first one, and those after a resize or a suspend.

memo is opt-in, as it is in React, because it isn't free and isn't always right:

  • Comparing the arguments costs something on every render, and == on a large argument walks all of it. A cheap component can cost less to re-run than to compare.
  • A function the parent creates while rendering, such as a lambda passed as a handler, is a new object every render and never equals the previous one, so the component always re-runs.
  • The component's output has to depend only on its arguments and its hooks. One that also reads a module-level value, or an argument that is mutated in place, keeps showing what it showed when it last ran.
  • In a list, an unkeyed memo component compares its arguments with whatever item was at its index last render, so when the list is reordered, most of them change and re-run. Key the items to compare each one with itself.

Performance walks through finding the components a frame re-runs, and each way memo and use_memo can miss or go stale.

docs.title: Keeping components pure
docs.text:
A component has to be pure: given the same arguments and hook state, it returns the same element, however many times it's called. A component that isn't re-run, memo or not, keeps showing the output from its last run, so one that also reads something else, such as a module-level value or the time, goes stale. To show the time, read it with use_clock. To show something else that changes on its own, such as a value polled from a server, keep it in state and update it from use_effect.

Pass check_purity=True to app in tests to catch an impure component: after each render, every component is run again with the same arguments and hooks, and if that builds a different tree, the app raises ImpureComponent naming the first component whose output differs. Elements are compared with ==, and where that fails, piece by piece, with handlers compared by their code and the values they captured, since a re-run creates new ones that never == the old ones. The second run also raises InconsistentHookExecution for a component that calls a different number of hooks, and checks use_memo the same way: each cached value is computed again, and one that differs raises StaleMemo. It costs as much as re-running everything, so leave check_purity off outside tests. use_ref covers what it catches for refs.

A decorator that marks a function as a component, used bare (@component) or with options.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION memo

If True, a render that would re-run this component only because its parent re-ran reuses its previous output instead when its arguments equal last render's, as React's memo does. It still re-runs when its own state changes. Its output MUST depend only on its arguments and its hooks, or the output it keeps goes stale; check_purity on counterweight.app.app catches that in tests.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

docs.title: with_key
docs.text:
with_key(key: str | None) -> Component

Returns a copy of this component with the given key. Across renders, a keyed component continues the sibling that had the same key last render, wherever it sat, so reordering keyed siblings moves their state and effects with them. An unkeyed component instead continues the unkeyed sibling at the same index. Changing a component's key remounts it with fresh state, and adding or removing a key counts as changing it. Sibling components MUST NOT share a key other than None; reconciling them raises DuplicateKey.

docs.title: Autocomplete
docs.text:
An autocomplete field suggests completions as you type, in a list that opens under the field and lays over whatever is there. The list has to reach past the box the field is in, which here is a form that scrolls inside a fill(1) panel, and so clips its children.

The field edits its text with use_text_input, which makes it focusable and handles typing, moving the cursor, and pasting, and leaves drawing the text and the list to the field. It draws the text in a row that scrolls sideways, with the cursor's cell holding the hook's cursor_cell handle, so a value wider than the field keeps the cursor in view.

PACKAGES = (
    "counterweight",
    "hypothesis",
    "more-itertools",
    "mypy",
    "pydantic",
    "pydantic-settings",
    "pytest",
    "pytest-asyncio",
    "pytest-xdist",
    "ruff",
    "waxy",
    "wcwidth",
)
GROUPS = ("bench", "dev", "docs", "lint", "test")
PYTHONS = ("3.13", "3.14", "3.15", "3.15t")
INDEXES = ("pypi", "testpypi", "pytorch-cpu", "pytorch-cu128")
RECIPES = ("codegen", "devlog", "docs-build", "docs-serve", "mutate", "pre-commit", "profile", "test", "upgrade")

SHOWN_ROWS = 5

CURSOR = (text_color("slate", 900) | text_bg("sky", 300)).text_style

below = Style(layout=waxy.Style(inset_top=waxy.Percent(1.0)))
above = Style(layout=waxy.Style(inset_bottom=waxy.Percent(1.0)))


def matches(text: str, candidates: tuple[str, ...]) -> list[str]:
    pattern = f"*{'*'.join(glob.escape(c) for c in text.lower())}*"
    return [candidate for candidate in candidates if fnmatchcase(candidate.lower(), pattern)]


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Completion:
    text: str
    highlighted: int
    is_dismissed: bool

    def edited(self, text: str) -> Completion:
        return self if text == self.text else Completion(text=text, highlighted=0, is_dismissed=False)


@component
def autocomplete(
    candidates: tuple[str, ...],
    screen_height: int,
    auto_focus: bool = False,
    list_clip: Style = clip_to_screen,
) -> Div:
    rects = use_rects()
    completion, set_completion = use_state(Completion(text="", highlighted=0, is_dismissed=False))
    highlighted_match, _ = use_state(ElementHandle)

    def edit(edit_text: Callable[[str], str]) -> None:
        set_completion(lambda c: c.edited(edit_text(c.text)))

    field = use_text_input(completion.text, edit, auto_focus=auto_focus)

    text, highlighted = completion.text, completion.highlighted
    shown = matches(text, candidates) if text else []
    is_open = field.focus.is_focused and not completion.is_dismissed and bool(shown)

    def choose(match: str) -> None:
        set_completion(Completion(text=match, highlighted=0, is_dismissed=True))

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        highlighted_in_view = ScrollIntoView(highlighted_match, block="nearest")
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Down) if is_open:
                set_completion(lambda c: replace(c, highlighted=(c.highlighted + 1) % len(shown)))
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Up) if is_open:
                set_completion(lambda c: replace(c, highlighted=(c.highlighted - 1) % len(shown)))
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter | Key.Tab) if is_open:
                choose(shown[highlighted])
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Escape) if is_open:
                set_completion(lambda c: replace(c, is_dismissed=True))
            case _:
                if (edited := response_controls(field.on_input(event, receiver))) is None:
                    return None
                return (*edited, highlighted_in_view)
        return highlighted_in_view

    room_above = rects.border.top
    room_below = screen_height - rects.border.bottom
    suggestions = Div(
        style=z(1)
        | position_absolute
        | (above if room_above > room_below else below)
        | inset_x(0)
        | list_clip
        | col
        | border
        | border_lightrounded
        | border_color("sky", 400)
        | max_height(SHOWN_ROWS + 2)
        | overflow_y_scroll,
        on_input=scroll_on_wheel(1),
        children=tuple(
            Text(
                content=match,
                style=pad_x(1) | (text_bg("sky", 800) if index == highlighted else text_bg("slate", 900)),
                handle=highlighted_match if index == highlighted else None,
                on_input=on_click(partial(choose, match)),
            )
            for index, match in enumerate(shown)
        ),
    )

    return Div(
        style=width(24) | (text_bg("slate", 700) if field.focus.is_focused else text_bg("slate", 800)),
        on_input=first(on_input, focus_receiver_on_press),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | overflow_x_scroll | stick_to_end_x,
                on_input=field.on_press,
                children=(
                    Text(content=field.before_cursor, style=text_wrap_none),
                    Text(
                        content=field.at_cursor,
                        style=text_wrap_none | Style(text_style=CURSOR if field.focus.is_focused else CellStyle()),
                        handle=field.cursor_cell,
                    ),
                    Text(content=field.after_cursor, style=text_wrap_none),
                ),
            ),
            *([suggestions] if is_open else []),
        ),
    )


@component
def labelled(label: str, field: Component) -> Div:
    return Div(style=row | gap(1), children=(Text(content=f"{label:>7}"), field))


@component
def root(list_clip: Style = clip_to_screen) -> Div:
    screen = use_rects()
    height = screen.border.height

    return Div(
        style=full | col,
        on_input=first(tab_focus, clear_focus),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=fill(1) | col | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
                children=(
                    Text(content=" Add a dependency ", style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | clip_to_border),
                    Div(
                        style=fill(1) | col | gap(1) | overflow_y_scroll,
                        on_input=scroll_on_wheel(1),
                        children=(
                            labelled("Package", autocomplete(PACKAGES, height, auto_focus=True, list_clip=list_clip)),
                            labelled("Group", autocomplete(GROUPS, height, list_clip=list_clip)),
                            labelled("Python", autocomplete(PYTHONS, height, list_clip=list_clip)),
                            labelled("Index", autocomplete(INDEXES, height, list_clip=list_clip)),
                        ),
                    ),
                ),
            ),
            Text(
                content="Type to see suggestions. Down and Up move through them, "
                "Enter or Tab chooses one, and Escape closes them.",
                style=fill(1) | pad(1) | text_wrap_pretty | text_color("slate", 400),
            ),
            labelled("just", autocomplete(RECIPES, height, list_clip=list_clip)),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Matching
docs.text:
A candidate matches when the typed letters appear in it in order, with anything between them, so py matches mypy as well as pytest. matches builds a pattern with a * between and around the typed letters, each escaped with glob.escape, so a typed [ or ? matches itself rather than starting a pattern. It lowercases both sides and compares them with fnmatchcase, since fnmatch folds case only where os.path.normcase does, which is on Windows alone.

The list shows every match, in the order of the candidates.

docs.title: The list
docs.text:
The list is a Div the field renders only while it's focused and has matches, so it closes when focus moves away: Tab with the list closed bubbles to the root's tab_focus, and a press anywhere that doesn't claim it bubbles to the root's clear_focus.

It's absolutely positioned against the field, so it doesn't push the fields below it down. inset_top=Percent(1.0) puts its top edge at the bottom of the field, and inset_x(0) makes it as wide as the field. It's raised with z(1), so it's drawn over the fields and text that follow it. It's at most SHOWN_ROWS matches tall, and scrolls the rest.

docs.title: Choosing a match
docs.text:
Down and Up move the highlight through the list, wrapping at the ends. The field keeps its text in one state with which match is highlighted and whether the list is dismissed, and the setter it passes to use_text_input applies each edit to that state, resetting the highlight whenever the edit changes the text, so moving the cursor leaves it where it was:

Escape closes the list too, and it stays closed until the text changes. Each of these keys is handled only while the list is open. Every other event goes to use_text_input's handler, which passes on the keys it doesn't edit with, so with the list closed, Tab moves focus and Enter bubbles to whatever handles it outside the field.

A press on a match chooses it, through on_click. on_click claims the press, so it never reaches the root's clear_focus, and focus stays in the field.

docs.title: A long list
docs.text:
The list is a scroll container with a maximum height, so a long list of matches stays a few rows tall, and the wheel scrolls it. Down and Up have to keep the highlighted match in view as they move it past either end, but focus stays in the field, so moving focus can't do it, as it does for a list whose options take focus.

The field gives one ElementHandle to whichever match is highlighted, and every key it handles returns ScrollIntoView for that handle, with block="nearest", beside whatever state the key changed, and after the controls use_text_input's handler returns for a key it edits with, which scroll the cursor into view. response_controls turns that handler's response into a tuple of controls, or None if it didn't handle the key, so the field can return them together. ScrollIntoView applies to the layout of the render that change causes, before it paints, and names the element that has the handle in that render: the newly highlighted match. So the list scrolls in the same frame the highlight moves, and only as far as it takes:

A key that resets the highlight, by changing the text, scrolls the first match back into view the same way, and one that closes the list names no element, so it scrolls nothing. The list is unclipped, so ScrollIntoView scrolls only the list, not the form around it: no container above an element with clip_to_screen clips it, so none has to scroll to show it.

This is how a web combobox does it, keeping focus in its input, marking the highlighted option with aria-activedescendant, and calling scrollIntoView({block: "nearest"}) on it each time the highlight moves.

docs.title: Border Healing
docs.text:
When border elements for certain border types are adjacent to each other and appear as if they should "join up", but don't because they belong to different elements, they will be joined up.

container_style = fill(1) | align_self_stretch | border_collapse
box_style = fill(1) | align_self_stretch | center_children


def box(s: str) -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=box_style | border | border_double,
        children=(
            Text(
                style=text_justify_center | text_color("cyan", 500),
                content=s,
            ),
        ),
    )


@component
def root() -> Div:
    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> AnyControl | None:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Space):
                return ToggleBorderHealing()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=row | container_style,
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col | container_style,
                children=(box("A1"), box("A2")),
            ),
            Div(
                style=col | container_style,
                children=(
                    Div(style=row | container_style, children=(box("B1"), box("B2"))),
                    Div(style=row | container_style, children=(box("C1"), box("C2"), box("C3"), box("C4"))),
                    Div(style=row | container_style, children=(box("D1"), box("D2"), box("D3"))),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Healing and clipping
docs.text:
A box that hides its overflow cuts off the borders inside it at its padding box, and the part that's cut off doesn't join anything. Here each container holds a box pushed up onto its top border. Where overflow is visible, the box's top corners are drawn on the container's border and join it; where it's hidden, they're clipped away, and the container's border stays straight:

@component
def clipped() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2),
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=border | border_light | size(16, 5) | overflow,
                children=(
                    Div(
                        style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(2) | size(11, 3) | border | border_light,
                        children=(Text(content=f" {name}"),),
                    ),
                ),
            )
            for name, overflow in (("visible", overflow_visible), ("hidden", overflow_hidden))
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌──┬─────────┬─┐  ┌──────────────┐
│  │ visible │ │  │  │ hidden  │ │
│  └─────────┘ │  │  └─────────┘ │
│              │  │              │
└──────────────┘  └──────────────┘

A box whose border sits just inside its container's border doesn't join it either, since the container's ─ and │ beside the box's corners don't point toward them.

Boxes that clip still join each other where their borders meet. Every box in the grid above is a fill(1) item, which hides its overflow, and each box's corners are inside its own clip, so they join across the shared edges.

docs.title: Healing across z
docs.text:
Healing doesn't compare z or border styles, so a raised box whose border lies on another box's border joins it as any border would:

@component
def raised() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(style=border | border_light | size(24, 3), children=(Text(content="A panel"),)),
            Text(
                content="A raised box",
                style=z(1) | position_absolute | inset_top(2) | inset_left(4) | border | border_light,
            ),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌──────────────────────┐
│A panel               │
└───┬────────────┬─────┘
    │A raised box│      
    └────────────┘

ScreenshotText 

┌──────────────────────┐
│A panel               │
└───┌────────────┐─────┘

    └────────────┘

An unclipped box, such as a dropdown, joins borders beneath it the same way. To keep a raised box from joining, keep its border off other borders. #74 tracks whether healing should require matching z and styles.

docs.title: Border Titles
docs.text:
To add title text to a border, use an absolutely-positioned Text inside a Div that provides the border, inset by -1 onto the border's row.

Give the title clip_to_border. A box that hides its overflow, as every fill(1) and other constraint item does, clips its children to its padding box, which would erase a title on its border. clip_to_border clips the title to the border box instead (see Drawing on the parent's border).

@component
def root() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | fill(1) | center_children | border | border_lightrounded | pad(1),
                children=(
                    Text(
                        style=position_absolute | inset_left(1) | inset_top(-1) | clip_to_border,
                        content=" Top-Left Title ",
                    ),
                    Text(
                        style=inset_top_center | inset_top(-1) | clip_to_border,
                        content=" Top-Center Title ",
                    ),
                    Text(
                        style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_right(1) | clip_to_border,
                        content=" Top-Right Title ",
                    ),
                    Text(
                        style=position_absolute | inset_bottom(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border,

docs.title: Draggable Components
docs.text:
To make a component draggable, position it absolutely at an offset kept in state, and give it a handler that claims button 1 presses. On the MouseDown, remember where the pointer was and what the offset was. On each MouseMoved, set the offset to where it started plus how far the pointer has moved since then, clamped so the component stays inside its parent.

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Grab:
    pointer: Position
    offset: Position


@component
def draggable(content: str, start: Position, bounds: Region) -> Text:
    offset, set_offset = use_state(start)
    grab: Ref[Grab | None] = use_ref(None)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case MouseDown(absolute=pointer, button=1):
                grab.current = Grab(pointer=pointer, offset=offset)
                return ()
            case MouseMoved(absolute=pointer, button=1) if grab.current is not None:
                target = grab.current.offset + (pointer - grab.current.pointer)
                box = receiver.rects.border
                set_offset(
                    Position(
                        x=clamp(0, target.x, bounds.width - box.width),
                        y=clamp(0, target.y, bounds.height - box.height),
                    )
                )
                return ()
            case MouseUp(button=1):
                grab.current = None
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=content,
        on_input=on_input,
        style=position_absolute | inset_left(offset.x) | inset_top(offset.y) | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
    )


@component
def root() -> Div:
    rects = use_rects()

    return Div(
        style=full | border | border_heavy,
        children=(
            draggable("Drag me!", Position(2, 1), rects.padding),
            draggable("No, me!", Position(20, 4), rects.padding),
        ),
    )

Claiming the MouseDown captures the press, so every move reaches the component until the button is released, even when the pointer moves faster than the component follows and leaves it behind.

docs.title: Keeping the grab in a ref
docs.text: The grab goes in a ref, not in state, because a handler sees the values of the render that built it. Setting state schedules a render; it doesn't change what offset or any other state holds in the handler. The terminal often reports a press and the first moves of a drag together, and Counterweight handles every event that has arrived before it renders again. If the grab were state, the moves after the press would read the grab from before the press, and the component would jump. A ref is one box shared by every call to the handler, so a move sees what the press just wrote.

docs.title: Setting the offset from the grab alone
docs.text: Each move computes the offset from the grab and the pointer, not from offset, so it doesn't matter how many moves arrive before the next render: every one of them sets where the component belongs for that pointer position, and the last one wins. Adding each move's distance to offset instead would need the previous move's pointer position, which is one more thing to keep in a ref.

docs.title: Keeping it inside its parent
docs.text:
An absolutely positioned element's insets place it relative to its parent's padding box, so an offset keeps the component inside its parent while it runs from 0 to the padding box's size less the component's own border box. The parent passes its padding box from use_rects as bounds, and the handler takes the component's size from its receiver, then clamps each axis.

The clamp happens when the offset is set, so the state always holds where the component is drawn, and the next press grabs it there. Once the pointer comes back inside, the component follows it again from the cell the press grabbed.

Both drags, as the mouse moves:

use_rects reports the previous frame's rectangles, and empty ones on the first render, which doesn't matter here, because handlers only run once the parent has been laid out. A parent that shrinks, such as when the terminal is resized, can leave a component outside it until it's dragged again. To keep it inside then too, clamp the offset when rendering as well, from the same bounds and the size the component gets from its own use_rects.

docs.title: Prefix Keys
docs.text:
A prefix key changes what the next key does, as tmux's Ctrl+B does: Ctrl+B, then c, opens a pane, while c on its own is typed into the focused one. Vim's modes and Emacs's chords are the same thing with more states. This one has panes that take typing, and Ctrl+B followed by c to open a pane, n to focus the next, or x to close one. Any other key after Ctrl+B is dropped.

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Pane:
    number: int
    handle: FocusHandle


def first_pane() -> tuple[Pane, ...]:
    return (Pane(number=1, handle=FocusHandle()),)


@component
def pane(number: int, handle: FocusHandle, prefix: InputHandler) -> Text:
    focus = use_focus(handle=handle, auto_focus=True)
    typed, set_typed = use_state("")

    def type_key(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=key) if len(key) == 1:
                set_typed(lambda typed: typed + key)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=f"{number}: {typed}",
        style=fill(1)
        | border
        | border_lightrounded
        | (border_color("amber", 400) if focus.is_focused else border_color("slate", 600)),
        on_input=first(prefix, type_key),
    )


@component
def root() -> Div:
    panes, set_panes = use_state(first_pane)
    is_armed = use_ref(False)
    shows_armed, set_shows_armed = use_state(False)

    def arm(value: bool) -> None:
        is_armed.current = value
        set_shows_armed(value)

    def prefixed(key: str, focused: FocusHandle | None) -> InputResponse:
        match key:
            case "c":
                handle = FocusHandle()
                set_panes(
                    lambda panes: (
                        *panes,
                        Pane(number=max((pane.number for pane in panes), default=0) + 1, handle=handle),
                    )
                )
                return FocusOn(handle)
            case "n":
                return FocusNext()
            case "x":
                set_panes(lambda panes: tuple(pane for pane in panes if pane.handle != focused))
                return FocusNext()
            case _:
                return ()

    def prefix(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.ControlB) if not is_armed.current:
                arm(True)
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=key) if is_armed.current:
                arm(False)
                return prefixed(key, receiver.focus_handle)
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | full,
        on_input=prefix,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | grow(1),
                children=tuple(pane(p.number, p.handle, prefix).with_key(str(p.number)) for p in panes),
            ),
            Text(
                content=("PREFIX " if shows_armed else "") + "ctrl+b, then c: new pane, n: next pane, x: close pane",
                style=text_color("slate", 900) | text_bg("amber", 400 if shows_armed else 200),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Keeping the mode in a ref
docs.text:
Whether the prefix is waiting for its key, is_armed, is a ref, not state, because a handler sees the state of the render that built it. A terminal often delivers Ctrl+B and the key after it in one read, such as when they're typed quickly or pasted, and Counterweight handles every event that has arrived before it renders again. If the mode were state, the handler for c would still see the prefix unarmed, and type c into the pane. A ref is one box shared by every call to the handler, so the c sees what the Ctrl+B just wrote.

Drawing the status bar does need state, since changing a ref doesn't render anything, and a component mustn't read a ref while rendering. So arm writes both: the ref for the handlers to read, and shows_armed for the status bar to draw.

docs.title: Putting the prefix first
docs.text:
Keys go to the focused pane first and bubble up from there, so a prefix handler on an ancestor alone would never see the c: the pane would type it first. Each pane puts the prefix ahead of its own typing with first(prefix, type_key), so the prefix decides before the pane does. The root's element has the prefix too, for when no pane is focused, such as after the last one closes.

The prefix claims Ctrl+B and the key after it, returning () or a control, and passes on everything else, so a key it doesn't bind reaches the pane, and anything the pane doesn't take reaches the root.

docs.title: Opening a pane focused
docs.text:
Opening a pane creates its focus handle in the handler, keeps it in state with the pane, and returns FocusOn with it. The pane doesn't exist until the next render, so FocusOn waits for that render, and the new pane is focused in the first frame that shows it. Keys that arrive in the same read as the c still go to the pane that was focused when they arrived.

The new pane's number comes from the latest panes, inside the update function passed to set_panes, rather than from the panes the render saw, so two panes opened in one read get different numbers, and different keys.

docs.title: Spinners
docs.text:
To show that something is still working, such as each step of a coding agent, animate a spinner with use_clock:

FRAMES = "⠋⠙⠹⠸⠼⠴⠦⠧⠇⠏"
FRAME_TIME = timedelta(milliseconds=80)


@component
def spinner(label: str) -> Text:
    elapsed = use_clock(FRAME_TIME).since_mount
    frame = FRAMES[elapsed // FRAME_TIME % len(FRAMES)]
    return Text(content=f"{frame} {label} ({elapsed // timedelta(seconds=1)}s)", style=text_color("amber", 400))


@component
def progress(done: tuple[str, ...], current: str) -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            *(Text(content=f"✓ {step}", style=text_color("emerald", 500)) for step in done),
            # Keyed by the step, so each new step remounts the spinner and restarts its time.
            spinner(current).with_key(current),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

✓ Read pyproject.toml                   
✓ Ran the tests                         
⠹ Fixing the failing test (4s)

Running, it spins at the pace the clock sets:

spinner reads the clock once per frame of the animation, and computes which frame to show from how long it has been mounted, so the animation keeps pace with real time however long the step takes (see Why compute from elapsed time?). The same reading gives the elapsed seconds beside the label.

Each frame re-runs spinner alone, since it's the only component that reads the clock. progress re-runs only when its steps change, and gives the spinner a new key for each step, which remounts it and starts its time again from zero.

docs.title: Canvas
docs.text:
A Canvas is a leaf element whose content box its painter draws, cell by cell, for pictures, plots, game boards and anything else that isn't text. A Text of chunks can draw the same cells, but layout measures and wraps a Text every frame, which a picture never needs. A canvas skips all of that: its painter says how big it is, and draws whatever box it ends up with.

This page covers drawing pixels, how a canvas is sized, loading an image, mouse input, and writing a painter of your own.

docs.title: Drawing Pixels
docs.text:
counterweight.painters.pixels splits a picture from how it's drawn:

  • Pixels is the picture: a width, a height, and RGBA bytes, with nothing about cells or terminals. Pixels.blank, Pixels.from_points and with_points build one from colors, and the constructor takes raw RGBA bytes from any decoder.
  • HalfBlocks is a painter that draws a Pixels in cells, two pixels to a cell, one above the other, as ▀ with the top pixel as its foreground and the bottom one as its background. A cell is about twice as tall as it is wide, so the pixels come out about square.
SKY_TOP = Color.from_hex("#1e1b4b")
SKY_BOTTOM = Color.from_hex("#f97316")
SUN = Color.from_hex("#fde047")
SEA = Color.from_hex("#0e7490")


def blend(a: Color, b: Color, t: float) -> Color:
    return Color(*(round(x + (y - x) * t) for x, y in zip(a, b, strict=True)))


def sunset(width: int, height: int) -> Pixels:
    """A sky that brightens toward the horizon, a sun setting on it, and the sea below."""
    horizon = height * 3 // 4
    radius = width / 4

    def color(x: int, y: int) -> Color:
        if y >= horizon:
            return SEA
        if (x + 0.5 - width / 2) ** 2 + (y + 0.5 - horizon) ** 2 < radius**2:
            return SUN
        return blend(SKY_TOP, SKY_BOTTOM, y / horizon)

    rgba = b"".join(bytes((*color(x, y), 255)) for y in range(height) for x in range(width))
    return Pixels(width, height, rgba)


SUNSET = sunset(16, 16)


@component
def picture() -> Canvas:
    return Canvas(painter=HalfBlocks(SUNSET), style=border)

A canvas compares its painter with == to the one it had last frame, and doesn't draw again while it's equal and its box is the same size. Two HalfBlocks are equal when their pixels' bytes, fit and position are, so a component that holds a Pixels in state can build its HalfBlocks in every render, and the canvas is drawn again only when the pixels or its box change. Changing a picture means making a new Pixels, as with_points does.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
A canvas is sized as HTML's replaced elements (<img>, <canvas>) are. Its painter's natural size is its intrinsic size, which it takes on each axis that its style and its parent's layout leave undetermined, as an <img> takes its picture's. A HalfBlocks is as wide as its picture and half as tall, rounded up.

def labeled(label: str, canvas: Canvas) -> Div:
    return Div(style=col | align_children_start, children=(Text(content=label), canvas))


@component
def sizing() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2) | align_children_start,
        children=(
            labeled("natural size", Canvas(painter=HalfBlocks(SUNSET), style=border)),
            labeled("width(10)", Canvas(painter=HalfBlocks(SUNSET), style=border | width(10))),
            labeled("height(4)", Canvas(painter=HalfBlocks(SUNSET), style=border | height(4))),
            Div(
                style=col | width(12),
                children=(
                    Text(content="min_width(0)"),
                    Div(
                        style=row,
                        children=(Canvas(painter=HalfBlocks(SUNSET), style=border | min_width(0)),),
                    ),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

  • A size from the style, or from a parent that stretches or flexes it, wins on its axis, and the painter draws at the size the canvas's content box ends up.
  • A painter that keeps its aspect ratio, as HalfBlocks does, gives a canvas sized on only one axis its other axis by that ratio, so width(10) or height(4) alone keeps the picture's proportions. The ratio is between content boxes, so a border or padding doesn't distort it.
  • In a flex row, a canvas shrinks no narrower than its intrinsic width, as an <img> doesn't, so a canvas wider than its row overflows it and draws over what's beside it. min_width(0) lets it shrink, as min-width: 0 does for an <img>.
  • A max_width on a canvas in a column that doesn't stretch its children, such as one with align_children_start, narrows it without shortening it. Set a width instead, or let the column stretch it.

docs.title: Fitting a Picture to Its Box
docs.text:
When the box isn't the picture's natural size, HalfBlocks's fit scales the picture as CSS's object-fit does, and position places it in the space left over as object-position does. fit is on the painter rather than the canvas's style, because only a painter with pixels has a picture to scale.

FITS: tuple[Fit, ...] = ("fill", "contain", "cover", "none", "scale-down")


@component
def fits() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(1),
        children=tuple(
            labeled(f'fit="{fit}"', Canvas(painter=HalfBlocks(SUNSET, fit=fit), style=border | size(22, 6)))
            for fit in FITS
        ),
    )

  • "fill", the default, stretches the picture to the box on each axis.
  • "contain" scales it to fit inside the box, keeping its proportions.
  • "cover" scales it to cover the box, keeping its proportions, and cuts off what overflows.
  • "none" leaves it at its natural size, cut off where it overflows.
  • "scale-down" is whichever of "none" and "contain" is smaller.

position is the fractions of the space left over on each axis to put to the left of and above the picture, (0.5, 0.5) by default, which centers it. It places the picture in whole pixels, so a picture can start halfway down a cell.

Each cell shows the pixels nearest the middle of its two halves, which is fast but rough when shrinking a photo a long way. For a smoother picture, scale it to the size you'll show it at first, such as with Pillow's Image.thumbnail.

docs.title: Transparency
docs.text: A pixel less than half opaque is transparent, and so is any part of the box the picture doesn't cover. A transparent half of a cell shows the canvas's background: its text_bg if its style sets one, and its content_color otherwise, so a canvas with only a content_color shows it everywhere the picture doesn't.

docs.title: Mouse Input
docs.text:
A canvas takes an on_input handler as any element does, and mouse events arrive in cells, as positions on the screen. HalfBlocks.pixels_at turns a cell of a box into the pixels of the picture that cell shows, scaled and placed by fit and position, so a paint program sets the pixels under the mouse:

BLANK = Pixels.blank(24, 16, Color.from_name("black"))
INK = Color.from_hex("#fbbf24")


@component
def paint() -> Div:
    pixels, set_pixels = use_state(BLANK)
    painter = HalfBlocks(pixels)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case MouseDown(absolute=a, button=1) | MouseMoved(absolute=a, button=1):
                content = receiver.rects.content
                under = painter.pixels_at(receiver.relative(a), content.width, content.height)
                set_pixels(lambda p: p.with_points(dict.fromkeys(under, INK)))
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(style=col | align_children_start, children=(Canvas(painter=painter, style=border, on_input=on_input),))

docs.title: Writing a Painter
docs.text:
A painter is any object with the three members of Painter: a natural_size in cells, whether it keeps_aspect_ratio, and draw(width, height), which returns rows of StyledGraphemes for a box of that size, top to bottom, each drawn rightward from the box's left edge. Cells past the box's edges are cut off, and any part of the box the rows don't reach shows the canvas's background. Whatever a cell's style leaves unset comes from the canvas, as it does for a Text's chunks, so a painter never needs the canvas's style.

A painter that takes whatever box it gets has a natural size of zero, and is sized with its style. This ruler draws a tick in every column of its box and a label in every tenth, however wide the box is:

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Ruler:
    """Draws a ruler as wide as whatever box it's given: a tick on every column, and a label on every tenth."""

    natural_size: tuple[int, int] = (0, 2)
    keeps_aspect_ratio: bool = False

    def draw(self, width: int, height: int) -> Rows:
        ticks = tuple(StyledGrapheme(grapheme="┴" if x % 10 == 0 else "╵" if x % 5 == 0 else "·") for x in range(width))
        labels = "".join(f"{x:<10}" for x in range(0, width, 10))[:width]
        label_style = CellStyle(foreground=Color.from_hex("#fbbf24"))
        return ticks, tuple(StyledGrapheme(grapheme=c, style=label_style) for c in labels)


@component
def ruler() -> Div:
    return Div(style=col, children=(Canvas(painter=Ruler(), style=border),))

Since a canvas draws again only when its painter isn't equal to the last one, draw must depend only on the painter and the size it's given. A frozen dataclass is the easiest way to get that: two built from the same values are equal, so a component can build its painter in every render.

docs.text:
Canvas(
    *,
    painter: Painter,
    style: Style = _DEFAULT_STYLE,
    on_input: InputHandler | None = None,
    handle: ElementHandle | None = None,
)

A leaf element whose content box its painter draws, cell by cell, instead of laying out text.

It's sized as HTML's replaced elements (<img>, <canvas>) are: its painter's natural_size is its intrinsic size, which it takes on each axis that its style and its parent's layout leave undetermined, and draw is called with the size its content box ends up. A painter that keeps its aspect ratio gives a canvas sized on only one axis the other by that ratio. In a flex row, a canvas shrinks no narrower than its intrinsic width, as an <img> doesn't, unless its style sets min_width(0).

A background that its painter leaves unset is the canvas's text_style background if its style sets one, and its content_color otherwise, so a cell the painter leaves transparent matches the rest of the box.

docs.text:
HalfBlocks(
    pixels: Pixels,
    fit: Fit = "fill",
    position: tuple[float, float] = (0.5, 0.5),
)

A Canvas painter that draws pixels two to a cell, one above the other, as a half block (▀) whose foreground is the top pixel and whose background is the bottom one. A cell is about twice as tall as it is wide, so the pixels are about square, and its natural size is the picture's width by half its height, rounded up.

In a box of another size, fit scales the picture as CSS's object-fit does, and position places it as object-position does, as the fractions of the space left over on each axis to put to its left and above it, so (0.5, 0.5), the default, centers it, and (0, 0) puts it in the top left corner. A picture larger than its box is cut off.

Each cell shows the pixels nearest the middle of its two halves. A pixel less than half opaque is transparent, and leaves its half of the cell to show the canvas's background, as does a half the picture doesn't cover.

docs.title: Wide Characters
docs.text:
A Text measures, wraps and paints its content by grapheme cluster, the unit a reader sees as one character, so an accented letter written with a combining mark or an emoji joined from several (👩‍💻) stays whole.

Counterweight measures each cluster with wcwidth's wcswidth. Most clusters take one terminal cell. CJK characters, most emoji and flags take two, and zero-width characters (zero-width spaces and joiners, bidirectional marks) take none and aren't drawn. No cluster takes more than two, which matches terminals that draw a cluster as one unit, such as Ghostty, foot and Windows Terminal. Terminals that add up the widths of a cluster's code points instead draw some clusters wider, such as a joined emoji as its separate parts, and text after one is drawn to the right of where layout put it.

A two-cell cluster is never split across lines or cut in half. When one would cross the right edge of its Text, it moves to the next line if the text wraps, or overflows the box with the rest of its line if it doesn't. Where a clip cuts across one, it is left out, with a space in its place.

docs.title: Control Characters
docs.text: Newlines (\n and \r\n) start a new line. Every other control character, such as tab or escape, is drawn as a symbol (␉, ␛) rather than written to the terminal, where it would run as a command instead of drawing anything.

docs.title: Headless Components
docs.text:
A headless component gives a component the behavior of a common control, such as which keys edit text and where the cursor goes, or which keys scroll a box, and leaves drawing it to the component, as Headless UI and React Aria do for the web. Each one is a hook in counterweight.headless, and counterweight.widgets draws each one way, for when you don't need your own look:

Hook Widget Behavior use_text_input text_input Edits one line of text use_text_area text_area Edits text that wraps onto rows use_scroll_area scroll_area Scrolls a box with the keys and the wheel use_terminal terminal Runs an interactive program in a box

docs.title: Styling the widgets
docs.text:
The text field widgets take a style, merged over their box's own style, for a size or a border, and styles, a TextFieldStyles that says how they draw their box while unfocused, focused, and unfocusable, their cursor, and their placeholder. Pass the fields you want to change, and share one TextFieldStyles between all the fields of a form:

AMBER = TextFieldStyles(
    box=border | border_heavy | border_color("slate", 500) | pad_x(1),
    focused_box=border_color("amber", 400),
    cursor=(text_color("slate", 900) | text_bg("amber", 300)).text_style,
    placeholder=CellStyle(italic=True) | text_color("slate", 400).text_style,
)


@component
def amber_sign_up() -> Div:
    name, set_name = use_state("")
    email, set_email = use_state("")
    return Div(
        style=col | width(30),
        on_input=tab_focus,
        children=(
            text_input(name, set_name, placeholder="Name", styles=AMBER, auto_focus=True),
            text_input(email, set_email, placeholder="Email", styles=AMBER),
        ),
    )

docs.title: use_scroll_area
docs.text:
use_scroll_area scrolls a box with the keys, the wheel and controls, and leaves drawing it to the component that calls it. It makes the component focusable, so Tab reaches it and the keys scroll it, gives the box the style that makes it a scroll container, and reports how far it's scrolled, for a "jump to latest" button or a position readout. For a ready-made box, use scroll_area, which is built on this hook.

This page covers the hook and that component. Scrolling covers the pieces they're built from, for a box that needs something they don't do.

docs.title: Using the hook
docs.text:
In a browser, a scroll container is keyboard-focusable: Firefox puts every one in the Tab order, Chrome only one that has nothing inside it that can take focus, and while it's focused, the arrows, PageUp, PageDown, Space, Home and End scroll it. Radix UI's ScrollArea gives a React component the same behavior and leaves drawing the box to it. use_scroll_area does the same for a component. It puts the area in the Tab order whatever is inside it, as Firefox does, since a hook can't see which of its descendants are focusable; pass in_focus_order=False for an area whose children should take Tab instead. It returns a handler, on_input, for the element the component returns, which is the one that's focused, and a style and an ElementHandle, viewport, for the element that scrolls. Those can be one element, or the one that scrolls can be inside the other, as Radix's viewport is inside its root, with things that stay put beside it.

This log puts its border and title on the element it returns, and its lines in the element that scrolls inside it, with stick_to_end=True, so it follows its newest line, and a button that jumps back to it while it's scrolled back:

@component
def deploy_log() -> Div:
    area = use_scroll_area(stick_to_end=True, auto_focus=True)

    return Div(
        style=col
        | border
        | border_lightrounded
        | size(30, 6)
        | (border_color("sky", 400) if area.focus.is_focused else border_color("slate", 600)),
        # The element that's focused, which keys, and wheel events and presses anywhere inside, reach.
        on_input=area.on_input,
        children=(
            Text(content=" Deploy log ", style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border),
            # The element that scrolls, with the area's style merged after fill(1), which hides overflow.
            Div(
                style=fill(1) | col | area.style,
                handle=area.viewport,
                children=tuple(Text(content=f"{i:>2} {event}") for i, event in enumerate(EVENTS, start=1)),
            ),
            # Beside the part that scrolls, so it stays over the last line.
            *(
                ()
                if area.is_at_end
                else (
                    Text(
                        content=" ↓ Jump to latest ",
                        style=position_absolute
                        | inset_bottom(0)
                        | inset_x(0)
                        | margin_x_auto
                        | fit_content_width
                        | text_bg("sky", 800),
                        on_input=on_click(lambda: area.to_end),
                    ),
                )
            ),
        ),
    )
