is_at_end says whether the area is scrolled to its end, which it is while its content fits, and to_end is the ScrollTo that scrolls it there, past any end, so it reaches the end of content that grew since the last render. is_at_start and to_start do the same for the start, and scroll is the Scroll they're read from, as use_scroll reports it, for a readout such as "rows 5-8 of 11". Like use_scroll, they report the previous frame's scroll, so the button appears a frame after the scroll that should show it.

The handler is on the element the component returns, so a wheel event or a press anywhere inside it reaches it, the button included, and the wheel scrolls the log from over the button too. A press that nothing inside the area claims focuses it, as a click focuses the nearest focusable element around it in a browser, so clicking the log focuses it, and clicking the button jumps without focusing it.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
While the area, or something inside it, is focused, a key that nothing inside it handles bubbles to its handler:

Key Scrolls Up, Down A row up or down Left, Right A column left or right PageUp, PageDown A page up or down: 87.5% of the height of the view, as in Chrome Space A page down Home, End To the start or the end

Home and End scroll vertically, as in a browser, except in an area that only scrolls sideways, which has nothing to scroll vertically, where they scroll to its first and last columns. Shift+Space pages up in a browser, but terminals send it as Space, so there's no key for that. page sets the size of a page, as for scroll_on_keys, and wheel_lines how far each notch of the wheel scrolls, three lines by default.

A key or a wheel event that would move the area past the end of its range bubbles on, so once a nested area reaches its end, the one around it scrolls, as the web chains scrolling from one container to the next. The handler judges that by the scroll as of the previous render, as is_at_end does, so an event that arrives in the same frame as a scroll before it is judged by the scroll before that.

docs.title: Which way it scrolls
docs.text: axis is "y" for an area that scrolls vertically, the default, "x" for one that scrolls sideways, or "both". The style clips the axis the area doesn't scroll, so a line too long for an area that scrolls vertically doesn't spill over its border or its siblings. For "y" it hides the overflow, so the area narrows beside its siblings as a box with hidden overflow does; for "x" it clips the overflow, so the area stays as tall as its content, as a wide code block in a document should. A browser does much the same: setting only overflow-y: scroll makes overflow-x auto.

docs.title: Merging the style
docs.text: The style sets the element's overflow, and its stickiness with stick_to_end, and nothing else. Merge it after the element's own style, or at least after anything that sets overflow: the constraint utilities fill, length, percentage and ratio hide their box's overflow, so area.style | fill(1) doesn't scroll, and fill(1) | area.style does.

docs.title: Sizing the area
docs.text:
The area's size is the caller's, as a scroll container's is on the web. A scroll container's automatic minimum size is 0 on the axes it scrolls (see Scroll containers), so an area with no size of its own shrinks to fit beside its siblings, and scrolls what doesn't fit. In a column that's already too short for everything in it, such as a document that scrolls, that can leave the area no rows at all. Give it the size you mean:

  • fill(1) takes the space its siblings leave, as for a pane beside a sidebar or above a prompt.
  • shrink(0) | max_height(8) makes it as tall as its content, up to eight rows, past which it scrolls, even in a column too short for everything in it, as the text area widget does.
  • height(10) or length(10) fixes it.

The hook doesn't add shrink(0) itself, since it can't tell which of those you mean, and in a row, shrink(0) keeps an area with no width of its own as wide as its longest line.

docs.title: Scrolling it from outside
docs.text:
The area scrolls the element with the viewport handle, so a parent that creates the handle with use_state(ElementHandle) and passes it to the hook can scroll the area with ScrollTo and ScrollBy, and read its scroll with use_scroll(handle). The chat example passes its transcript's handle to the transcript's scroll area, so the root jumps the transcript to its end when a message is sent, and Shift+PageUp and Shift+PageDown page it while the prompt has focus, which takes PageUp and PageDown itself to move its cursor. Tab moves focus to the transcript, where PageUp and PageDown scroll it.

Pass a FocusHandle as handle to focus the area from outside with FocusOn, and in_focus_order=False to leave it out of Tab's order, as tabindex="-1" does, for an area that a press or a FocusOn focuses but Tab passes by, such as a page's body.

docs.title: A styled scroll area
docs.text:
scroll_area puts its children in a bordered box that scrolls, and takes the hook's parameters, a style merged over its own, for a size, and styles for its colors. A browser draws a focus ring around a focused scroll container as an outline, which takes no space; a terminal draws nothing outside a box, so its border changes color with focus instead, as the text field widgets' borders do, and its content stays where it is as focus comes and goes:

SOURCE = (
    "def deploy(image: str, steps: tuple[int, ...] = (10, 50, 100)) -> None:",
    "    for percent in steps:",
    "        shift_traffic(image, percent)",
)


@component
def panes() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(1),
        on_input=tab_focus,
        children=(
            scroll_area(
                tuple(Text(content=event) for event in EVENTS),
                style=size(24, 6),
                auto_focus=True,
            ),
            scroll_area(
                tuple(Text(content=line) for line in SOURCE),
                axis="x",
                style=size(24, 6),
            ),
        ),
    )

For a box without a border, pass ScrollAreaStyles(box=default) with a focused_box that takes no space, such as a background color.

docs.title: counterweight.headless.use_scroll_area
docs.text:
use_scroll_area(
    axis: ScrollAxis = "y",
    stick_to_end: bool = False,
    viewport: ElementHandle | None = None,
    wheel_lines: int = 3,
    page: float = PAGE_FRACTION,
    auto_focus: bool = False,
    handle: FocusHandle | None = None,
    is_focusable: bool = True,
    in_focus_order: bool = True,
) -> ScrollArea

Scrolls a box with the keys, the wheel and controls, leaving how it's drawn to the calling component, as Radix UI's ScrollArea does for the web. The hook makes the calling component focusable, as browsers make a scroll container focusable, so Tab reaches it and the keys scroll it.

The calling component returns the element that's focused, which takes on_input, and draws the content in the element that scrolls, which takes viewport and style. They can be one element, or the scrolling one can be inside the other, with things that stay put while it scrolls, such as a title or a "jump to latest" button, beside it.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION axis

Which way the area scrolls: "y" vertically, "x" sideways, or "both".

TYPE: ScrollAxis DEFAULT: 'y'

stick_to_end

Whether the viewport stays scrolled to its end on the area's axes as its content grows, as for a log or a chat (see Following the end).

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

viewport

The element handle for the element that scrolls, which a parent creates with use_state(ElementHandle) to scroll the area or read its scroll from outside it. If None, the hook creates one on the first render and keeps it.

TYPE: ElementHandle | None DEFAULT: None

wheel_lines

How many lines each notch of the wheel scrolls.

TYPE: int DEFAULT: 3

page

How much of the height of the view PageUp, PageDown and Space scroll, as for scroll_on_keys.

TYPE: float DEFAULT: PAGE_FRACTION

auto_focus

Passed to use_focus.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

handle

The focus handle passed to use_focus.

TYPE: FocusHandle | None DEFAULT: None

is_focusable

Passed to use_focus.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: True

in_focus_order

Passed to use_focus, where False leaves the area out of Tab's order, as tabindex="-1" does for a scroll container.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: True

RETURNS DESCRIPTION ScrollArea

The style and the element handle for the element that scrolls, how far it's scrolled,

ScrollArea

and the handler that scrolls it, for the element the calling component returns.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

If page isn't positive.

docs.title: style instance-attribute
docs.text:
style: Style

The style that makes the element viewport names a scroll container on the area's axes, and sticks it to its end on them if stick_to_end was passed, for the calling component to merge over that element's own style: style=fill(1) | col | area.style. On the axis it doesn't scroll, it clips the content, so a line too long for an area that scrolls vertically doesn't spill over its border: with hidden overflow there, so the area narrows beside its siblings, or for an area that scrolls sideways, with clipped overflow, so it stays as tall as its content. It MUST be merged after any style that sets overflow, such as the constraint utilities fill, length, percentage and ratio, which hide it, or the element doesn't scroll. It sets nothing else, so the element's size and layout are the caller's.

docs.title: viewport instance-attribute
docs.text:
viewport: ElementHandle

The element handle for the calling component to give the element that scrolls: the one passed to the hook, or one the hook creates. The area's handler and its controls scroll that element, and ScrollTo, ScrollBy and use_scroll reach it through the handle from anywhere.

docs.title: scroll instance-attribute
docs.text:
scroll: Scroll

How far the viewport is scrolled, as use_scroll reports it.

docs.title: is_at_start instance-attribute
docs.text:
is_at_start: bool

Whether the viewport is scrolled to the start of its content on each of the area's axes, as of scroll.

docs.title: is_at_end instance-attribute
docs.text:
is_at_end: bool

Whether the viewport is scrolled to the end of its content on each of the area's axes, as of scroll, which is also true while the content fits, so a "jump to latest" button can show while it's false.

docs.title: to_start instance-attribute
docs.text:
to_start: ScrollTo

The control that scrolls the viewport to the start of its content on the area's axes.

docs.title: to_end instance-attribute
docs.text:
to_end: ScrollTo

The control that scrolls the viewport to the end of its content on the area's axes, wherever the end is when it applies, so it reaches the end of content that grew since the last render.

docs.title: focus instance-attribute
docs.text:
focus: Focus

Whether the calling component is focused, and its focus handle, as use_focus returns them.

docs.title: on_input instance-attribute
docs.text:
on_input: InputHandler

The handler that scrolls the viewport, for the calling component to put on the element it returns, which is the one that's focused, and which a wheel event or a press anywhere inside it bubbles to. For the keys that scroll a page in a browser, it returns a ScrollBy or ScrollTo for the viewport: Up and Down by a row, Left and Right by a column, PageUp, PageDown and Space by a page (see page_down), and Home and End to the start and the end: vertically, or for an area that only scrolls sideways, sideways. For the wheel, it scrolls by wheel_lines toward the wheel's direction, as scroll_on_wheel does, Shift with the vertical wheel included. It returns None for a key or a wheel event that would move the viewport past the end of its range, as of scroll, so the event bubbles to the next scroll container out. For a MouseDown, it returns FocusOn for the component while it's focusable, so a press that nothing inside the area claims focuses it, as a click focuses the nearest focusable element around it in a browser. It returns None for anything else.

docs.title: use_text_area
docs.text:
use_text_area edits text that wraps onto rows: it handles typing, deleting, moving the cursor along a row and between rows, and pasting, and leaves drawing to the component that calls it. It wraps the value itself, at the width the component gives it, so the cursor moves between the rows the value is drawn on. For a ready-made box, use text_area, which is built on this hook.

This page covers the hook and that component. Selection isn't supported yet.

docs.title: Using the hook
docs.text:
As with use_text_input, the calling component owns the value and passes it with its setter, and the hook owns the cursor and makes the component focusable. It also takes the width to wrap at, which here is the content width that use_rects reports for the box. The box gets its width from its parent, not from its text, since the text is wrapped to fit it. The hook returns the rows, joined by line breaks, split around the cursor, so the component draws them with text_wrap_none, without wrapping them again:

CURSOR = (text_color("slate", 900) | text_bg("amber", 300)).text_style


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Conversation:
    messages: tuple[str, ...]
    draft: str


@component
def composer(draft: str, edit_draft: Callable[[Callable[[str], str]], None], send: Callable[[], None]) -> Text:
    rects = use_rects()
    field = use_text_area(draft, edit_draft, width=rects.content.width, auto_focus=True)

    def on_enter(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter):
                send()
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=(
            Chunk(content=field.before_cursor),
            Chunk(content=field.at_cursor, style=CURSOR),
            Chunk(content=field.after_cursor),
        ),
        style=border | border_lightrounded | border_color("amber", 400) | pad_x(1) | text_wrap_none,
        on_input=first(field.on_input, field.on_press, on_enter),
    )


@component
def chat() -> Div:
    conversation, set_conversation = use_state(Conversation(messages=(), draft=""))

    def edit_draft(edit: Callable[[str], str]) -> None:
        set_conversation(lambda c: Conversation(messages=c.messages, draft=edit(c.draft)))

    def send() -> None:
        set_conversation(lambda c: Conversation(messages=(*c.messages, c.draft), draft=""))

    return Div(
        style=col | size(34, 9) | gap(1),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=fill(1) | col | justify_children_end | gap(1) | overflow_y_scroll | stick_to_end_y,
                on_input=scroll_on_wheel(1),
                children=tuple(
                    Text(content=message, style=text_wrap_pretty | text_color("slate", 400))
                    for message in conversation.messages
                ),
            ),
            composer(conversation.draft, edit_draft, send),
        ),
    )

Enter isn't an edit, so it bubbles, and here the composer takes it to send the draft. Alt+Enter and Ctrl+J insert a line break:

ScreenshotText 

╭────────────────────────────────╮
│ Rows wrap to fit the box as    │
│ you type                       │
│ and Ctrl+J starts a line       │
╰────────────────────────────────╯

Enter sends it, keeping its line break:

ScreenshotText 

Rows wrap to fit the box as you   
type                              
and Ctrl+J starts a line

│                                │
╰────────────────────────────────╯

The conversation holds the messages and the draft together, so send reads the latest draft from the conversation it updates, rather than the draft this render saw, which misses keys typed since.

The messages are in a scroll container that fills the space above the composer, with stick_to_end_y, so it stays scrolled to the newest message, and justify_children_end, so the first few messages sit just above the composer, as chats show them. Older messages scroll up out of view, and the wheel scrolls back to them:

Typing the messages, with Ctrl+J for the line break and Enter to send each one:

docs.title: Line breaks
docs.text:
Pass enter_inserts_newline=True for Enter to insert a line break, as in a text editor, rather than bubble, as for a form or a chat that submits on Enter. Alt+Enter and Ctrl+J insert one either way. Shift+Enter can't stand in for them: most terminals send Shift+Enter as plain Enter, so terminal programs that submit on Enter, chat prompts among them, take Alt+Enter for a new line. Alt+Enter arrives from terminals that send Alt as an escape, as most do by default, and Ctrl+J from all of them.

A paste keeps its line breaks, however they're written, and expands each tab to spaces up to the next tab stop, every tab_size columns (4 by default), counting the line's text before the cursor, so pasted code keeps its indentation and the alignment of its columns:

ScreenshotText 

╭────────────────────────────╮
│ if done:                   │
│     ship()                 │
│     return                 │
╰────────────────────────────╯

Tab stops are counted in characters, as highlight counts them, so a wide character before a tab, such as 日, pushes what follows one column further than a tab stop. A browser's <textarea> keeps the tab, and CSS's tab-size sets how wide it's drawn; counterweight's text is drawn without tab stops, so the paste expands them instead.

docs.title: How the text wraps
docs.text: A row breaks after the last whitespace that fits, or wherever it fills when a word is wider than a row. Rows are filled one at a time, as text editors fill them, rather than evened out as text_wrap_pretty evens out a paragraph, so an edit rewraps its line only from the row above the cursor onward. The whitespace at a break stays at the end of its row, taking its cells, and a cell is kept after the end of each line, so wherever the cursor is, there's a cell to draw it in: a line that exactly fills its rows puts the cursor at its end on a row of its own.

docs.title: Keeping the cursor in view
docs.text:
A text area in a scroll container, such as one with a max_height, has to scroll as the cursor moves past its edge. The hook returns a cursor_row ElementHandle for the element the component draws the cursor's row in, and its handler returns ScrollIntoView for that handle, with block="nearest", for each key press and paste it handles. That applies to the layout of the render the edit causes, so the container scrolls in the same frame the cursor moves, and only as far as it takes, as a browser's <textarea> scrolls to its caret.

The cursor starts at the end of the value, so give a scroll container that holds the rows stick_to_end_y, which starts it scrolled to its end, so the cursor is in view from the start, as a browser keeps a focused <textarea>'s caret in view, rather than showing the top of a value that's already taller than the container.

To use it, draw the cursor's row as an element of its own and give it the handle. before_cursor and after_cursor separate rows with line breaks, so the rows above the cursor's are everything in before_cursor up to its last line break, and the rows below are everything in after_cursor after its first. The styled text area draws those as a Text each, around the cursor's row. A component that draws all the rows in one element can leave out the handle, and ScrollIntoView then scrolls nothing.

docs.title: Moving the cursor with a press
docs.text: A click in a browser's <textarea> focuses it and puts the caret where it lands. The hook can't know where the component draws the rows, so it returns a second handler, on_press, for the element the rows are drawn in, from the top-left corner of its content box. It reads a press of the left button as a cell of the rows, moved by that element's scroll if it's a scroll container, puts the cursor on the character drawn across that cell, or at the end of the row past its text, taking a press above the first row or below the last as one on that row, and focuses the component. The composer above draws its rows in the element it returns, so it puts both handlers there: first(field.on_input, field.on_press, on_enter).

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
The keys are use_text_input's, with these acting on rows:

Key Edit Up, Ctrl+P Move to the row above, at the same column, or to the start from the first row Down, Ctrl+N Move to the row below, at the same column, or to the end from the last row Home Move to the start of the row Ctrl+A Move to the start of the row, or to the start from the start of a row End Move to the end of the row Ctrl+E Move to the end of the row, or to the end from the end of a row Ctrl+U Delete to the start of the row Ctrl+K Delete to the end of the row PageUp Move a page of rows up, at the same column, or to the start from the first row PageDown Move a page of rows down, at the same column, or to the end from the last row Ctrl+J, Alt+Enter Insert a line break Enter Insert a line break, with enter_inserts_newline=True

Up and Down keep aiming for the column they started from, so the cursor comes back to it after passing through a shorter row. The end of a row that wraps is the start of the next, so End on one moves to its last character, usually the whitespace it wrapped at. Left, Right, Backspace and Delete step over a line break as one character, and the word keys treat it as whitespace. Ctrl+T swaps characters within a line, so it does nothing at the start of one.

PageUp and PageDown move the cursor, as they move a browser's caret in a <textarea>, rather than bubbling to a scroll container around the text area, which would scroll the text area itself out of view. When the element the handler is on is a scroll container, a page is as many rows as scroll_on_keys pages it by, 87.5% of the height of its view, and the handler scrolls it by a page too, so the cursor stays where it was in the view. When it isn't, its content box holds every row, so a page is 87.5% of that.

docs.title: Validating and transforming
docs.text: The setter works as it does for use_text_input: it's called with a function from the latest value to the edited one, and wrapping it validates or transforms each edit. The cursor stays where it is when the setter rejects an edit, and moves to the end of the value when the value changes other than by an edit.

docs.title: A styled text area
docs.text:
text_area draws a bordered box around the rows, wrapped at the width of its box, with the cursor highlighted while it's focused, and takes focus when it's pressed, with the cursor where the press lands. It takes the hook's parameters, other than width, a placeholder to show in an empty box, a style merged over its own, and styles for its colors. It's as wide as its parent or its style makes it, and grows to fit its rows, up to a max_height in its style, even in a column too short for everything in it:

@component
def notes() -> Div:
    text, set_text = use_state("")
    return Div(
        style=col | width(30),
        children=(
            text_area(
                text,
                set_text,
                placeholder="Notes",
                style=max_height(6),
                enter_inserts_newline=True,
                auto_focus=True,
            ),
        ),
    )

on_input: InputHandler

The handler that edits the value, for the calling component to put on the element it returns. It returns ScrollIntoView for cursor_row for each event it edits with, after a ScrollBy of a page for PageUp and PageDown when that element is a scroll container, and None for every event while that element isn't focused, and for the key presses it doesn't edit with, such as Tab, Escape, and Enter unless it inserts a line break, so they bubble to the element's ancestors.

docs.title: on_press instance-attribute
docs.text:
on_press: InputHandler

The handler that moves the cursor to where a press lands, as a click in a browser's <textarea> does, for the calling component to put on the element it draws the rows in, from the top-left corner of that element's content box, scrolled by that element's scroll if it's a scroll container. For a press of the left button, it moves the cursor to the cluster drawn across the cell pressed, or to the end of its row past the row's text, or to the first row or the last from above or below them, and returns FocusOn for the component with ScrollIntoView for cursor_row. It returns None for every other event, and for every event while the component isn't focusable.

A bordered box for editing text that wraps onto rows, built on use_text_area, which takes value, set_value, enter_inserts_newline, tab_size and the focus parameters, handle being a focus handle. It draws the cursor as a highlighted cell while it's focused, and a press on it focuses it, and on its text moves the cursor there. It's as wide as its parent or its style makes it, and grows to fit its rows, up to a max_height, past which it scrolls, keeping the cursor in view, and the wheel scrolls it. It starts scrolled to its end, where the cursor starts.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION placeholder

TYPE: str DEFAULT: ''

docs.title: use_text_input
docs.text:
use_text_input edits one line of text: it handles typing, deleting, moving the cursor, and pasting, and leaves drawing to the component that calls it, as Headless UI and React Aria do for the web. The component styles the text and the cursor however it likes, in whatever layout it's part of. For a ready-made box, use text_input, which is built on this hook.

This page covers the hook and that component. For text that wraps onto rows, use use_text_area. Selection isn't supported yet.

docs.title: Using the hook
docs.text:
The calling component owns the value, as with React's controlled <input>, and passes it to the hook with its setter. The hook owns the cursor, makes the component focusable, and returns the value split around the cursor, with the handler that edits it:

FRUITS = ("apple", "banana", "cherry", "grape", "lemon", "mango", "orange", "papaya")

CURSOR = (text_color("slate", 900) | text_bg("amber", 300)).text_style


@component
def search_box(query: str, set_query: Setter[str]) -> Text:
    field = use_text_input(query, set_query, auto_focus=True)
    cursor = CURSOR if field.focus.is_focused else CellStyle()
    return Text(
        content=(
            Chunk(content="search: ", style=text_color("amber", 400).text_style),
            Chunk(content=field.before_cursor),
            Chunk(content=field.at_cursor, style=cursor),
            Chunk(content=field.after_cursor),
        ),
        on_input=first(field.on_input, focus_receiver_on_press),
    )


@component
def search() -> Div:
    query, set_query = use_state("")
    results, _ = use_state(ElementHandle)
    matches = [fruit for fruit in FRUITS if query in fruit]

    def scroll_results(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Up):
                return ScrollBy(results, y=-1)
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Down):
                return ScrollBy(results, y=1)
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | gap(1),
        on_input=scroll_results,
        children=(
            search_box(query, set_query),
            Div(
                style=col | max_height(5) | overflow_y_scroll,
                handle=results,
                on_input=scroll_on_wheel(1),
                children=(Text(content="\n".join(matches) or "no matches", style=text_color("slate", 400)),),
            ),
        ),
    )

before_cursor, at_cursor and after_cursor together are the value, except that at_cursor is a space when the cursor is at the end of the value, so there's always a cell to draw the cursor in. The hook also returns cursor, the cursor's offset into the value in code points, so value[:cursor] is the text before it. Here the cursor is a highlighted cell, drawn only while the search box is focused:

ScreenshotText 

search:                       

apple                         
banana                        
cherry                        
grape                         
lemon

Typing edits the value, and the list below it re-renders from the new value:

ScreenshotText 

search: an                    

banana                        
mango                         
orange

Scrolling the list with Down, then typing and deleting, as it runs:

Left, three times, moves the cursor back between the m and the n of mngo, and an a typed there lands at the cursor:

ScreenshotText 

search: mango                 

mango

Put field.on_input on the element the component returns, which is the one that's focused. The handler ignores everything while that element isn't focused, and returns None for the keys it doesn't edit with, such as Enter, Tab, Up and Down, so they bubble on to a form that submits on Enter or moves focus on Tab. Here the search takes Up and Down as they bubble past the box, and scrolls the list of matches, which is at most five rows tall:

ScreenshotText 

search:                       

cherry                        
grape                         
lemon                         
mango                         
orange

Compose it with focus_receiver_on_press for the component to take focus when it's pressed, and with handlers of your own: first(field.on_input, on_enter) handles a key the field passes on, and first(on_ctrl_k, field.on_input) takes over a key the field would handle.

docs.title: Moving the cursor with a press
docs.text: A click in a browser's <input> focuses it and puts the caret where it lands. The hook can't know where the component draws the value, so it returns a second handler, on_press, for the element the value is drawn in, which may be inside the one the component returns. It reads a press of the left button as a cell of the value, counted from the left edge of that element's content box and moved by its scroll if it's a scroll container, puts the cursor on the character drawn across that cell, or at the end of the value past it, and focuses the component. In the command line below, it's on the row that scrolls the value rather than on the one that holds the $ prompt too.

docs.title: Scrolling a long value
docs.text:
A browser's <input> scrolls a value wider than the box sideways, keeping the caret in view. The hook does its part of that: it returns a cursor_cell element handle (an ElementHandle, which names an element, unlike the focus handle the hook's handle parameter takes), and its handler returns ScrollIntoView for that handle, with block="nearest" and inline="nearest", for each key press and paste it handles. The control applies to the layout of the render the edit causes, so the value scrolls in the same frame the cursor moves, and only as far as it takes.

To use it, draw at_cursor as an element of its own, give it the handle, and put the three parts in a row that scrolls sideways, with text_wrap_none so none of them wraps. Draw a cell after the value while the cursor is off its end, so the value is as wide wherever the cursor is, and doesn't move under the pointer when a press takes the cursor off the end:

@component
def command_line() -> Div:
    command, set_command = use_state("")
    field = use_text_input(command, set_command, auto_focus=True)
    cursor = CURSOR if field.focus.is_focused else CellStyle()
    return Div(
        style=row | width(24),
        on_input=first(field.on_input, focus_receiver_on_press),
        children=(
            Text(content="$ ", style=text_color("amber", 400)),
            Div(
                style=row | overflow_x_scroll | stick_to_end_x,
                on_input=field.on_press,
                children=(
                    Text(content=field.before_cursor, style=text_wrap_none),
                    Text(
                        content=field.at_cursor,
                        style=text_wrap_none | Style(text_style=cursor),
                        handle=field.cursor_cell,
                    ),
                    Text(
                        content=field.after_cursor + (" " if field.cursor < len(command) else ""),
                        style=text_wrap_none,
                    ),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

$  "Scroll long values"

Home moves the cursor to the start, and the row scrolls back to it:

ScreenshotText 

$ git commit -m "Scroll

The cursor starts at the end of the value, so the row has stick_to_end_x, which starts it scrolled to its end when the value is already wider than the box. The same ScrollIntoView scrolls every scroll container above the cell, so a field in a scrolling form comes back into view as soon as you type in it. A component that draws the value in one element can leave out the handle, and ScrollIntoView then scrolls nothing.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
The handler follows Readline's default bindings, which most terminal programs share:

Key Edit Text Insert it at the cursor Left, Ctrl+B Move one character left Right, Ctrl+F Move one character right Home, Ctrl+A, Ctrl+Home Move to the start End, Ctrl+E, Ctrl+End Move to the end Ctrl+Left, Alt+Left, Alt+B Move to the start of this word or the previous one Ctrl+Right, Alt+Right, Alt+F Move to the end of this word or the next one Backspace Delete the character before the cursor Delete, Ctrl+D Delete the character at the cursor Ctrl+W Delete back to the start of the whitespace-separated word Alt+Backspace Delete back to the start of this word or the previous one Ctrl+Delete, Alt+Delete, Alt+D Delete to the end of this word or the next one Ctrl+U Delete to the start Ctrl+K Delete to the end Ctrl+T Swap the characters before and at the cursor, or the last two at the end

A character is a grapheme cluster, so the cursor steps over an emoji or an accented letter whole. A word is a run of letters and digits, so Alt+Backspace stops at punctuation, as Readline's backward-kill-word does, where Ctrl+W, its unix-word-rubout, deletes back to whitespace: from the end of cd ../src, Alt+Backspace leaves cd ../ and Ctrl+W leaves cd. The Alt keys arrive from terminals that send Alt as an escape, as most do by default. Alt+Enter isn't an edit, so it bubbles as Enter does, as Key.AltEnter.

A paste inserts its text in one edit, with each line break and tab turned into a space and any other control characters dropped, on terminals that support bracketed paste. On others, the pasted text arrives as typed keys, and its line breaks arrive as Enter, or as Ctrl+J from a terminal that sends them as line feeds.

docs.title: Validating and transforming
docs.text:
The setter that use_text_input takes is called with a function from the latest value to the edited one, rather than with the edited value. Several key presses can arrive between renders, as when typing fast, and each edit has to apply to the result of the one before, which the value the component rendered with doesn't have yet. A use_state setter takes such a function and applies it right away.

To validate or transform an edit, wrap the setter in one that applies the edit itself and decides what to keep. This one keeps only digits:

def digits_only(set_value: Setter[str]) -> Callable[[Callable[[str], str]], None]:
    def set_digits(edit: Callable[[str], str]) -> None:
        set_value(lambda value: edited if (edited := edit(value)).isdigit() or not edited else value)

    return set_digits


@component
def sign_up() -> Div:
    name, set_name = use_state("")
    age, set_age = use_state("")
    return Div(
        style=col | width(30),
        on_input=tab_focus,
        children=(
            text_input(name, set_name, placeholder="Name", auto_focus=True),
            text_input(age, digits_only(set_age), placeholder="Age"),
        ),
    )

Typing 3x6 into the age field gives 36, since the x would have made the value something other than digits:

ScreenshotText 

╭────────────────────────────╮
│ Ada Lovelace               │
╰────────────────────────────╯
╭────────────────────────────╮
│ 36                         │
╰────────────────────────────╯

The cursor stays where it is when the setter rejects an edit, and when the value changes other than by an edit, such as when a form clears it after submitting or fills in an earlier entry, the cursor moves to the end of the new value.

docs.title: A styled text input
docs.text:
text_input draws a bordered box around the value, with the cursor highlighted while it's focused, and takes focus when it's pressed, with the cursor where the press lands. It takes the hook's parameters, a placeholder to show in an empty box, a style merged over its own, such as a width, and styles for its colors. The sign-up form above uses it, and shows its placeholders when it starts:

ScreenshotText 

╭────────────────────────────╮
│ Name                       │
╰────────────────────────────╯
╭────────────────────────────╮
│ Age                        │
╰────────────────────────────╯

A value wider than the box scrolls inside its border, keeping the cursor in view:

ScreenshotText 

╭────────────────────────────╮
│ ing, Countess of Lovelace  │
╰────────────────────────────╯
╭────────────────────────────╮
│ Age                        │
╰────────────────────────────╯

Like an <input>, it doesn't grow to fit its value: beside other elements in a row, it shrinks to fit, and scrolls.

docs.title: counterweight.headless.use_text_input
docs.text:
use_text_input(
    value: str,
    set_value: Callable[[Callable[[str], str]], None],
    auto_focus: bool = False,
    handle: FocusHandle | None = None,
    is_focusable: bool = True,
    in_focus_order: bool = True,
) -> TextInput

Edits one line of text, leaving how it's drawn to the calling component. The calling component owns the value, and the hook owns the cursor and makes the component focusable.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION value

The text being edited.

TYPE: str

set_value

Called with a function from the latest value to the edited one for each edit, which it MUST call before returning, as a use_state setter does. Several key presses can arrive between renders, as when typing fast, so an edit applies to the latest value rather than to value, which is the one this render saw. Validate or transform an edit by wrapping the setter: lambda edit: set_value(lambda v: new if (new := edit(v)).isdigit() or not new else v) keeps only digits, and lets the value be emptied. Each edit also calls it before and after with a function that returns the value it's given, to read the latest value, and then the one the edit settled at: the cursor moves with an edit unless the setter left the value as it was before it.

TYPE: Callable[[Callable[[str], str]], None]

auto_focus

Passed to use_focus.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

handle

The focus handle passed to use_focus.

TYPE: FocusHandle | None DEFAULT: None

is_focusable

Passed to use_focus.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: True

in_focus_order

Passed to use_focus.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: True

RETURNS DESCRIPTION TextInput

The value split around the cursor, for the calling component to draw,

TextInput

the handler that edits it, for the calling component to put on the element it returns,

TextInput

and the handler that moves the cursor to a press, for the element it draws the value in.

TextInput

The cursor starts at the end of the value, and moves to the end when the value changes other than by an edit.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Counterweight uses "hooks", inspired by React hooks, to manage state and side effects in components. The headless components, such as use_text_input, are hooks too, built on these, that give a component a common control's behavior.

A component MUST call the same hooks in the same order on every render, because each hook finds its state by its position in that order. Don't call a hook inside a condition, a loop whose length can change, or after an early return. A render that calls a different hook at some position, or a different number of hooks than the previous render, raises InconsistentHookExecution.

When a component seems to need a hook only some of the time, or one hook per item, move that hook down into a child component that owns it. A parent can't conditionally call a hook, but it can conditionally render a component, and each component has its own hooks.

from counterweight.components import component
from counterweight.elements import Div, Text
from counterweight.hooks import use_state


@component
def settings(is_advanced: bool) -> Div:
    if is_advanced:
        level, set_level = use_state(3)  # wrong: raises when is_advanced changes
    ...

Here the hook moves into an advanced_settings component, which the parent renders only when it's needed:

@component
def advanced_settings() -> Text:
    level, set_level = use_state(3)
    return Text(content=f"level {level}")


@component
def settings(is_advanced: bool) -> Div:
    return Div(children=(advanced_settings(),) if is_advanced else ())

Showing advanced_settings mounts it with fresh state, and hiding it unmounts it, which discards that state. If the state should outlive the child, keep it in the parent and pass it down instead.

The same move handles a hook per item: render a component per item, rather than calling the hook in a loop over the items. See Components for how to key those components so each one's state follows its item.

docs.title: use_clock
docs.text:
use_clock gives a component the time, so it can show a clock, an uptime, or a timer while staying pure. A component that reads the time any other way, such as with datetime.now(), keeps showing the time from whenever it last ran.

@component
def wall_clock() -> Text:
    tick = use_clock(timedelta(minutes=1))
    return Text(content=f"{tick.now:%H:%M %Z}", style=text_color("amber", 400))


@component
def uptime() -> Text:
    tick = use_clock(timedelta(seconds=1))
    seconds = tick.since_start // timedelta(seconds=1)
    return Text(content=f"Up {seconds // 3600}:{seconds // 60 % 60:02}:{seconds % 60:02}")


@component
def status_bar() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | justify_children_space_between | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
        children=(uptime(), wall_clock()),
    )
ScreenshotText 

╭──────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Up 1:02:05                 16:11 UTC │
╰──────────────────────────────────────╯

docs.title: Ticks
docs.text:
Each call reads the clock every interval. A component takes a reading when it mounts, and again on its first render after each new tick starts, re-running then if nothing else made it. Every render in between gets the same reading, so re-running the component for any other reason doesn't change what it shows.

Ticks start at whole multiples of interval on the wall clock, so wall_clock re-runs as the minute turns, along with uptime, rather than a minute after the app started. Components that take a reading in the same frame get the same one, so two clocks on screen never disagree.

Each tick re-runs the components that read the clock and nothing else, so call use_clock in the component that shows the time, not in one that also renders things that don't change with it. See Performance.

docs.title: Time zones
docs.text:
The app's clock reads the wall-clock time in UTC, so an app shows the same time wherever it runs unless it asks for another zone. Give app a SystemClock with a timezone to read the time in that zone instead:

await app(status_bar(), clock=SystemClock(timezone=ZoneInfo("America/New_York")))

Ticks follow the clock's zone too, so an interval of a day ticks at that zone's midnight. Converting a UTC reading with tick.now.astimezone(zone) shows the right time, but its ticks still start on UTC's boundaries: a day-long tick at UTC's midnight rather than the zone's, and an hour-long tick off the zone's hour where it's offset by a fraction of one, such as India's.

docs.title: Timing from an event
docs.text:
since_mount is how long the component has been mounted. To time something from an event, such as a key press, render a component that reads the clock and give it a new key when the event happens, which remounts it and starts its since_mount again from zero:

@component
def lap_time() -> Text:
    elapsed = use_clock(timedelta(seconds=1)).since_mount
    return Text(content=f"{elapsed // timedelta(seconds=1)} s")


@component
def lap_timer() -> Div:
    laps, set_laps = use_state(1)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Space):
                set_laps(lambda laps: laps + 1)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=row | gap(1),
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            Text(content=f"Lap {laps}:", style=text_color("slate", 400)),
            # A new key each lap remounts lap_time, so its time since mounting starts again from zero.
            lap_time().with_key(str(laps)),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

Lap 2: 42 s

Each press of Space starts the next lap from zero:

A handler sees the reading from the latest tick, so a time it records, such as the lap time when a lap ends, is up to one interval early. Choose an interval as fine as the precision the time needs. A timer that can be paused and resumed loses up to that much on each pause, since it carries the time recorded at the pause into the next run.

docs.title: Why compute from elapsed time?
docs.text:
Compute whatever changes over time, such as an animation frame or a countdown, from since_mount or since_start. Don't keep a running total in state and add to it each tick:

@component
def spinner() -> Text:
    frame, set_frame = use_state(0)

    async def step() -> None:
        while True:
            await sleep(0.1)
            set_frame(lambda frame: frame + 1)  # wrong: falls further behind each step

    use_effect(step, deps=())

    return Text(content="|/-\\"[frame % 4])

Each step counts a full interval, but takes longer: sleep wakes up late, and a render and any other work run before the next step starts. The total falls behind the real elapsed time by a little more each step, and the gap only grows. Measured on an otherwise idle event loop, steps of 10 ms counted 2 seconds when 2.05 had passed. Adding up the real time between steps instead fixes the drift, but anything that misses a step or repeats one, such as an effect that restarts, still breaks the total.

Elapsed time from use_clock is the difference between two readings of a monotonic clock, so a value computed from it can't drift, however long the component runs:

@component
def spinner() -> Text:
    frame = use_clock(timedelta(milliseconds=100)).since_mount // timedelta(milliseconds=100)
    return Text(content="|/-\\"[frame % 4])

It also needs no state or effect, so a tick re-renders once instead of twice.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Pass a FrozenClock to app to fix the time, and move it on with AdvanceClock in the autopilot, so a test or a screenshot doesn't depend on when it runs or how long it takes:

async def test_the_lap_timer_counts_from_the_last_lap() -> None:
    await app(
        lap_timer(),
        headless=True,
        clock=FrozenClock(datetime(2026, 3, 14, 15, 9, 26, tzinfo=UTC)),
        autopilot=[
            AdvanceClock(by=timedelta(seconds=75)),
            KeyPressed(key=Key.Space),
            AdvanceClock(by=timedelta(seconds=42)),
            Screenshot.to_file(Path("lap-timer.txt")),
            Quit(),
        ],
        check_purity=True,
    )

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.use_clock
docs.text:
use_clock(interval: timedelta) -> Tick
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION interval

How often the component reads the clock. Ticks start at whole multiples of interval past midnight on the wall clock, in the clock's timezone (for an interval that divides a day), so components reading the clock every second and every minute both re-run as the minute turns.

TYPE: timedelta

RETURNS DESCRIPTION Tick

A reading of the app's clock, taken when the component mounts, and again on the first render after each new tick starts, with the component re-running then if nothing else made it. Between those, every render returns the same reading, so the component's output stays a function of its arguments and hooks. Components that take a reading in the same frame get the same one, whatever their intervals.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

docs.title: use_controls
docs.text:
An input handler acts on the app by returning controls, but an effect, or a callback that a program or a timer calls, has no event to return them for. use_controls gives a component a sender that hands the app a control from anywhere:

from asyncio import sleep

from counterweight.components import component
from counterweight.controls import Quit
from counterweight.elements import Text
from counterweight.hooks import use_controls, use_effect


@component
def farewell() -> Text:
    send_control = use_controls()

    async def quit_soon() -> None:
        await sleep(3)
        send_control(Quit())

    use_effect(quit_soon, deps=())

    return Text(content="Quitting in three seconds...")

The multiplexer example quits the same way when its last pane's shell exits, and moves focus with FocusNext when the focused pane's shell exits.

The app handles a sent control as it handles one a handler returns, after the events already waiting, so state set just before sending it changes the same frame the control does. Every render returns an equal sender, so it can be left out of an effect's deps.

Sends the app controls from outside an input handler, such as from an effect, or a callback a program or a timer calls. An input handler returns its controls instead.

ControlSender

ControlSender

ControlSender

ControlSender

ControlSender

docs.title: Effect Cancellation
docs.text:
Effects are canceled by the framework when one of the following conditions is met:

  • The component that created the effect is unmounted.
  • The effect's dependencies change and the effect's setup function is going to be re-run.

Effect cancellation is synchronous

Note that the effect is synchronously cancelled (i.e., the Task that represents the effect is cancelled and then awaited; see this discussion) before the next render cycle starts. Assuming that you do not mess with the cancellation yourself from inside the effect setup function, the effect will definitely stop running before the next frame is rendered.

Within a render, every effect that is being cancelled is cancelled concurrently, and all of them finish before any effect's setup function starts, so an effect that holds something exclusive (a subscription, a terminal mode) releases it before its own re-run or a sibling's effect can acquire it.

docs.title: use_focus
docs.text:
Each key press goes to one element: the focused one. A component becomes focusable by calling use_focus, and when it's focused, its top-level element, the one it returns, receives every key press first. The key then bubbles to that element's ancestors, until a handler returns something other than None. When nothing is focused, key presses go to the root component's element alone.

This page covers making components focusable and moving focus between them. How a key press travels once it reaches the focused element is on the Events page.

docs.title: Making a component focusable
docs.text:
@component
def counter() -> Text:
    focus = use_focus(auto_focus=True)
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Up):
                set_count(lambda count: count + 1)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=str(count),
        style=text_bg("indigo", 700) if focus.is_focused else default,
        on_input=on_input,
    )

focus.is_focused says whether the component is focused, so it can draw a focus ring, and auto_focus=True focuses it when it mounts while nothing else is focused.

Put a focusable component's key handler on the element it returns. Elements inside that one never receive key presses, since they're descendants of the focused element rather than ancestors. For the same reason, a component deep in the tree can't own a global shortcut: a help overlay toggled with ? puts that binding on the root component's element, or on an ancestor of whatever is focused, which every key press bubbles through unless a handler below it stops it.

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
This order form uses every way focus moves. Its fields take keys rather than text: the size and the wrapping paper cycle with Left and Right, the quantity steps with Up and Down, and gift wrap toggles with Space.

SIZES = ("Small", "Medium", "Large")
PAPERS = ("Stripes", "Dots", "Plain")
TIPS = ("Enter moves to the next field", "Press a label to focus its field", "Tab stays inside the dialog")


def marked(focus: Focus, content: str) -> str:
    return f"{'▸' if focus.is_focused else ' '} {content}"


def field_style(focus: Focus, is_focusable: bool = True) -> Style:
    if not is_focusable:
        return text_color("slate", 600)
    return text_bg("indigo", 700) | text_color("slate", 50) if focus.is_focused else text_color("slate", 300)


@component
def choice_field(
    options: tuple[str, ...], handle: FocusHandle, auto_focus: bool = False, is_focusable: bool = True
) -> Text:
    focus = use_focus(auto_focus=auto_focus, handle=handle, is_focusable=is_focusable)
    index, set_index = use_state(0)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Left):
                set_index(lambda i: (i - 1) % len(options))
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Right):
                set_index(lambda i: (i + 1) % len(options))
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=marked(focus, f"< {options[index]} >"),
        style=field_style(focus, is_focusable),
        on_input=first(on_input, focus_receiver_on_press),
    )


@component
def quantity_field(handle: FocusHandle) -> Text:
    focus = use_focus(handle=handle)
    quantity, set_quantity = use_state(1)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Up):
                set_quantity(lambda q: q + 1)
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Down):
                set_quantity(lambda q: max(q - 1, 1))
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=marked(focus, f"{quantity} ▴▾"),
        style=field_style(focus),
        on_input=first(on_input, focus_receiver_on_press),
    )


@component
def toggle_field(is_on: bool, set_on: Setter[bool], handle: FocusHandle) -> Text:
    focus = use_focus(handle=handle)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Space):
                set_on(toggle)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=marked(focus, "[x]" if is_on else "[ ]"),
        style=field_style(focus),
        on_input=first(on_input, focus_receiver_on_press),
    )


@component
def help_panel() -> Div:
    # A press focuses it, but Enter and Tab never stop on it.
    focus = use_focus(in_focus_order=False)
    page, set_page = use_state(0)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Left):
                set_page(lambda p: (p - 1) % len(TIPS))
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Right):
                set_page(lambda p: (p + 1) % len(TIPS))
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=border
        | border_lightrounded
        | pad_x(1)
        | (border_color("indigo", 400) if focus.is_focused else border_color("slate", 600)),
        on_input=first(on_input, focus_receiver_on_press),
        children=(
            Text(
                style=position_absolute | inset_left(1) | inset_top(-1) | clip_to_border,
                content=f" {marked(focus, f'Tip {page + 1}/{len(TIPS)}')} ",
            ),
            Text(content=TIPS[page], style=text_color("slate", 400)),
        ),
    )


@component
def button(
    label: str, action: Callable[[], InputResponse], auto_focus: bool = False, handle: FocusHandle | None = None
) -> Text:
    focus = use_focus(auto_focus=auto_focus, handle=handle)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter):
                return action()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=marked(focus, label),
        style=pad_x(1) | border | border_lightrounded | field_style(focus),
        on_input=first(on_input, each(on_click(action), focus_receiver_on_press)),
    )


dialog_box = position_absolute | inset(0) | margin_auto | fit_content_width | fit_content_height


@component
def confirmation(close: Callable[[], None], return_to: FocusHandle) -> Div:
    def close_and_return() -> InputResponse:
        close()
        return FocusOn(return_to)

    return Div(
        style=dialog_box | col | align_children_center | border | border_double | pad_x(2),
        # Tab from either button reaches this element before the form's, and cycles between the two.
        on_input=tab_focus,
        children=(
            Text(content="Place this order?"),
            Div(
                style=row | gap(1),
                children=(
                    button("Confirm", close_and_return),
                    button("Cancel", close_and_return, auto_focus=True),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )


@component
def labelled(label: str, handle: FocusHandle, field: Component) -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(1),
        children=(Text(content=f"{label:<10}", on_input=focus_on_press(handle)), field),
    )


@component
def order_form() -> Div:
    size, _ = use_state(FocusHandle)
    quantity, _ = use_state(FocusHandle)
    gift_wrap, _ = use_state(FocusHandle)
    paper, _ = use_state(FocusHandle)
    submit, _ = use_state(FocusHandle)
    is_wrapped, set_wrapped = use_state(False)
    is_confirming, set_confirming = use_state(False)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter):
                return FocusNext(within=receiver.subtree)
            case _:
                return None

    def open_confirmation() -> InputResponse:
        set_confirming(True)
        # With nothing focused, the dialog's Cancel button takes focus as it mounts.
        return ClearFocus()

    return Div(
        style=col | gap(1) | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
        on_input=first(on_input, tab_focus),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col,
                children=(
                    labelled("Size", size, choice_field(SIZES, size, auto_focus=True)),
                    labelled("Quantity", quantity, quantity_field(quantity)),
                    labelled("Gift wrap", gift_wrap, toggle_field(is_wrapped, set_wrapped, gift_wrap)),
                    labelled("Paper", paper, choice_field(PAPERS, paper, is_focusable=is_wrapped)),
                ),
            ),
            help_panel(),
            Div(style=row, children=(button("Submit", open_confirmation, handle=submit),)),
            *([confirmation(close=lambda: set_confirming(False), return_to=submit)] if is_confirming else []),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Moving focus
docs.text:
Focus moves only through controls, auto_focus, and the focused component going away. No key or press does anything to focus unless a handler on its path returns a control that does:

  • FocusNext and FocusPrevious move to the next or previous component in the focus order, which is tree order, wrapping at the ends.
  • FocusOn focuses the component with a given focus handle, including one that mounts in the render its handler causes.
  • ClearFocus clears focus, so key presses go to the root component's element.

The library handlers return these for the common bindings: tab_focus for Tab and Shift+Tab, focus_receiver_on_press and focus_on_press for a press, and clear_focus for a press that should blur. An app without tab_focus on some element has no Tab navigation, and a focusable component without focus_receiver_on_press doesn't take focus when it's clicked. An app that wants Escape to clear focus binds it to ClearFocus() on its root.

Focus also changes when a render leaves the focused component unable to keep it. Unmounting it, hiding it, or making it unfocusable clears focus, rather than moving it to whichever component took the departed one's place. A component that mounts with auto_focus=True in the same render can then take focus.

Wherever focus moves, the newly focused component's element is scrolled into view in any scroll container it's in, by as little as it takes, as browsers do.

docs.title: Focusing a component you render
docs.text:
A FocusHandle names a focusable component for FocusOn. use_focus creates one on the component's first render and keeps it, but a parent that needs to focus a child it renders creates the handle itself, before the child mounts, and passes it down:

@component
def labelled_input(label: str) -> Div:
    input_handle, _ = use_state(FocusHandle)
    value, set_value = use_state("")
    return Div(
        children=(
            Text(content=label, on_input=focus_on_press(input_handle)),
            text_input(value, set_value, handle=input_handle),
        ),
    )

A child that can be focused from outside takes a handle: FocusHandle | None = None parameter and passes it on to use_focus, as text_input and the headless components do. Keep the handle in use_state: one built with FocusHandle() on every render makes use_focus raise ChangedFocusHandle on the second. Two mounted components given the same handle raise DuplicateFocusHandle. The handle never changes while the component is mounted, so it's safe in an effect's deps.

docs.title: Focusing a component as it mounts
docs.text:
A handler that adds a component can focus it too: it creates the new component's handle, keeps it in state with whatever else describes the component, and returns FocusOn with it:

@component
def notes() -> Div:
    handles, set_handles = use_state(tuple[FocusHandle, ...]())

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.ControlN):
                handle = FocusHandle()
                set_handles(lambda handles: (*handles, handle))
                return FocusOn(handle)
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(on_input=on_input, children=tuple(note(handle) for handle in handles))

The note doesn't exist until the next render, so FocusOn waits for it: a FocusOn whose handle names no component that can take focus yet focuses that component in the next render, before the frame is drawn, so the new note is focused in the first frame that shows it. It's how a browser's <dialog> focuses a field inside it as showModal() opens it. A control that moves focus after it, in the same handler or a later one before that render, wins, and a FocusOn whose component doesn't take focus in that render does nothing.

docs.title: Moving focus within part of the tree
docs.text:
FocusNext and FocusPrevious take within, a Subtree that limits them to the focusable components inside one element, including the element itself. A handler gets its own element's from its receiver, as receiver.subtree. From focus outside the subtree, they go to its first or last focusable component.

tab_focus passes its receiver's subtree, so on the root component's element it moves through the whole tree, and on a dialog's element, which Tab from a field inside the dialog bubbles to first, it keeps Tab inside the dialog. A form that moves to its next field on Enter does the same thing for Enter, from its own element's handler.

A dialog traps Tab and nothing else. A press beside it still reaches whatever is drawn there, and if focus clears while the dialog is open, because its focused field unmounted, key presses go to the root, whose tab_focus can move focus out of the dialog.

docs.title: Taking a component out of focus
docs.text:
Two parameters take a mounted, visible component partly or wholly out of focus, each like a browser attribute:

  • is_focusable=False makes it unfocusable, like disabled, for a field that's disabled until another is filled in. Nothing can focus it, and if it's focused, focus clears. It still receives the mouse events routed to it, so a press on it is still claimed by its focus_receiver_on_press, which then does nothing.
  • in_focus_order=False takes it out of the focus order only, like tabindex="-1", for a component that should take focus when it's pressed or named, but isn't a Tab stop. FocusNext and FocusPrevious skip it, while FocusOn, auto_focus and a press still focus it, and it keeps focus once it has it. From it, FocusNext and FocusPrevious move to its neighbors in tree order.

Either way the component keeps its focus handle and its place in tree order, so it's back in the focus order where it was when the parameter flips back, though making a component focusable again doesn't focus it. They're parameters, rather than a use_focus call to skip, because a component can't call a hook conditionally.

docs.title: When focus changes
docs.text:
Every key press in a batch of input is routed with the focus as it is when it arrives, so a Tab followed by a letter delivers the letter to the newly focused component. A key press that mounts an auto_focus component, or that mounts one and returns FocusOn for it, doesn't send the next key press in its batch there, since the component doesn't exist until the next render.

A control that moves focus re-renders the components that gained and lost focus, as a state change would, so is_focused is current on the next frame. When a render moves focus itself, to an auto_focus component that mounted or to the component a FocusOn waited for, or away from a focused component that unmounted, hid, or became unfocusable, the components that gained and lost focus re-render before the frame is drawn, so an auto_focus component is focused in the first frame that shows it. An auto_focus component that hides itself because it gained focus would move focus again, so it raises UnsettledFocus instead, and so does one that a waiting FocusOn focuses. One that a control focuses and that hides itself because it gained focus loses focus in the same render, like any focused component that hides, and is drawn unfocused.

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.use_focus
docs.text:
use_focus(
    auto_focus: bool = False,
    handle: FocusHandle | None = None,
    is_focusable: bool = True,
    in_focus_order: bool = True,
) -> Focus

Makes the calling component focusable. Its top-level element, the one it returns, is the one that's focused, so a component that handles key presses puts its handler on that element. A component can call it only once.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION auto_focus

Whether the component takes focus when it mounts visible and focusable while nothing is focused. When several mount in the same render, the first in tree order takes focus. A component that mounts hidden or unfocusable doesn't take focus when it's shown or made focusable later.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

handle

The handle that names the component, which a parent creates with use_state(FocusHandle) to focus a child it renders with FocusOn. If None, use_focus creates one on the first render and keeps it. Every render MUST pass the same handle as the first, or use_focus raises ChangedFocusHandle, and two mounted components given the same handle raise DuplicateFocusHandle.

TYPE: FocusHandle | None DEFAULT: None

is_focusable

Whether the component can be focused, like a browser's disabled attribute when False. Nothing can focus an unfocusable component, and making the focused component unfocusable clears focus. It still receives the mouse events routed to it.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: True

in_focus_order

Whether FocusNext and FocusPrevious stop on the component, like a browser's tabindex="-1" when False. A component out of the focus order can still be focused with FocusOn, auto_focus, or a press, and keeps focus once it has it.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: True

RETURNS DESCRIPTION Focus

Whether the component is focused, and its handle, which is the same object on every render.

docs.title: use_memo
docs.text:
use_memo keeps a value from one render to the next, computing it again only when its dependencies change. Use it for:

  • An expensive value derived from arguments or state, such as a sorted or filtered list.
  • An unchanging part of a component's output. A component that returns the same element object as last render keeps the components inside it from re-running.
  • A handler passed to a memo component. A handler defined inline is a new object every render, so the memo component's arguments never equal last render's.
from counterweight.components import component
from counterweight.elements import Div, Text
from counterweight.hooks import use_memo, use_state


@component
def file_list(paths: tuple[str, ...]) -> Div:
    descending, set_descending = use_state(False)

    ordered = use_memo(lambda: sorted(paths, reverse=descending), deps=(paths, descending))

    return Div(children=tuple(Text(content=path) for path in ordered))

file_list sorts paths again only when paths or descending changes, not on every render its parent causes.

A handler to keep stable is use_memo(lambda: handler, deps).

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
deps has to list every value compute reads that can change between renders: arguments, state, and anything computed from them. A value left out keeps the cached result from updating when it changes. For a cached handler, that means the handler keeps acting on the value it captured when it was cached. When a handler only needs the latest state to compute the next state, pass a function to the setter (set_count(lambda count: count + 1)), which needs no dependency on count.

Since hooks are found by their position, use_memo can't be called once per item in a loop whose length can change. To cache something per item, render a component per item and call use_memo in it, or declare that component memo.

Passing check_purity=True to app in tests catches a missing dependency: each use_memo whose deps didn't change also calls compute, and raises StaleMemo if the result differs from the cached value. Handlers are compared by their code and the values they captured, as in Keeping components pure.

docs.title: use_memo or functools.lru_cache?
docs.text:
Both cache a computed value, but they differ in who owns it. A use_memo value belongs to one mounted component. An lru_cache value belongs to a function, and every caller in the process shares it. So cache a pure function of its arguments with lru_cache, and use use_memo for a value that belongs to the component.

use_memo lru_cache Shared by One component instance Every caller, across instances, renders and apps Keeps One value, for the latest deps Up to maxsize values, keyed by arguments Freed When the component unmounts When evicted, or never with maxsize=None Hits when deps equal last render's (==) The arguments equal a cached call's (hash, then ==) Goes stale when compute reads a value missing from deps The function reads something besides its arguments Defined Inside the component At module level

Prefer lru_cache when:

  • The computation reads only its arguments. Its key is its dependency list, so that list can't be incomplete.
  • Many components compute the same thing, such as rows formatting the same column widths. They all share one cache.
  • The inputs alternate, such as a sort order toggled back and forth. lru_cache keeps both results, while use_memo keeps one and recomputes on every toggle.

The example above, rewritten that way:

from functools import lru_cache


@lru_cache(maxsize=64)
def sorted_paths(paths: tuple[str, ...], descending: bool) -> tuple[str, ...]:
    return tuple(sorted(paths, reverse=descending))


@component
def file_list(paths: tuple[str, ...]) -> Div:
    descending, set_descending = use_state(False)

    return Div(children=tuple(Text(content=path) for path in sorted_paths(paths, descending)))

Prefer use_memo when:

  • The value captures the component's state or setters, as a handler does.
  • The inputs can't be hashed, such as lists, dicts and most mutable objects.
  • The value should go away with the component. A module-level cache keeps every argument and result it holds alive until they're evicted, and carries them between tests and between apps run in the same process.
  • The value is part of the component's output, such as an element whose children shouldn't re-run. That's meant for one instance, not for every instance that happens to pass equal arguments.
  • Each instance computes from its own input, such as a document per message in a transcript. A render with more instances than the cache's maxsize asks for more keys than it holds, in the same order every render, so each key is evicted before it's asked for again and nothing hits. use_memo keeps one value per instance, however many instances there are.

Don't put lru_cache on a function defined inside a component: every render defines a new function with an empty cache, so it never hits.

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.use_memo
docs.text:
use_memo(
    compute: Getter[T], deps: tuple[object, ...]
) -> T
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION compute

A zero-argument function that computes the value. It runs while the component renders: on the first render, and on every render whose deps changed.

TYPE: Getter[T]

deps

The values compute depends on. If any of them change (compared with ==), compute runs again. () computes the value once, when the component mounts. Unlike use_effect's, these can't be None: to compute on every render, don't use this hook.

TYPE: tuple[object, ...]

RETURNS DESCRIPTION T

The value compute returned when deps last changed. It is the same object on every render until then, so an element returned from it keeps the components below it from re-running, and a handler returned from it can be passed to a memo component without making it re-run. The cached value MUST depend only on deps; check_purity on counterweight.app.app catches a value that goes stale.

docs.title: Measuring another element
docs.text: Given an ElementHandle, use_rects reports the rectangles of the element with that handle instead of the calling component's own top-level element, as a React component measures an element through a ref and a ResizeObserver. That's how a component measures an element a child component draws, such as the viewport of a scroll_area it passes the handle to as viewport. The handle comes from use_state(ElementHandle), so it's the same on every render. A handle that named no visible element in the previous render reports empty rectangles, as the first render does.

docs.title: When it renders again
docs.text: use_rects reports the previous frame's rectangles, and a component that calls it renders again as soon as any of the rectangles it read move, whether its own state changed or something else, such as a sibling growing, moved them. A component whose size depends on the rectangles it reads should settle: one that grows whenever it reads its own size renders without end.

docs.title: use_ref
docs.text: use_ref keeps a mutable box, a Ref, for as long as the component is mounted. Changing ref.current doesn't render anything, which is what sets a ref apart from state: it holds what the component needs to remember but doesn't show.

docs.title: Using a ref outside of rendering
docs.text:
Read and write current in handlers and effects, which run after a render, not while rendering.

from counterweight.components import component
from counterweight.elements import Text
from counterweight.events import InputEvent, InputResponse, KeyPressed, Receiver
from counterweight.hooks import use_focus, use_ref, use_state
from counterweight.keys import Key


@component
def line_entry() -> Text:
    use_focus(auto_focus=True)
    typed = use_ref(list[str]())
    line, set_line = use_state("")

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter):
                set_line("".join(typed.current))
                typed.current.clear()
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=key):
                typed.current.append(key)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(content=line, on_input=on_input)

line_entry collects keys without rendering, and renders only when Enter sets line. Rendering reads line, never typed. It shows a ref, not how to take text: it has no cursor or Backspace, and drops pastes. For a field, use use_text_input.

Refs fit:

  • Values a handler builds up before it sets state, as typed does above.
  • Values a later event needs before the next render, such as where a drag began: a handler sees the state of the render that built it, so an event handled in the same batch as the one that set the state doesn't see the new value.
  • Objects outside the tree, such as a task or a client, that a handler or an effect uses.
  • Something expensive to build once, with a function as the initial value: use_ref(lambda: build_index()) calls build_index only on the first render.

docs.title: Not reading or writing a ref while rendering
docs.text:
A component has to be pure: given the same arguments and hook state, it returns the same element. A ref changes without a render, so it isn't part of that state, and a render can skip a component and keep its previous output.

Writing a ref while rendering happens once per run, and which renders run a component depends on what else changed:

@component
def counts_renders() -> Text:
    renders = use_ref(0)
    renders.current += 1
    return Text(content=f"rendered {renders.current} times")

The count goes up only on the renders that re-run counts_renders, so it says nothing reliable. Count something you can name instead, such as the events a handler saw, in state.

Reading a ref while rendering shows whatever it held when the component last ran:

@component
def shows_change(value: int) -> Text:
    previous = use_ref(value)
    text = f"{previous.current} -> {value}"
    previous.current = value
    return Text(content=text)

Once previous holds value, running shows_change again shows value -> value. Keep the previous value in state, and set it together with the current one.

Reading current once to start with, such as passing use_ref(lambda: build_index()).current to a child, is fine as long as nothing changes it afterward.

With check_purity on, the second run of every component gets copies of its refs, so assigning current there leaves the component's refs alone, and a component whose output depends on what a ref held raises ImpureComponent. The copies hold the same objects, so changing the object current holds, such as appending to a list, still reaches the component's ref.
