docs.title: use_state
docs.text:
use_state gives a component a value that persists across renders, and a setter that changes it. Setting a different value re-renders the component.

@component
def counter() -> Text:
    count, set_count = use_state(0)
    ...

docs.title: Updating state from its previous value
docs.text:
When the new state depends on the old, pass the setter a function

count is the value as of the render that built the handler, and nothing updates it until the next render. A setter given a value replaces the state with it, so every update computed from count before the next render starts from the same stale count, and only the last one survives. No error is raised: the other updates just vanish.

Given a function, the setter calls it right away with the latest state, updates included, and stores what it returns:

set_count(count + 1)            # wrong: loses updates made since this render
set_count(lambda c: c + 1)      # right: builds on the latest state

Several updates can land before the next render in ways that are easy to miss, because each looks like one update when you read the code.

Two updates in one handler. Each count + 1 is computed from the same count:

def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    set_count(count + 1)
    set_count(count + 1)  # count goes from 0 to 1, not 2
    return ()

Key presses that arrive together. Counterweight routes every event it has read before rendering again, and a terminal delivers keys together whenever they come faster than one per frame: fast typing, a held key repeating, or text pasted into a terminal without bracketed paste. Each key press's handler sees the same text:

text, set_text = use_state("")


def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    match event:
        case KeyPressed(key=key) if len(key) == 1:
            set_text(text + key)  # "abc" typed in one burst leaves text as "c"
            return ()
        case _:
            return None

This one hides from tests: an autopilot renders after each event it sends, so every key press there sees the latest text, and so does slow typing by hand. Write set_text(lambda t: t + key). For a text field, use_text_input does this for you, along with the cursor, the editing keys and pastes.

An effect that outlives its render. An effect closes over the values from the render that started it, and one with deps=() keeps them for as long as the component is mounted:

count, set_count = use_state(0)


async def tick() -> None:
    while True:
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
        set_count(count + 1)  # count stays at 1, since this count is always 0


use_effect(tick, deps=())

Pass a value only when the new state doesn't depend on the old, as in set_query("") to clear a field or set_selected(item.id) to select an item. Toggling a flag depends on it, so it takes a function too: toggle, as in set_open(toggle).

The setter is the same object on every render, so a handler that updates state only through functions captures nothing that goes stale, and can be built once with use_memo or passed to a memo component.

use_state(
    initial_value: Getter[T] | T,

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION initial_value

The initial value of the state. It can either be the initial value itself, or a zero-argument function that returns the initial value.

TYPE: Getter[T] | T

RETURNS DESCRIPTION T

The current value of the state (i.e., for the current render cycle).

Setter[T]

A function that can be called to update the value of the state (e.g., in an event handler). It can either be called with the new value of the state, or a function that takes the current value of the state and returns the new value of the state. When the new value depends on the current one, pass a function: a value computed from the state a render saw loses every update made since, such as from other key presses read before the next render (see Updating state from its previous value). If the value is not equal to the current of the state, Counterweight will trigger a render cycle. It is the same object on every render, so it can be left out of an effect's deps, and including it never reruns the effect. Once the component unmounts, calling it does nothing.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Controls are objects that can be returned from an element's on_input handler to instruct Counterweight to take some action during the render loop, such as gracefully quitting the application or playing the terminal "bell" sound.

A handler returns one control (return Quit()), or a tuple of controls, which Counterweight applies in order (return Bell(), Screenshot.to_file(path)), skipping any None in it, as merge skips None styles. Returning (), a tuple of no controls, says the handler handled the event with nothing more to do, and returning any control or tuple stops the event, as () does (see Events). Code outside a handler, such as an effect, sends controls with use_controls.

docs.title: Scrolling
docs.text: These controls scroll a scroll container. scroll_on_wheel returns ScrollBy for the wheel, and scroll_on_keys returns ScrollBy for the keys that scroll by a step or a page, and ScrollTo for Home and End. ScrollIntoView brings an element into view in every container above it: moving focus applies it to the newly focused element, use_text_area's handler returns it for the cursor's row, and the autocomplete recipe returns it for the highlighted match.

    x: int | None = None,
    y: int | None = None,

It applies to the layout of the next render, before that render paints, after anchoring and sticking to the end, and in order with the other scroll controls returned since the last render, so a handler that returns it beside a state change scrolls the content that change lays out. It does nothing if target names no mounted, visible scroll container then.

docs.text:
ScrollIntoView(
    target: ElementHandle | Subtree,
    block: ScrollAlignment = "start",
    inline: ScrollAlignment = "nearest",
)

Scroll each scroll container above the element target names so the element's border box is in view, from the innermost container out, as the web's scrollIntoView does, aligning it as block says vertically and as inline says horizontally, with the web's defaults. On each axis, "start" puts the element's start edge at the start edge of the container's view, "center" its center at the view's center, and "end" its end edge at the view's end edge. "nearest" does whichever of "start" and "end" scrolls least, and doesn't scroll at all if the element is already wholly in view, or covers the whole view. Each offset is clamped to the range its container scrolls through.

It applies as ScrollTo does, to the layout of the next render, so a handler that returns it beside a state change, such as moving a highlight through a long list, shows the scroll in the same frame as the change. The element target names is the one with that element handle in the next render, so an element handle moved onto a newly highlighted element names the new one. It does nothing if target names no mounted, visible element then, and it stops at an element with clip_to_screen, since no container above that element clips it.

docs.title: Handling Input
docs.text:
Div and Text elements take an on_input handler, which Counterweight calls with key presses, pastes, and mouse events, along with a Receiver describing the element the event is delivered to. A handler matches on the event, so one case can cover a key and a mouse event alike:

def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    match event:
        case KeyPressed(key=Key.Space) | MouseDown(button=1):
            set_is_open(toggle)
            return ()
        case _:
            return None

The library handlers cover the common cases, such as on_click for a press released inside the element, and scroll_on_wheel and scroll_on_keys for a scroll container.

A handler's return value says whether the event was its to handle:

  • None means it wasn't, and the event bubbles on to the element's parent.
  • Anything else means it was, and the event stops there. That is a control for Counterweight to apply (return Quit()), a tuple of controls applied in order (return Bell(), Screenshot.to_file(path)), or (), a tuple of no controls, when there's nothing else to do. A None inside a tuple is skipped, so a control can be conditional (return Bell() if is_full else None, Screenshot.to_file(path)), and a tuple still stops the event when every item in it is None.

Return () (or the controls) from every case that does something, so an ancestor that handles the same event doesn't act on it too.

Don't chain handlers with or

() is falsy, so handler_a(event, receiver) or handler_b(event, receiver) calls handler_b even when handler_a handled the event. Compose handlers with first and each instead.

A handler that only cares about keys still receives mouse events, including every movement of the pointer over its element. One that matches many keys can return early on anything else, which keeps its cases about keys alone:

def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    if not isinstance(event, KeyPressed):
        return None

    match event.key:
        case Key.ControlC:
            return Quit()
        case Key.Tab:
            set_tab(lambda t: (t + 1) % len(TABS))
            return ()
        case _:
            return None

The receiver describes the element the event is delivered to. Its rectangles tell a handler where in the element a mouse event landed:

def on_input(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    match event:
        case MouseDown(absolute=position, button=1):
            set_clicked(receiver.relative(position))
            return ()
        case _:
            return None

Its is_focused, focus_handle and subtree serve the focus handlers: whether the element is focused, the focus handle that names its component if the component is focusable, and the element and its descendants, for moving focus among them. The subtree also names the element for the scroll controls, and scroll says how far the element is scrolled if it's a scroll container, which scroll_on_keys reads to tell how far a page is and whether it's reached an end.

A handler that calls another, as the autocomplete recipe calls a text field's, reads what it returned with response_controls, which turns any response into a tuple of controls, or None if the inner handler didn't handle the event.

docs.title: Routing Input Events
docs.text: Each input event has one target element. Counterweight calls the target's on_input handler, then each of its ancestors' in turn, up to the root component's element, until one returns something other than None. The ancestors are the element tree's, not the screen's, so an absolutely positioned child bubbles to its parent even where it's drawn outside it. Each element receives the same event, with its own receiver: a parent's rects are its own, and its is_target is False.

docs.title: Key Presses
docs.text:
The target of a key press is the focused element, or the root component's element when nothing is focused. A key press bubbles from the focused element through its ancestors, and never reaches its siblings, so two components that handle the same keys don't both act on one press. When nothing is focused, only the root component's handler receives key presses, and its receiver's is_target is True, though its is_focused is False.

A focusable component's key handler goes on the element the component returns, which is the one that's focused. Handlers on the elements inside it never receive key presses, and a component deep in the tree can't own a global shortcut: put the shortcut on the root component's element, which every key press bubbles to unless a handler on the way stops it.

docs.title: Mouse Events
docs.text: The target of a mouse event is the element drawn on top at the pointer: the last element in paint order whose border box contains it. An element's margin isn't part of it, so a press in a margin reaches whatever lies beneath. A pointer over none of the root component's elements, when the root's element is smaller than the terminal, targets the root's element, though its rectangles don't contain the pointer.

docs.title: Presses
docs.text:
A press runs from the first mouse button going down to the last one coming up, as in the web's Pointer Events. Its first MouseDown is routed like any mouse event, and the element whose handler stops it captures the press: the press's later events, each MouseMoved with a button held and each MouseDown and MouseUp of the buttons pressed and released while it lasts, go to that element alone, as their target, wherever the pointer is, and stop there whatever its handler returns. A second button pressed during a press joins it rather than starting a new one, so a handler that acts on one button matches on button, as on_click does for button 1. So a drag keeps reaching the element it started on however fast the pointer moves, and a release outside the element still reaches it, which a handler can tell from its receiver's rectangles.

The rest of a press that nothing stopped, or whose element has since unmounted, reaches no handler, and neither does a MouseUp for a button the press doesn't hold, so an element never receives the end of a press it didn't see begin: a release over a button after a press somewhere else doesn't click it. A handler that wants a press's moves stops its MouseDown, even with nothing to do for it:

def on_input(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    match event:
        case MouseDown(button=1):
            return ()
        case MouseMoved(absolute=position, button=1):
            set_end(receiver.relative(position))
            return ()
        case _:
            return None

A MouseMoved with no button held ends a press whose release the terminal never reported, such as when focus moves to another window mid-drag, and so does a MouseDown for a button the press already holds. Both are routed by the pointer's position, and the MouseDown starts a new press. Scroll wheel events aren't part of a press, so they always target the element under the pointer, even mid-drag.

Since the press goes to whichever element stops its MouseDown, the innermost element with a handler for presses owns the whole press: a press on a button inside a draggable panel clicks the button and doesn't drag the panel. on_click builds a handler for the commonest case.

docs.title: Handling Keyboard Events
docs.text: Each time a key is pressed, Counterweight emits a KeyPressed event that holds which key was pressed, and routes it to the focused element. Enter and Ctrl+J are different keys, Key.Enter and Key.ControlJ, so a text area can insert a line break on Ctrl+J while Enter submits a form.

docs.title: counterweight.events.KeyPressed dataclass
docs.text: KeyPressed(key: str)

docs.title: key instance-attribute
docs.text:
key: str

The Key for a control or special key (Key.Enter, Key.Up, Key.F1), or for one pressed with Alt (Key.AltEnter, Key.AltUp, Key.ControlAltA), the text typed: one grapheme cluster, such as "a", "é" or "👩‍💻", or alt+ and the text, for text typed with Alt, such as "alt+b" or "alt+B" (Alt with Shift and B). Text pasted in a terminal without bracketed paste arrives as a key press per grapheme cluster; in one with it, the text arrives as one Pasted.

docs.title: Keys pressed with Alt
docs.text:
Terminals send a key pressed with Alt as ESC followed by what the key sends on its own (xterm's metaSendsEscape, which most terminals do by default), and Counterweight reads the two as one key press: Key.AltEnter for Alt+Enter, Key.AltBackspace for Alt+Backspace, Key.ControlAltA for Ctrl+Alt+A, and "alt+b" for Alt+B, which is alt+ and the text the key types, so Alt+Shift+B is "alt+B". Arrow, navigation and function keys pressed with Alt are Key.AltUp, Key.AltPageDown, Key.AltF1 and so on, whether the terminal sends Alt in their escape sequence, as xterm does, or as an ESC before it, as rxvt does.

def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    match event:
        case KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter):
            send()
            return ()
        case KeyPressed(key="alt+n"):
            start_new_chat()
            return ()
        case _:
            return None

The DOM's KeyboardEvent reports Alt in altKey, beside a key that doesn't change, as Counterweight's mouse events report it in is_alt_held. A key press names Alt in its key instead, as it names Control and Shift (Key.ControlLeft, Key.ShiftUp), so a handler that matches Key.Enter doesn't also take Alt+Enter, and a text field never types the b of Alt+B, since text is always one grapheme cluster, and "alt+b" isn't.

An Escape pressed on its own and then a key sends the same bytes as Alt with the key, so Counterweight tells them apart by time, as terminal programs do: an ESC at the end of the input that has arrived waits up to 50 milliseconds for more, as it waits for the rest of an escape sequence, and is Alt with the key that arrives in that time, or the Escape key once it passes. Two ESCs are two presses of Escape rather than Alt+Escape, so pressing Escape twice quickly is never lost. ESC [ and ESC O also begin escape sequences, so Alt+[ and Alt+Shift+O arrive as "alt+[" and "alt+O" only when no key follows them within that time.

A terminal that doesn't send Alt as an escape never sends these keys. One that sets the high bit of the byte for Alt instead (xterm with metaSendsEscape off and eightBitInput on) sends another character, as does macOS's Option key, which types characters such as ∫ for Option+B unless the terminal is set to send it as Meta (Terminal.app's "Use Option as Meta key", or iTerm2's "Esc+" for the Option key). Run counterweight check-input to see which events a terminal's keys arrive as.

docs.title: Keys the terminal would act on
docs.text:
A terminal acts on a few Ctrl keys itself unless the program reading it asks otherwise: Ctrl+C and Ctrl+\ send signals that interrupt and kill the program, Ctrl+Z one that stops it, and Ctrl+S and Ctrl+Q pause and resume its output. Counterweight asks otherwise, as tmux does: it reads the terminal raw, so every one of those keys arrives as a key press (Key.ControlC, Key.ControlBackslash, Key.ControlZ, Key.ControlS and Key.ControlQ), and an editor can save on Ctrl+S, or an app can pass Ctrl+C on to a program it runs.

A key press that no handler on its path claims then takes its default from app's unclaimed_keys, as a browser takes a key's default action unless a listener prevents it. DEFAULT_UNCLAIMED_KEYS gives Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z what they'd do in a terminal: Ctrl+C quits, and Ctrl+Z suspends the app as a shell job, with Suspend.to_shell(), until the shell resumes it with fg. A handler that claims one of them keeps it from taking its default, and unclaimed_keys changes the defaults for the whole app:

# No defaults: Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z do nothing unless a handler handles them.
asyncio.run(app(root(), unclaimed_keys={}))

# Ctrl+Q quits too, as well as Ctrl+C.
asyncio.run(app(root(), unclaimed_keys=DEFAULT_UNCLAIMED_KEYS | {Key.ControlQ: Quit()}))

A key the terminal would turn into a signal only does something once the app reads it, so an app whose render loop is stuck, such as in a handler that never returns, can't be quit with Ctrl+C. Stop it from outside with kill: the first interrupt quits it as Ctrl+C would, and a second one goes to whatever handled interrupts before the app started. A focused component that claims every key, such as one that passes keys on to a program, takes Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z too, so an app that has one needs another way to quit, such as a key that it doesn't claim.

docs.title: counterweight.app.DEFAULT_UNCLAIMED_KEYS module-attribute
docs.text:
DEFAULT_UNCLAIMED_KEYS: Mapping[str, AnyControl] = (
    frozendict(
        {
            Key.ControlC: Quit(),
            Key.ControlZ: Suspend.to_shell(),
        }
    )
)

What app does with a key press no handler claims, by default: Ctrl+C quits, and Ctrl+Z suspends the application as a shell job, as they do to a program in a terminal.

docs.title: Handling Pastes
docs.text: Counterweight turns on the terminal's bracketed paste mode, so text pasted into the terminal arrives as one Pasted event holding all of it, rather than as a key press per character, and it's routed to the focused element, as a key press is. A handler that only matches key presses never sees it, so a paste can't trigger a binding by holding the binding's key. use_text_input and use_text_area insert it in one edit. Terminals without bracketed paste send pasted text as typed keys, with its line breaks as Enter, or as Ctrl+J from a terminal that sends them as line feeds.

docs.title: Handling Mouse Events
docs.text:
Each time the state of the mouse changes, Counterweight emits a single mouse event, one of MouseMoved, MouseDown, MouseUp, MouseScrolledDown, MouseScrolledUp, MouseScrolledLeft, or MouseScrolledRight.

Each mouse event says which modifier keys were held, as the DOM's MouseEvent does, in is_shift_held, is_alt_held and is_control_held, so a handler can match a modified press or turn of the wheel:

def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    match event:
        case MouseDown(button=1, is_control_held=True):
            set_selected(lambda selected: selected ^ {item})
            return ()
        case MouseDown(button=1):
            set_selected({item})
            return ()
        case _:
            return None

Terminals keep some combinations for themselves and never report them to the app: most select text for Shift with a press, even while the app tracks the mouse, and some scroll their own scrollback for Shift with the wheel or open links for Control with a press. So a modifier works best as a shortcut for something the app offers another way too. counterweight check-input --mouse shows the events a terminal reports.

For example, consider the following series of mouse actions and corresponding events:

Action Event Mouse starts at position (0, 0) No event emitted Mouse moves to position (1, 0) MouseMoved(absolute=Position(x=1, y=0), button=None) Mouse button 1 is pressed MouseDown(absolute=Position(x=1, y=0), button=1) Mouse moves to position (1, 1) MouseMoved(absolute=Position(x=1, y=1), button=1) Mouse button 1 is released MouseUp(absolute=Position(x=1, y=1), button=1) Mouse button 3 is pressed MouseDown(absolute=Position(x=1, y=1), button=3) Mouse moves to position (2, 2) and mouse button 3 is released simultaneously MouseUp(absolute=Position(x=2, y=2), button=3)

Mouse Button Identifiers

Mouse buttons are identified by numbers instead of names (e.g., "left", "middle", "right") because the button numbers are the same regardless of whether the mouse is configured for left-handed or right-handed use.

Number Button for Right-Handed Mouse Button for Left-Handed Mouse 1 Left Right 2 Middle Middle 3 Right Left 8 Back Back 9 Forward Forward

You should always use the numbers instead of names to refer to mouse buttons to ensure that your application works as expected for both left-handed and right-handed users.

use_mouse vs. on_input

use_mouse and an element's on_input handler both see the mouse, but use_mouse is a hook and on_input is an event handler. use_mouse is more efficient when a component depends only on the current state of the mouse (e.g., the current position, or whether a button is currently pressed), while on_input is more convenient when a component needs to respond to changes in the mouse state, (e.g., a button release MouseUp). use_mouse sees every change, while a handler sees only the events routed to its element.

docs.title: Handlers
docs.text:
counterweight.handlers holds handlers for common behaviors, and combinators that compose several handlers into the one an element's on_input takes. Nothing happens to an input event unless a handler on its path does it, so a behavior an element should have is a handler composed onto it.

from counterweight.handlers import each, first, on_click

# A button that sends a message when clicked.
Text(content="Send", on_input=on_click(send))

# A row that selects itself when clicked, and handles keys while focused
# (it's the top-level element of a component that calls use_focus).
Div(children=..., on_input=first(row_keys, on_click(select)))

Each library handler is a pure function of the event and the receiver, so it can be tested by calling it, without running an app.

docs.title: Composing Handlers
docs.text: first tries handlers in order and stops at the first that handles the event, so the order states their precedence. In first(on_click(open_menu), drag_panel), drag_panel never sees a button 1 press, which on_click handles. each runs every handler and combines their controls, which is how two handlers that both act on a MouseDown share one element: only the element that stops a press's first MouseDown receives the rest of it, so they can't sit on an element and its parent.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.first
docs.text:
first(*handlers: InputHandler) -> InputHandler

A handler that calls each of handlers in turn with the same event and receiver, and returns the first response that isn't None, () included, without calling the rest. It returns None if none of them responds.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.each
docs.text:
each(*handlers: InputHandler) -> InputHandler

A handler that calls every one of handlers with the same event and receiver. If any responds with something other than None, it returns a tuple of every control they returned, in the order of handlers, which is () if every response was (). It returns None if none of them responds.

docs.title: Headless Components
docs.text:
A headless component returns its behavior as a handler, on_input, for the component to put on the element it returns, composed with any others:

field = use_text_input(value, set_value)
Text(content=..., on_input=first(field.on_input, submit_on_enter, focus_receiver_on_press))

The hook's handler returns None for the keys it doesn't edit with, such as Enter and Tab, so a handler after it in first, or on an ancestor, gets them.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.on_click
docs.text:
on_click(
    action: Callable[[], InputResponse],
) -> InputHandler

A handler that claims a button 1 MouseDown, and so every later event of the press, and on the press's MouseUp, calls action if the release is over the element: inside its border box, and inside its clip, where it's painted. It returns the controls action returns, or () if action returns None. It returns None for anything else, such as a key or a pointer move with no button held.

docs.title: Focus
docs.text:
Nothing moves focus unless a handler returns a control that does, so Tab navigation and click-to-focus are handlers an app composes in:

from counterweight.handlers import clear_focus, each, first, focus_receiver_on_press, on_click, tab_focus

# The root: Tab navigation, after the app's own shortcuts,
# and a blur for presses that nothing below the root claims.
Div(children=..., on_input=first(app_shortcuts, tab_focus, clear_focus))

# A focusable button. Both handlers claim the press, so each runs both.
focus = use_focus()
Text(content="Send", style=ring if focus.is_focused else plain, on_input=each(on_click(send), focus_receiver_on_press))

# A button that isn't focusable, and blurs whatever is when it's clicked.
Text(content="Clear", on_input=each(on_click(clear), clear_focus))

tab_focus moves within the element it's attached to, so on the root component's element it moves through the whole tree, and on a dialog's element it keeps Tab inside the dialog. A focused component that wants Tab for itself, such as a code editor that indents with it, handles it and returns (), so it never bubbles to tab_focus. The headless text components don't: they pass Tab on, so it moves focus out of them.

Every handler here that acts on a press claims its MouseDown, so of nested elements with press handlers, the innermost takes the press: with focus_receiver_on_press on nested focusable components, a press focuses the innermost one under the pointer. A press on a non-focusable element that claims presses, such as a button made with on_click, leaves focus where it was, unless the element composes clear_focus in too.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.tab_focus
docs.text:
tab_focus(
    event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver
) -> InputResponse

A handler that moves focus to the next focusable component inside its element for Tab, and to the previous one for Shift+Tab, wrapping at the ends. On the root component's element it moves through the whole tree; on a modal's, it keeps Tab inside the modal. It returns None for anything else.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.focus_receiver_on_press
docs.text:
focus_receiver_on_press(
    event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver
) -> InputResponse

A handler that claims a MouseDown and focuses the component whose element received it. It goes on the element a focusable component returns, the one whose receiver carries its focus_handle. It returns None for anything else.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

For a MouseDown whose receiver has no focus_handle, because the component never called use_focus, or the handler is on an inner element.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.focus_on_press
docs.text:
focus_on_press(handle: FocusHandle) -> InputHandler

A handler that claims a MouseDown and focuses the component with handle, such as a label focusing the input beside it, whatever element received the press. It returns None for anything else.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.clear_focus
docs.text:
clear_focus(
    event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver
) -> InputResponse

A handler that claims a MouseDown and clears focus. On the root component's element it blurs on a press nothing below it claimed; composed into a non-focusable element's own press handler, it blurs on the presses that element claims. It returns None for anything else.

docs.title: Scrolling
docs.text:
Nothing scrolls a scroll container unless a handler returns a control that does, so a container the wheel scrolls composes scroll_on_wheel in, and one the keyboard scrolls composes scroll_on_keys in, on a focusable component's element:

from counterweight.handlers import first, scroll_on_keys, scroll_on_wheel

use_focus()
Div(style=fill(1) | col | overflow_y_scroll, on_input=first(scroll_on_keys(), scroll_on_wheel()), children=...)

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.scroll_on_wheel
docs.text:
scroll_on_wheel(lines: int = 3) -> InputHandler

A handler that scrolls the scroll container it's on by lines toward the wheel's direction for each MouseScrolledUp, MouseScrolledDown, MouseScrolledLeft and MouseScrolledRight, which is three lines by default, as desktop platforms scroll for each notch of the wheel. With Shift held, the vertical wheel scrolls sideways, as browsers on Windows and Linux do: up scrolls left and down scrolls right. It returns None for a wheel event that would move the container past the end of its range, so the event bubbles to the next scroll container out, as the web chains scrolling, and for anything else.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

For a wheel event whose receiver isn't a scroll container.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.scroll_on_keys
docs.text:
scroll_on_keys(page: float = PAGE_FRACTION) -> InputHandler

A handler that scrolls the scroll container it's on for the keys that scroll a page in a browser: Up and Down by a row, Left and Right by a column, PageUp and PageDown by page times the height of the view (see page_down), and Home and End to the start and the end of the content. A key press reaches it while the container, or an element inside it, is focused, so the container is usually the top-level element of a component that calls use_focus, and a focused element inside that handles a key itself stops it first. It returns None for a key that would move the container past the end of its range, so the key bubbles to the next scroll container out, as scroll_on_wheel does with the wheel, and for anything else.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

If page isn't positive, and for one of those keys when its receiver isn't a scroll container.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.page_down
docs.text:
page_down(
    target: ElementHandle | Subtree,
    scroll: Scroll,
    fraction: float = PAGE_FRACTION,
) -> ScrollBy

The ScrollBy that scrolls the scroll container target names, scrolled as scroll says, down by fraction of the height of its view, rounded down, and at least one row.

The default is Chrome's, so on a 24-row view a page is 21 rows, and 3 stay in view. fraction=0.5 is less's half page for d, and fraction=1.0 its whole page for Space, with nothing kept.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

If fraction isn't positive.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.page_up
docs.text:
page_up(
    target: ElementHandle | Subtree,
    scroll: Scroll,
    fraction: float = PAGE_FRACTION,
) -> ScrollBy

The ScrollBy that scrolls the scroll container target names up by a page, as page_down scrolls it down.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

If fraction isn't positive.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
These pages show how to get each layout effect, with every technique that achieves it, shown as code beside its screenshot. Where a technique has a well-known failure, the failure is shown too.

Each example labels its boxes with the styles that produced them. The examples are components; they all assume these imports:

import waxy

from counterweight.components import component
from counterweight.elements import Div, Text
from counterweight.styles.utilities import *

waxy provides the values that styles are built from, for the cases no utility covers.

To run one, call the component and pass the result to counterweight.app.app, as in app(root()).

Start with Choosing a layout model, which says when to reach for flexbox and when for grid. Then read How layout sizes things: the defaults it describes explain most surprises in the other pages.

docs.title: Alignment and Distribution
docs.text:
A container places its children along two axes. The justify_children_* utilities distribute them along the main axis (across a row, down a col), and the align_children_* utilities place them on the cross axis. A child can override its parent's cross-axis alignment for itself with align_self_*.

The examples on this page title each panel with this helper, which draws its text over the top border:

def title(content: str) -> Text:
    return Text(content=f" {content} ", style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border)

docs.title: Distributing children along the main axis
docs.text:
The justify_children_* utilities share out the free space a row or column has left over after its children take their sizes. Children that grow leave no free space, so these only matter when nothing claims it.

@component
def justify() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=row | justify | border,
                children=(
                    title(name),
                    Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="a"),
                    Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="bb"),
                    Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="ccc"),
                ),
            )
            for name, justify in (
                ("justify_children_start", justify_children_start),
                ("justify_children_center", justify_children_center),
                ("justify_children_end", justify_children_end),
                ("justify_children_space_between", justify_children_space_between),
                ("justify_children_space_around", justify_children_space_around),
                ("justify_children_space_evenly", justify_children_space_evenly),
            )
        ),
    )

def align() -> Div:

        style=row,

docs.title: Centering a box
docs.text:
Center a box on both axes with center_children, which is justify_children_center | align_children_center. It works in a grid too: there it centers the grid's tracks, and a grid with no template sizes its one track to fit its lone child. To center a box over other content rather than among it, see A dialog centered over the app.

@component
def center() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | center_children | fill(1) | border,
                children=(title("flexbox"), Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="centered")),
            ),
            Div(
                style=display_grid | center_children | fill(1) | border,
                children=(title("grid"), Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="centered")),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Content larger than its container
docs.text:
The *_center and *_end utilities are CSS's safe alignments: content too large for its container starts at the container's start edge and overflows only past the end, so its beginning stays in view. Each has an *_unsafe counterpart with CSS's default behavior, which centers or end-aligns the content anyway and overflows past the start edge too. These containers are fill(1) items, which clip what overflows them, so the unsafe one cuts off the content's beginning as well as its end.

@component
def overflow() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=col | justify | fill(1) | border,
                children=(title(name), Text(content=TALL)),
            )
            for name, justify in (
                ("justify_children_center", justify_children_center),
                ("justify_children_center_unsafe", justify_children_center_unsafe),
            )
        ),
    )

docs.title: App Shells
docs.text: These whole-screen layouts combine the techniques from the other pages. Each root fills the screen and is split with flexbox: fixed parts take a length or their content's size, and the part that fills takes fill(1). When that part holds more than fits, such as a log, a transcript or a long document, make it a scroll container with overflow_y_scroll, so its content scrolls inside it while the fixed parts stay put. Splitting space shows the same splits with grid, and Choosing a layout model builds a whole shell both ways.

docs.title: Choosing a Layout Model
docs.text: The other pages in this section show how to get each effect with flexbox and with grid. This one helps you decide which of the two to use for a container.

docs.title: Who owns the sizes
docs.text:
Flexbox and grid can build most of the same layouts. What differs is where the sizes are written. In a grid, the parent lists them as track templates, and the children fill the tracks in order. In flexbox, each child carries its own size, and the parent only sets the direction. In short, grid is top-down and flexbox is bottom-up.

Here is one app shell built both ways, with the same result:

FlexboxGrid 
@component
def shell_flex() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | fill(1),
                children=(
                    Text(style=length(20) | border, content="sidebar:\nlength(20)"),
                    Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="main:\nfill(1)"),
                ),
            ),
            Text(style=length(1) | text_bg("slate", 700), content=" status: length(1)"),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌──────────────────┐┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│sidebar:          ││main:                                 │
│length(20)        ││fill(1)                               │
│                  ││                                      │
│                  ││                                      │
│                  ││                                      │
└──────────────────┘└──────────────────────────────────────┘

@component
def shell_grid() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(20, fr(1)) | grid_template_rows(fr(1), 1),
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="sidebar:\n20"),
            Text(style=border, content="main:\nfr(1)"),
            Text(style=grid_column(1, span(2)) | text_bg("slate", 700), content=" status: 1"),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌──────────────────┐┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│sidebar:          ││main:                                 │
│20                ││fr(1)                                 │
│                  ││                                      │
│                  ││                                      │
│                  ││                                      │
└──────────────────┘└──────────────────────────────────────┘

So choose by which should own the sizes: the container, or each child.

docs.title: Flexbox or grid?
docs.text:
Use grid when the container owns the arrangement: a fixed set of slots known up front, such as an app shell or a dashboard, or columns that must line up across rows.

Grid costs locality. A child's size lives on its parent, away from the component that draws it, and children fill the tracks in order, so a child the template didn't plan for starts a new implicit row, and the rows split the height between them. A flexbox row takes the same extra child as one more column. Auto flow shows how grid adds the tracks.

GridFlexbox 
@component
def extra_child_grid() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(fr(1), fr(1)),
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="fr(1)"),
            Text(style=border, content="fr(1)"),
            Text(style=border, content="a third child"),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText

│fr(1)                ││fr(1)               │
└─────────────────────┘└────────────────────┘
┌─────────────────────┐                      
│a third child        │                      
└─────────────────────┘                      

@component
def extra_child_flex() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=(
            Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="fill(1)"),
            Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="fill(1)"),
            Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="fill(1)"),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌─────────────┐┌─────────────┐┌─────────────┐
│fill(1)      ││fill(1)      ││fill(1)      │
│             ││             ││             │
│             ││             ││             │
│             ││             ││             │
└─────────────┘└─────────────┘└─────────────┘

Use flexbox when each child owns its size: a variable number of children (lists, toolbars, tags), content-sized items, wrapping, or a component that keeps its size wherever it's placed, such as a sidebar that's always length(24).

Flexbox costs alignment across rows: two rows' columns line up only if each child in them repeats the same size. In a grid they line up for free, as in Dashboard tiles.

docs.title: Mixing them
docs.text:
The choice is per container, not per app. Any child of a grid can be a flexbox container, and any flexbox child can be a grid. A common split for a terminal app is a grid for the screen, whose panes are a fixed set known up front, and flexbox inside each pane, for the lists, toolbars and status items whose number varies. Here the grid places the panes, the sidebar is a col of items, and the status bar is a row that pushes its items to either end:

@component
def mixed() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(20, fr(1)) | grid_template_rows(fr(1), 1),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col | border,
                children=(Text(content="inbox"), Text(content="drafts"), Text(content="sent")),
            ),
            Text(style=border, content="main: fr(1)"),
            Div(
                style=row | justify_children_space_between | grid_column(1, span(2)),
                children=(
                    Text(style=text_bg("slate", 700), content=" status: row"),
                    Text(style=text_bg("slate", 700), content="justify_children_space_between "),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText

│inbox             ││main: fr(1)                           │
│drafts            ││                                      │
│sent              ││                                      │
│                  ││                                      │
│                  ││                                      │

docs.title: Coming from ratatui?
docs.text:
Ratatui splits an area by a list of constraints on the parent, and never lets content push back: it hands each widget a rectangle to draw into. Grid with fr tracks has the same structure, and the constraint utilities give the same sizes in flexbox, with each child holding its own constraint. A few things behave differently.

Conflicts overflow instead of giving way. Ratatui shrinks lower-priority constraints until the areas fit inside the parent, so Length(30) twice in 40 cells comes out 20 and 20. Flexbox has no priorities, and the constraint utilities don't shrink, so length(30) twice overflows, as in the top row below. Decide which child gives way and say so: shrink(1) lets a length shrink below its basis, as on both children in the bottom row, and fill(1) takes whatever is left, or nothing.

@component
def conflict() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | width(42) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=length(30) | border, content="length(30)"),
                    Text(style=length(30) | border, content="length(30)"),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | width(42) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=length(30) | shrink(1) | border, content="length(30)\n| shrink(1)"),
                    Text(style=length(30) | shrink(1) | border, content="length(30)\n| shrink(1)"),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

Percentages don't subtract gaps. Ratatui takes spacing out of the area first; a CSS percentage is a share of the whole parent, so two halves and a gap overflow. Use fill(1) for equal shares.

Flex::Legacy, which gives leftover space to the last constraint, has no counterpart. Put grow(1) on the child that should take it. The other Flex modes are the justify_children_* utilities of the same names, and ratatui's full-size cross axis is flexbox's default stretch (see Alignment and distribution).

docs.title: Clipping
docs.text: A box's content can be larger than the box. Its overflow, as in CSS's overflow, decides whether what doesn't fit is drawn anyway or cut off. This page covers cutting it off, how a box draws on its parent's border when its parent cuts things off, and how a box such as a dropdown escapes the clip altogether.

docs.title: Hiding overflow
docs.text:
By default a box's overflow is visible: children that don't fit are drawn past its padding box, over its border and whatever lies beyond. overflow_hidden clips them to its padding box instead, so nothing inside the box is drawn outside its border. overflow_scroll clips them the same way, and lets them scroll. A Text's lines overflow its box the same way, and overflow_hidden on the Text clips them to its own padding box (see Text in layout).

@component
def hidden() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2),
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=col,
                children=(
                    Div(
                        style=col | border | height(4) | width(20) | overflow,
                        children=tuple(Text(content=f"line {i}") for i in range(1, 7)),
                    ),
                    Text(content="below"),
                ),
            )
            for overflow in (overflow_visible, overflow_hidden)
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐
│line 1            │  │line 1            │
│line 2            │  │line 2            │
└line 3            ┘  └──────────────────┘
below                 below               
 line 5                                   
 line 6

Layout doesn't change: the clipped children are just as large, and only the part inside the box is drawn. The constraint utilities, length, percentage, ratio and fill, hide their box's overflow, so a constrained box always clips its children.

overflow_clip clips the same way. The two differ in layout, as they do in CSS: a flex item with overflow_hidden can shrink below its content's size, while one with overflow_clip keeps the content's size as its minimum, as a visible one does (see Content sets a minimum size).

docs.title: Clipping one axis
docs.text:
overflow_x_hidden clips only at the left and right of the padding box, and overflow_y_hidden only at the top and bottom. The overflow_x_* and overflow_y_* utilities each set one axis, so they combine with each other, as overflow_x_hidden | overflow_y_clip.

@component
def one_axis() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(8),
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=border | height(4) | width(16) | overflow,
                children=(Text(content=LINES, style=height(6)),),
            )
            for overflow in (overflow_x_hidden, overflow_y_hidden)
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐
│line 1 of a lo│        │line 1 of a lon
│line 2 of a lo│        │line 2 of a lon
└line 3 of a lo┘        └──────────────┘

docs.title: Clipping applies whatever the z
docs.text:
A clip cuts off everything inside the box, wherever it's positioned and however high its z, as on the web: a raised menu inside a box that hides its overflow is cut off at the box's padding box, unless it escapes every clip.

@component
def raised() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col | border | size(30, 5) | overflow_hidden,
                children=(
                    Text(content="File  Edit  View"),
                    Text(
                        content="Open…\nSave\nSave As…\nQuit",
                        style=z(1) | position_absolute | inset_top(1) | inset_left(0) | border | border_heavy,
                    ),
                ),
            ),
            Text(content="The menu is cut off inside the box's border,\nhowever high its z."),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌────────────────────────────┐                  
│File  Edit  View            │                  
│┏━━━━━━━━┓                  │                  
│┃Open…   ┃                  │                  
└────────────────────────────┘                  
The menu is cut off inside the box's border,    
however high its z.

Nested boxes that clip combine: a box inside two of them is drawn only where both let it.

docs.title: Drawing on the parent's border
docs.text:
A border title is positioned on its parent's border, outside the padding box, so a parent that hides its overflow clips it away. clip_to_border clips a box to its parent's border box instead, so it can draw on the border and is still cut off at the border's outer edge. clip_to_padding is the default.

@component
def clip_to() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=fill(1) | border | pad_x(1),
                children=(
                    Text(content=f" {name} ", style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip),
                    Text(content="fill(1) hides its overflow"),
                ),
            )
            for name, clip in (("clip_to_padding", clip_to_padding), ("clip_to_border", clip_to_border))
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌────────────────────────────┐┌─ clip_to_border ───────────┐
│ fill(1) hides its overflow ││ fill(1) hides its overflow │
└────────────────────────────┘└────────────────────────────┘

A parent whose overflow is visible clips nothing, so the two agree there, but a title that sets clip_to_border keeps working when its parent starts to clip. CSS has no equivalent property: its overflow-clip-margin widens the clip for every child of the box that sets it, where clip_to is set on the child, so a title can reach the border while the rest of the content stops at the padding box.

docs.title: Escaping every clip
docs.text:
A dropdown or an autocomplete list has to reach past the box it opens from, even when that box, or one around it, clips. clip_to_screen makes a box unclipped: no ancestor clips it, so only the edge of the screen cuts it off.

@component
def unclipped() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col | border | size(30, 5) | overflow_hidden,
                children=(
                    Text(content="File  Edit  View"),
                    Text(
                        content="Open…\nSave\nSave As…\nQuit",
                        style=z(1)
                        | position_absolute
                        | inset_top(1)
                        | inset_left(0)
                        | clip_to_screen
                        | border
                        | border_heavy,
                    ),
                ),
            ),
            Text(content="With clip_to_screen, the menu\nreaches past the box.", style=pad_left(11)),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌────────────────────────────┐                  
│File  Edit  View            │                  
│┏━━━━━━━━┓                  │                  
│┃Open…   ┃                  │                  
└┃Save    ┃──────────────────┘                  
 ┃Save As…┃With clip_to_screen, the menu        
 ┃Quit    ┃reaches past the box.

Everything else about an unclipped box is as usual. It's positioned against its parent, so the menu stays under its menu bar. It's drawn in the usual order, so it needs a z to draw over what follows it, and a box elsewhere with a higher z still covers it. Its own overflow still clips its children, whose clips start from the screen. It receives the mouse wherever it's drawn, including outside its ancestors.

On the web, a dropdown escapes a clip with position: fixed, which positions it against the viewport, so the page then has to work out where its anchor is, in script or with anchor positioning. An unclipped box keeps its parent as the box it's positioned against, so it's anchored already. The autocomplete recipe builds a complete one.

A scroll container clips to its padding box too, so in a list of titled panels that scrolls, a panel scrolled partly out of view loses the same part of its title as of its border. A title clipped to the screen would be drawn past the scroll container's edge instead.

PANELS = ElementHandle()


@component
def scrolled_panels() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | size(24, 6) | overflow_y_scroll,
        handle=PANELS,
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=border | border_lightrounded | height(3) | shrink(0),
                children=(
                    Text(
                        content=f" {title} ", style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border
                    ),
                    Text(content=body),
                ),
            )
            for title, body in (("web", "3 replicas"), ("worker", "8 replicas"), ("cron", "1 replica"))
        ),
    )

docs.title: Percentage insets and borders
docs.text:
Insets on an absolutely positioned box are measured from its parent's padding box, as in CSS, so inset_top=Percent(1.0) puts the box's top edge at the bottom of the padding box, which is the bottom border's row when the parent has a border.

below_parent = Style(layout=waxy.Style(position=waxy.Position.Absolute, inset_top=waxy.Percent(1.0)))


@component
def percent_inset() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=border | width(30) | pad_x(1),
        children=(
            Text(content="inset_top=Percent(1.0)"),
            Text(content=" on the border row ", style=below_parent | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Clipping and the mouse
docs.text:
A box receives the mouse only where it's drawn. Over a part of a box that's clipped away, mouse events go to whatever is drawn there instead, use_hovered reports the mouse outside the box, and on_click doesn't click it.

use_rects still reports each box whole, since a box that's partly clipped is still where layout put it. Its clip is the region the box's ancestors let it draw in, and its visible is the part of its border box inside that region, or None when none of it is.

docs.title: Grids and Wrapping
docs.text: display_grid lays a container's children out in rows and columns at once. The container lists its tracks with grid_template_columns and grid_template_rows, and each child fills the next free cell, or the cells it asks for. The examples on this page size every track with fr(1), one share of the grid's free space.

docs.title: Dashboard tiles
docs.text:
Equal tracks on both axes give a grid of equal tiles, and gap separates them.

@component
def tiles() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(fr(1), fr(1), fr(1)) | grid_template_rows(fr(1), fr(1)) | gap(1),
        children=tuple(Text(style=border, content=f"tile {n}") for n in range(1, 7)),
    )

docs.title: Cells spanning tracks
docs.text:
grid_column and grid_row place a child by grid line, counted from 1, and span(n) stretches it across n tracks. Children without a placement fill the cells that are left, in order.

Place a spanning child on both axes, as both are here. A child placed on rows alone is placed before one placed on columns alone, whatever their order among the children, so mixing the two can push a child into an extra row below the template.

@component
def spans() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(fr(1), fr(1), fr(1)) | grid_template_rows(fr(1), fr(1), fr(1)),
        children=(
            Text(
                style=grid_row(1) | grid_column(1, span(2)) | border | border_heavy,
                content="grid_row(1)\ngrid_column(1, span(2))",
            ),
            Text(
                style=grid_row(1, span(3)) | grid_column(3) | border | border_heavy,
                content="grid_row(\n  1, span(3),\n)\ngrid_column(3)",
            ),
            Text(style=border, content="auto"),
            Text(style=border, content="auto"),
            Text(style=border, content="auto"),
            Text(style=border, content="auto"),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Auto flow
docs.text:
Children beyond the template's cells get new tracks, which the grid adds as it needs them. By default, children fill each row in turn and the grid adds rows, like the seventh child on the left. grid_auto_flow_column fills each column in turn and adds columns instead.

@component
def auto_flow() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(fr(1), fr(1), fr(1)) | fill(1) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(
                        content=" grid_template_columns(fr(1), fr(1), fr(1)) ",
                        style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border,
                    ),
                    *(Text(style=border, content=str(n)) for n in range(1, 8)),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=display_grid
                | grid_template_rows(fr(1), fr(1), fr(1))
                | grid_auto_flow_column
                | fill(1)
                | border
                | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(
                        content=" grid_template_rows(fr(1), fr(1), fr(1)) ",
                        style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border,
                    ),
                    Text(
                        content=" grid_auto_flow_column ",
                        style=position_absolute | inset_bottom(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border,
                    ),
                    *(Text(style=border, content=str(n)) for n in range(1, 8)),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.text:

@component
def wrap() -> Div:

        style=row | flex_wrap | align_children_start | gap_width(1),
        children=tuple(Text(style=border | pad_x(1), content=tag) for tag in TAGS),

docs.title: How Layout Sizes Things
docs.text:
Counterweight lays out elements with Taffy, which implements CSS flexbox and grid with their CSS defaults:

  • flex_direction is row.
  • flex_grow is 0, so children don't grow into free space on the main axis.
  • flex_shrink is 1, so children shrink when they don't fit.
  • align_items is stretch, so children fill their parent on the cross axis.
  • Sizes are border-box: a width includes the border and padding.

Together, these mean a child takes its content's size along its parent's direction, and its parent's full size across it.

docs.title: Children take their content size along the main axis
docs.text:
In a row, each child is as wide as its content and as tall as the row:

@component
def row_defaults() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="one"),
            Text(style=border, content="two two"),
            Text(style=border, content="three three three"),
        ),
    )

│   ││       ││                 │

The space to the right is free space that no child claimed. Splitting space shows how to hand it out.

docs.text:
In a col, the axes swap: each child is as tall as its content and as wide as the column.

@component
def col_defaults() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="one"),
            Text(style=border, content="two two"),
            Text(style=border, content="three three three"),

docs.title: The root fills the screen
docs.text:
The app places the root component in a grid cell the size of the terminal, and the root stretches to fill it, whatever its content. Content wider than the terminal can't widen the root: the wide line overflows the root, drawing over its border, and the edge of the screen cuts it off. overflow_hidden on the root would clip it at the root's padding box instead.

@component
def root_fills_screen() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_heavy,
        children=(Text(content="root: col | border | border_heavy"), Text(content=WIDE)),
    )

docs.title: Content sets a minimum size
docs.text:
A flex item can't shrink below its content's minimum size, which CSS calls the automatic minimum size. For a Text that doesn't wrap, that minimum is the whole line; for one that wraps, it's the widest word. In the top row below, two grow(1) children with long lines can't take half the row each, so they overflow it.

fill(1) has no automatic minimum, so in the bottom row the same two children split the row evenly. It hides the child's overflow, and CSS gives a box that hides its overflow a minimum size of zero. Hiding its overflow also clips each Text's line at its own padding box. min_width(0) (or min_height(0) in a col) lowers the minimum the same way on its own axis, but leaves the overflow visible, so each line would run past its box.

@component
def automatic_minimum() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=grow(1) | border, content=LONG),
                    Text(style=grow(1) | border, content=LONG),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=fill(1) | border, content=LONG),
                    Text(style=fill(1) | border, content=LONG),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Text doesn't wrap unless asked to
docs.text:
A Text renders each line of its content on one row. A line wider than the box overflows it, as text does in CSS, drawing over the box's border and past it, as in the top box below. overflow_hidden clips the line at the box's padding box, as in the middle one, and a wrap mode such as text_wrap_stable breaks lines to fit the box's width instead, as in the bottom one. Text in layout shows how wrapping text sizes itself, and Text wrapping compares the wrap modes.

@component
def wrapping() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(style=width(24) | border, content=PARAGRAPH),
            Text(style=width(24) | border | overflow_hidden, content=PARAGRAPH),
            Text(style=width(24) | border | text_wrap_stable, content=PARAGRAPH),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Layering
docs.text: Most boxes sit where layout puts them, side by side. Positioning moves a box off that spot, so it can overlap others, and z decides which of the overlapping boxes is drawn on top.

docs.title: Relative positioning
docs.text:
position_relative with insets moves a box from where layout placed it, without moving anything else: its siblings keep the space it would have taken. Insets are measured in cells, and inset_top(2) moves the box down two rows.

def relative() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | align_children_start | gap(3),
        children=(

            Text(

                content="position_relative\ninset_top(2)\ninset_left(2)",
            ),
            Text(style=border, content="third"),

docs.title: Controlling overlap with z
docs.text:
Where boxes overlap, the one with the higher z is drawn on top. Boxes with equal z are drawn in the order they appear in the tree, each parent before its children, and a box that sets no z counts as 0.

@component
def root() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(
                style=z(1)
                | position_absolute
                | inset_left(6)
                | inset_top(6)
                | border
                | border_lightrounded
                | margin(1)
                | margin_color("purple", 600),
                content="z = +1",
            ),
            Text(
                style=z(0)
                | position_absolute
                | inset_left(4)
                | inset_top(3)
                | border
                | border_lightrounded
                | margin(1)
                | margin_color("teal", 600),
                content="z =  0",
            ),
            Text(
                style=z(-1)
                | position_absolute
                | inset_left(0)
                | inset_top(0)
                | border
                | border_lightrounded
                | margin(1)
                | margin_color("red", 600),
                content="z = -1",
            ),
            Text(
                style=z(2)
                | position_absolute
                | inset_left(13)
                | inset_top(3)
                | border
                | border_lightrounded
                | margin(1)
                | margin_color("amber", 600),
                content="z = +2",

docs.title: Stacking contexts
docs.text:
z only orders boxes within a stacking context, as CSS's z-index does. A box that sets z, z(0) included, forms one: it and everything inside it are drawn together, as one layer at its z, and the z of a box inside it orders that box only among the others inside it. A box that sets no z forms none, so the boxes inside it are layered alongside it, among the boxes of the nearest stacking context around it. The app's root always forms one.

So a box is always drawn beneath the boxes inside it, whatever z they set. A negative z puts a box beneath the other boxes of its stacking context, but still over the box that forms the context.

A z(1) dropdown inside a toolbar that sets no z joins the stacking context around the toolbar, so it's drawn over the content below the toolbar:

def menu_bar(toolbar_style: Style) -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=toolbar_style | row | gap(2) | border | pad_x(1),
                children=(
                    Text(content="file"),
                    Text(content="edit"),
                    Text(
                        style=z(1) | position_absolute | inset_top(2) | inset_left(0) | border | border_heavy,
                        content="new\nopen\nsave\nquit",
                    ),
                ),
            ),
            Text(style=border, content="The page's content"),
        ),
    )


@component
def dropdown_escapes() -> Div:
    return menu_bar(toolbar_style=Style())


@component
def dropdown_scoped() -> Div:
    return menu_bar(toolbar_style=z(0))

The whole toolbar is drawn at 0, and the page's content, which comes after it in the tree, is drawn over the dropdown, leaving only the part of the dropdown that hangs below the page visible.

docs.title: A dialog centered over the app
docs.text:
To center a box over its parent, as CSS does, position it absolutely with insets of 0, auto margins, and a fit-content size. The insets make its whole parent the space to place it in, the fit-content size keeps it as small as its content, and the auto margins split the space left over evenly on each side, whether or not the parent centers its children. A margin paints nothing unless its element sets margin_color, so the app's content shows around the dialog. The dialog is drawn over the content because it comes after it; a dialog that comes earlier in the tree needs a higher z.

An absolutely positioned box is always placed in its own parent, never a more distant ancestor or the screen, so a dialog centers over the whole app only when it's a child of an element that fills the screen, such as the root component's element here. A dialog rendered deeper in the tree centers over its own parent.

dialog_box = position_absolute | inset(0) | margin_auto | fit_content_width | fit_content_height


@component
def dialog() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="header"),
            Text(
                style=fill(1) | border | text_wrap_stable,
                content="The app's content stays where it is, and the dialog draws over it. " * 4,
            ),
            Text(
                style=dialog_box | border | border_double | pad_x(2) | pad_y(1),
                content="a dialog centered over the app",
            ),
        ),
    )

Known issue: parents with a border, and grids

The layout engine, Taffy, mismeasures auto margins on an absolutely positioned box in two kinds of parent. In a flex parent with a border, the dialog lands one cell right of and below center, because the space its margins split includes the parent's border. In a grid parent, the auto margins are ignored, so the dialog sits at the parent's top-left corner. A parent with padding and no border centers it correctly.

docs.title: A badge pinned to a corner
docs.text:
Negative insets reach past the parent's padding box onto its border. inset_top(-1) puts a box on the top border, and inset_right(-1) on the right border. clip_to_border keeps the badges visible if the parent hides its overflow.

@component

docs.title: Scrolling
docs.text: A box whose overflow is Scroll is a scroll container: its content can be larger than it, and it shows the part its offset scrolls into view. This page covers making one, scrolling it with the wheel, the keyboard and from handlers, scrolling an element into view, and reading how far it's scrolled. Clipping covers how a scroll container cuts off what's outside its padding box, which it does as a box with hidden overflow does.

docs.title: Scroll areas
docs.text:
Most scrolling boxes want the same things: the wheel and the keys scroll them, Tab and a click focus them, as browsers make a scroll container focusable, and a style that scrolls even beside a constraint utility that hides overflow. use_scroll_area gives a component all of those, and leaves drawing it to the component, and scroll_area is a bordered box built on it:

SOURCE = (
    "def deploy(image: str, steps: tuple[int, ...] = (10, 50, 100)) -> None:",
    "    for percent in steps:",
    "        shift_traffic(image, percent)",
)


@component
def panes() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(1),
        on_input=tab_focus,
        children=(
            scroll_area(
                tuple(Text(content=event) for event in EVENTS),
                style=size(24, 6),
                auto_focus=True,
            ),
            scroll_area(
                tuple(Text(content=line) for line in SOURCE),
                axis="x",
                style=size(24, 6),
            ),
        ),
    )

The rest of this page covers the pieces they're built from, for a box that needs something they don't do.

docs.title: Scroll containers
docs.text:
overflow_scroll makes a box a scroll container on both axes, and overflow_x_scroll and overflow_y_scroll on one, as CSS's overflow: scroll does. On an axis it scrolls, the box clips its children to its padding box, and moves them up and left by its offset.

Counterweight holds each scroll container's offset, as a browser holds an element's scrollTop, so a box scrolls without any state in the component that renders it. It starts at 0, the start of the content. After every layout, it moves to keep the content in view where it was (see Keeping the content in view), and is clamped to how far the content reaches, so when the content shrinks, the box scrolls back as far as it has to. A scroll container that unmounts or is hidden loses its offset, and starts at 0 again when it comes back.

How far a box can scroll is how far its content reaches past its padding box, as on the web. That includes its absolutely positioned descendants, so a dropdown that opens past the bottom of a scrolling form lets the form scroll down to show it (see the autocomplete recipe).

A scroll container's automatic minimum size is 0, as one with hidden overflow's is (see Content sets a minimum size), so a flex item that scrolls shrinks to fit beside its siblings instead of growing to fit its content. That's usually what a scrolling pane wants; give it a size, or shrink(0), when it should be as large as its content up to some limit.

A Text doesn't scroll its own text, nor a Canvas what it draws, so either one whose overflow is Scroll raises ValueError: put a long Text or a large Canvas in a Div that scrolls.

docs.title: Scrolling with the wheel
docs.text:
Nothing scrolls unless a handler scrolls it, as with every other input, so a scroll container that the wheel should scroll composes scroll_on_wheel into its on_input. A titled pane puts its border and title on a box around the part that scrolls, so they stay put while the content moves:

@component
def pane() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | size(30, 6),
        children=(
            Text(content=" Deploy log ", style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border),
            Div(
                style=fill(1) | col | overflow_y_scroll,
                on_input=scroll_on_wheel(),
                children=tuple(Text(content=f"{i:>2} {event}") for i, event in enumerate(EVENTS, start=1)),
            ),
        ),
    )

A wheel event goes to the element under the pointer and bubbles from there, so of nested scroll containers, the innermost under the pointer scrolls. scroll_on_wheel lets an event that would move its container past either end of its range bubble on, so once the inner one reaches its end, the wheel scrolls the one around it, as the web chains scrolling from one container to the next.

With Shift held, scroll_on_wheel scrolls sideways for the vertical wheel, as browsers on Windows and Linux do, so a mouse without a sideways wheel can scroll a container that only scrolls sideways, such as a wide code block. The wheel event still says which way the wheel turned and that Shift was held, as Firefox's does, rather than reporting a sideways turn, as Chrome's does, so a handler before scroll_on_wheel can give Shift with the wheel a meaning of its own. Some terminals keep Shift with the wheel for their own scrollback and never report it, so a sideways wheel or a trackpad's sideways swipe is the only way to scroll sideways there.

docs.title: Scrolling with the keyboard
docs.text:
scroll_on_keys scrolls for the keys that scroll a page in a browser: the arrow keys by a row or a column, PageUp and PageDown by a page, and Home and End to the start and the end. A key press goes to the focused element and bubbles from there, so a container the keys scroll is usually a focusable component's top-level element, and the keys scroll it while it, or anything inside it, is focused. Like scroll_on_wheel, it lets a key that would move its container past either end of its range bubble on, to the next container out.

A page is 87.5% of the height of the view, rounded down, as in Chrome, so the last lines of one page stay in view at the top of the next, to read on from. page_down and page_up return the ScrollBy for a page of any size, for apps that bind paging to other keys, such as less's Space for a whole page and d and u for half of one:

def less_keys(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    # Receiver.scroll is None only off a scroll container, and this handler is only on one.
    if receiver.scroll is None:
        return None
    match event:
        case KeyPressed(key=" "):
            return page_down(receiver.subtree, receiver.scroll, fraction=1.0)
        case KeyPressed(key="d"):
            return page_down(receiver.subtree, receiver.scroll, fraction=0.5)
        case KeyPressed(key="u"):
            return page_up(receiver.subtree, receiver.scroll, fraction=0.5)
        case _:
            return None


@component
def pager() -> Div:
    focus = use_focus(auto_focus=True)

    return Div(
        style=col
        | border
        | border_lightrounded
        | size(30, 8)
        | overflow_y_scroll
        | (border_color("sky", 400) if focus.is_focused else border_color("slate", 600)),
        on_input=first(less_keys, scroll_on_keys(), scroll_on_wheel()),
        children=tuple(Text(content=f"{i:>2} {EVENTS[i % len(EVENTS)]}") for i in range(30)),
    )

docs.title: Scrolling from a handler
docs.text:
The ScrollTo and ScrollBy controls scroll a container to an offset, or by an amount, clamped to its range. A handler on the scroll container itself names it by its receiver's subtree, as scroll_on_wheel does. A handler anywhere else names it by an element handle, an ElementHandle, as a React component reaches a DOM node through a ref: create one with use_state(ElementHandle), and pass it to the element's handle.

@component
def controlled() -> Div:
    log, _ = use_state(ElementHandle)

    return Div(
        style=col | gap(1),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | gap(2),
                children=(
                    Text(content="[ Top ]", on_input=on_click(lambda: ScrollTo(log, y=0))),
                    Text(content="[ Bottom ]", on_input=on_click(lambda: ScrollTo(log, y=len(EVENTS)))),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=col | border | border_lightrounded | size(30, 5) | overflow_y_scroll,
                handle=log,
                children=tuple(Text(content=f"{i:>2} {event}") for i, event in enumerate(EVENTS, start=1)),
            ),
        ),
    )
