╭────────────────────────────╮
│ 9 traffic shifted to 100%  │
│10 old replicas drained     │
│11 deploy finished          │

Two mounted elements given the same element handle raise DuplicateElementHandle, and a control whose handle names no mounted scroll container does nothing.

Scroll controls apply to the layout of the render after the handler that returns them, before that render paints, in the order they were returned, and after anchoring and sticking to the end have placed the content, so each moves the view from where those left it. So a handler that adds a line to a log and returns ScrollBy(log, y=1) beside the state change scrolls by a row of the log that has the new line, in the same frame. That's where Counterweight differs from the web: a browser's scrollBy scrolls the page as it stands while the handler runs, before React renders the state change, and a React app that wants to scroll the content that change lays out calls it from useLayoutEffect instead, which is what scroll controls do. A handler that runs later in the same batch of input sees the controls returned before it: its receiver's scroll is moved by each ScrollTo and ScrollBy since the last render, clamped to the range as of that render, so scroll_on_keys passes a key on once an earlier key has scrolled its container to the end.

docs.title: Scrolling an element into view
docs.text:
ScrollIntoView scrolls to an element rather than to an offset, as the web's scrollIntoView does: it scrolls each scroll container above the element, from the innermost out, until the element is in view. Its block says where the element goes vertically: "start", the default, puts its top at the top of the view, "center" in the middle, "end" at the bottom, and "nearest" scrolls as little as it takes, and not at all if the element is already in view. inline says the same horizontally, and is "nearest" by default. It stops at an element with clip_to_screen, since no container above that element clips it, so none has to scroll to show it.

A table of contents scrolls each section's heading to the top of the pane it's in:

SECTIONS = (
    ("Install", "Add counterweight to your project with uv."),
    ("Components", "A component is a function that returns an element."),
    ("Hooks", "Hooks keep state and run effects for a component."),
    ("Styles", "Styles are merged from small utilities with |."),
)


@component
def contents() -> Div:
    headings, _ = use_state(lambda: tuple(ElementHandle() for _ in SECTIONS))

    return Div(
        style=row | size(40, 6),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col | width(14) | border_right | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
                children=tuple(
                    Text(
                        content=title,
                        style=text_color("sky", 300),
                        on_input=on_click(partial(ScrollIntoView, heading)),
                    )
                    for (title, _), heading in zip(SECTIONS, headings, strict=True)
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=fill(1) | col | gap(1) | pad_x(1) | overflow_y_scroll,
                on_input=scroll_on_wheel(1),
                children=tuple(
                    Div(
                        style=col,
                        children=(
                            Text(content=title, style=text_color("amber", 400), handle=heading),
                            Text(content=body, style=text_wrap_pretty),
                        ),
                    )
                    for (title, body), heading in zip(SECTIONS, headings, strict=True)
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

Like the other scroll controls, it applies to the layout of the render after the handler that returns it, as React's useLayoutEffect would call scrollIntoView after the DOM updates and before the browser paints. So a handler that changes state and returns ScrollIntoView beside it shows both in the same frame, and the handle names the element that has it in that render, not the one before. A list that moves a highlight with Down puts one element handle on whichever item is highlighted, and returns ScrollIntoView(handle, block="nearest") beside the state change that moves it: the handle has moved to the new item by the time the control applies (see the autocomplete recipe). use_text_area does the same for its cursor: it returns a cursor_row element handle for the element the cursor's row is drawn in, and its handler returns ScrollIntoView for it with block="nearest" beside each edit, so a text area in a scroll container keeps the cursor in view as it moves between rows.

Moving focus scrolls the newly focused element into view with block="nearest", as browsers do, so Tab never leaves focus on something out of sight. That includes a component that takes focus with auto_focus as it mounts.

ScrollIntoView scrolls in one step. The web's behavior: "smooth" animates the scroll across frames, which Counterweight has no design for yet: a fixed number of frames and a fixed duration are both plausible.

docs.title: Reading the scroll
docs.text:
use_scroll returns a Scroll: how far the calling component's top-level element is scrolled, how far it can be, and the size of its padding box, the part of the content in view. Given an ElementHandle, it reports on the element with that handle instead, as a React component reads another element's scrollTop through a ref (see Jumping to the end). A handler's Receiver carries the same for a receiving element that's a scroll container, which is how scroll_on_wheel knows whether its container can move any further.

Like use_rects, use_scroll reports the previous frame's scroll, and a component that calls it renders again as soon as it changes. A list too long to render whole can render only the rows in view, with empty boxes above and below them so the content is as tall as every row would make it, as React's windowing libraries do:

ROWS = 100_000


@component
def windowed_row(i: int) -> Text:
    return Text(content=f"row {i:,} of {ROWS:,}")


@component
def windowed() -> Div:
    scroll = use_scroll()

    # Render the rows in view, with a screen's worth of rows on each side
    # so a scroll shows rows, not blank space, before this re-renders,
    # and an empty box above and below for the rest, so the content is as tall as every row.
    overscan = scroll.view_height
    first = max(0, scroll.offset.y - overscan)
    last = min(ROWS, scroll.offset.y + scroll.view_height + overscan)

    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | size(30, 6) | overflow_y_scroll,
        on_input=scroll_on_wheel(),
        children=(
            Div(style=height(first) | shrink(0)),
            # Keyed, so a row keeps its node as the window moves, and scroll anchoring follows the row.
            *(windowed_row(i).with_key(str(i)) for i in range(first, last)),
            Div(style=height(ROWS - last) | shrink(0)),
        ),
    )

╭────────────────────────────╮
│row 6 of 100,000            │
│row 7 of 100,000            │
│row 8 of 100,000            │
│row 9 of 100,000            │

The rows on each side of the view cover the frame between a scroll and the render that follows it, which would otherwise show the empty boxes. The rows are keyed components, so each keeps its place as the window moves (see Keeping the content in view).

docs.title: Keeping the content in view
docs.text:
When content changes above what's in view, an offset that stayed put would show different content: a message dropped from the top of a transcript would pull everything up by its height. So a scroll container keeps what's in view where it is, as browsers do with scroll anchoring. Before each layout, it picks an anchor: the first node in view, or, for a node only partly in view, the first of its descendants in view. After the layout, it moves its offset so the anchor's top edge is as far from the top of the view as it was. Content that changes below the anchor, or inside it, doesn't move the view; content that changes above it moves the view with it.

The anchor is a node, so it follows what each node shows from one render to the next. Siblings without keys continue the sibling at the same index, so when items drop off the front of an unkeyed list, every node shows the item after the one it did, and the view lurches forward by however far that moved the anchor. Give each item of a list whose front changes its own key, as React asks of a list (see When position isn't identity).

As on the web:

  • A container scrolled to the top doesn't anchor, so content added above the top pushes the rest down into view.
  • Anchoring moves only the vertical offset.
  • overflow_anchor_none turns it off: on a scroll container, its offset only gets clamped, and on an element inside one, neither it nor anything inside it is picked as the anchor. An element with clip_to_screen is never picked either.
  • A container whose anchor unmounted or was hidden only clamps its offset.

docs.title: Following the end
docs.text:
A log or a transcript should stay scrolled to its end as lines arrive, so the newest is always in view, until the reader scrolls back to read something earlier. stick_to_end_y does that: a container that's scrolled to its end before a layout is scrolled to its end after it, and one that isn't is anchored as usual. stick_to_end_x does the same horizontally, stick_to_end on both axes, and unstick turns it off. A container whose content fits is at its end, so a log that starts short follows its end from its first line, and one that mounts already overflowing starts at its end.

This log keeps its newest eight lines, adds one a second, and sticks to its end:

KEPT_LINES = 8


@component
def request_line(number: int) -> Text:
    return Text(content=f"{number:>3} GET /items/{number} 200")


@component
def tail() -> Div:
    tick = use_clock(timedelta(seconds=1))
    # A line a second, keeping the newest few.
    newest = 4 + int(tick.since_mount.total_seconds())

    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | size(30, 6) | overflow_y_scroll | stick_to_end_y,
        on_input=scroll_on_wheel(1),
        # Keyed, so a line keeps its node, which anchoring follows, as older lines drop off the top.
        children=tuple(request_line(n).with_key(str(n)) for n in range(max(0, newest - KEPT_LINES), newest)),
    )

docs.title: Jumping to the end
docs.text:
Counterweight doesn't draw scrollbars (#417), as most terminal apps don't, so a reader scrolled back through a log has no sign of how far the end is. A button over the last line that appears once the log is scrolled back, and jumps to the end, gives them one:

@component
def jump_to_end() -> Div:
    log, _ = use_state(ElementHandle)
    scroll = use_scroll(log)

    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | size(30, 6),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=fill(1) | col | overflow_y_scroll | stick_to_end_y,
                handle=log,
                on_input=scroll_on_wheel(1),
                children=tuple(Text(content=f"{i:>2} {event}") for i, event in enumerate(EVENTS, start=1)),
            ),
            # A sibling of the log, not a child, so it stays over the last line as the log scrolls.
            *(
                ()
                if scroll.offset.y == scroll.max_offset.y
                else (
                    Text(
                        content=" ↓ Jump to end ",
                        style=position_absolute
                        | inset_bottom(0)
                        | inset_x(0)
                        | margin_x_auto
                        | fit_content_width
                        | text_bg("sky", 800),
                        on_input=on_click(lambda: ScrollTo(log, y=scroll.max_offset.y)),
                    ),
                )
            ),
        ),
    )

Scrolling back, then clicking the button:

The button is a sibling of the log in a box around it, not a child of the log, because a scroll container moves everything inside it by its offset, absolutely positioned elements included, so a button inside the log would scroll away with the lines. Being outside the log, it reads the log's scroll with use_scroll(log). That's the previous frame's scroll, so the button appears a frame after the scroll that should show it, which nobody notices for a button that comes and goes. A wheel event over the button goes to the box around the log, not the log, so the wheel doesn't scroll it there. use_scroll_area puts its handler on the box around the part that scrolls, so its is_at_end and to_end make the same button from inside the component, and the wheel scrolls the log from over the button too.

docs.title: Where scrolled boxes are
docs.text: Scrolling moves boxes, so everything that reports where a box is reports where it's painted: use_rects, a receiver's rects, the element the mouse is over, and use_hovered. A box scrolled partly out of view is still whole there, with its visible region the part in view, as for any box that's clipped.

docs.title: counterweight.focus.ElementHandle dataclass
docs.text:
ElementHandle()

An opaque token that names one element, as a React ref names a DOM node: a scroll container for ScrollTo, ScrollBy and use_scroll, or an element to bring into view with ScrollIntoView, such as the cursor's row a text area draws with its cursor_row.

It's an identity token, equal only to itself, so it can exist before the element it names has mounted: a component creates one with use_state(ElementHandle) and passes it to an element's handle. Two mounted elements given the same handle raise DuplicateElementHandle.

docs.title: __repr__
docs.text:
__repr__() -> str

Names the handle by its identity, since that's all that tells two handles apart.

docs.title: counterweight.shadow.DuplicateElementHandle
docs.text: Raised when two mounted elements are given the same ElementHandle, which leaves it naming neither.

docs.title: Sizing One Box
docs.text: A box that doesn't set its own size takes its content size along its parent's main axis, and stretches across it (see How layout sizes things). The utilities on this page override either.

docs.title: A fixed size
docs.text:
width, height and size set a box's size in cells. An axis left unset keeps its default: the height(4) box below still stretches across the column.

@component
def fixed() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(style=size(24, 4) | border, content="size(24, 4)"),
            Text(style=width(36) | border, content="width(36)"),
            Text(style=height(4) | border, content="height(4)"),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Fit to content
docs.text:
Along the main axis, a box already fits its content. Across it, a box stretches unless its alignment says otherwise: align_self_start (or any alignment except stretch) shrinks it to its content.

@component
def fit() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="stretched by its col"),
            Text(style=align_self_start | border, content="align_self_start"),
        ),

docs.title: Sizing keywords
docs.text:
The sizing keywords set a box's width or height from its content, whichever axis it is on:

  • min_content_width is as narrow as the content goes without breaking a word: for wrapping text, its widest word.
  • max_content_width is as wide as the content is unwrapped.
  • fit_content_width is the max-content width, capped at the space available (but never below the min-content width), as a wrapping paragraph is in CSS. It differs from max_content_width only when the content doesn't fit.
  • stretch_width fills the space available, after the box's margins.

Each has a _height counterpart. Here each box is the only child of a row:

KEYWORDS = {
    "min_content_width": min_content_width,
    "max_content_width": max_content_width,
    "fit_content_width": fit_content_width,
    "stretch_width": stretch_width,
}


@component
def content_keywords() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=row,
                children=(Text(style=keyword | border | text_wrap_stable, content=f"{name} sizes this"),),
            )
            for name, keyword in KEYWORDS.items()
        ),
    )

└─────────────────┘

└────────────────────────────┘          
┌────────────────────────────┐          
│fit_content_width sizes this│          
└────────────────────────────┘          
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐

In a col, a width keyword doesn't size wrapping text correctly: taffy measures the box's height at the column's full width, before applying the keyword, and doesn't measure it again. Below, min_content_width keeps the one row its text takes at full width, so sizes this, wrapped onto a second row, overflows the box and is drawn over its bottom border. A max_content_width box wider than the column keeps extra rows for the same reason. Put the box in a row, as above, or in a grid.

@component
def content_keywords_col() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=tuple(
            Text(style=keyword | border | text_wrap_stable, content=f"{name} sizes this")
            for name, keyword in KEYWORDS.items()
        ),
    )

@component
def filling() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="content height"),
            Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="fill(1): the rest of the col"),
            Div(
                style=row,
                children=(Text(style=full_width | border, content="full_width: the whole row"),),

docs.text:
max_width and max_height cap a box that would otherwise grow; min_width and min_height stop one shrinking. In the top row, the first box would take half the row but stops at 20 cells. In the bottom row, two 30-cell boxes don't fit in 40 cells, so both shrink, but the first stops at 24 cells and the second gives up the rest.

@component
def clamped() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row,
                children=(
                    Text(style=fill(1) | max_width(20) | border, content="fill(1)\nmax_width(20)"),
                    Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="fill(1)"),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | width(40) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=width(30) | min_width(24) | border, content="width(30)\nmin_width(24)"),
                    Text(style=width(30) | border, content="width(30)"),
                ),
            ),

docs.text:
aspect_ratio sets a box's width divided by its height, so a box with a width and an aspect ratio gets its height from them. Terminal cells are about twice as tall as they are wide, so aspect_ratio(1) looks tall, and aspect_ratio(2) is the one that looks square. The parent here sets align_children_start: a box stretched across a row has its height from the row, and its aspect ratio has nothing to set.

@component
def aspect() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | align_children_start,
        children=(
            Text(style=width(18) | aspect_ratio(1) | border, content="width(18)\naspect_ratio(1)"),
            Text(style=width(18) | aspect_ratio(2) | border, content="width(18)\naspect_ratio(2)"),
        ),
    )

docs.text:
Sizes include the border and padding by default, so a width(24) box is 24 cells wide overall. With content_box, the size applies to the content alone, and the border and padding are added outside it: here 24 cells of content, 4 of padding and 2 of border.

@component
def box_sizing() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | align_children_start,
        children=(
            Text(style=width(24) | pad_x(2) | border, content="width(24)"),
            Text(style=content_box | width(24) | pad_x(2) | border, content="content_box | width(24)"),

docs.title: The box model
docs.text:
Counterweight's layout follows the CSS box model. Every element's box is four nested rectangles:

  • Content: where the element's content goes. A Div's content is its children, and a Text's content is its text.
  • Padding: space between the content and the border.
  • Border: the box-drawing characters around the padding.
  • Margin: space between the border and the element's neighbors.

The example below colors each rectangle:

@component
def root() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=fill(1)
                | content_color("green", 500)
                | padding_color("orange", 500)
                | pad_x(2)
                | pad_y(1)
                | border
                | border_lightrounded
                | border_bg("blue", 500)
                | margin_color("red", 500)
                | margin_x(2)
                | margin_y(1)
            ),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

  ╭────────────────────────╮  
  │                        │  
  │                        │  
  │                        │  
  │                        │  
  │                        │  
  │                        │  
  ╰────────────────────────╯

Terminal cells are not square

Terminal cells are about twice as tall as they are wide, so one row of vertical padding or margin looks about as big as two columns of horizontal. The example above uses twice as much horizontal spacing as vertical for that reason, and horizontal spacing alone is often enough.

docs.title: Gap, margin and padding
docs.text:
All three put space around children, but they belong to different elements:

  • gap is set on the parent, and puts space between its children only.
  • margin is set on a child, and puts space all around it, including at the ends of the row. Margins don't collapse into each other, so two children with margin_x(1) are two cells apart.
  • pad is set on the parent, and puts space between its border and all of its children.

margin_sides and pad_sides set each side separately, in the order of CSS's four-value shorthands: top, right, bottom, left.

margin_color and padding_color color the margin and padding, in red and blue here. As on the web, a margin is painted only where its element sets margin_color, and content_color fills the box inside the margin, so a margin otherwise leaves whatever lies beneath it visible.

@component
def gap_margin_pad() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | gap(2) | border | border_heavy,
                children=tuple(Text(style=border, content=f"gap(2) on the row {n}") for n in range(2)),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | border | border_heavy,
                children=tuple(
                    Text(style=margin_x(1) | margin_color("red", 600) | border, content=f"margin_x(1) {n}")
                    for n in range(2)
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | pad_x(2) | padding_color("blue", 600) | border | border_heavy,
                children=tuple(Text(style=border, content=f"pad_x(2) on the row {n}") for n in range(2)),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Sharing borders between neighbors
docs.text:
border_collapse on a parent overlaps its children's borders by one cell, so neighbors share a border instead of drawing two side by side. Where the shared borders meet, border healing joins them with the right junction characters.

@component
def collapse() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row,
                children=tuple(Text(style=border, content="side by side") for _ in range(3)),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | border_collapse,
                children=tuple(Text(style=border, content="border_collapse") for _ in range(3)),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Borders on some sides
docs.text:
Borders work as they do in Tailwind. A side is drawn where its border width is 1, and layout reserves a cell for it. border sets all four sides, border_top, border_bottom, border_left and border_right set one, and border_x and border_y set a pair. Each has a _0 form, such as border_right_0, that takes its sides away. Sides start at 0, so border_top | border_left draws just those two.

Merging is ordered, as it is for every style: the right side wins. border | border_right_0 leaves the right side off, but border_right_0 | border turns it back on.

The border kind only chooses the characters, and defaults to BorderKind.Light, so border alone draws a light border and border | border_heavy a heavy one. A kind with no widths draws nothing. border_none removes the border along with its space. border_sides sets all four sides at once from a set of side names.

@component
def sides() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | align_children_start | gap(2),
        children=(
            Text(style=border_y, content="border_y"),
            Text(style=border_top | border_left, content="border_top\n| border_left"),
            Text(style=border | border_right_0, content="border\n| border_right_0"),
            Text(style=border_right_0 | border, content="border_right_0\n| border"),
        ),
    )

border_y  │border_top     │border            │border_right_0│
────────  │| border_left  │| border_right_0  │| border      │
                          └────────────────  └──────────────┘

docs.text:
border_contract(n) stops each edge n cells short at an end next to a side that isn't drawn.

@component
def contract() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | align_children_start | gap(2),
        children=(
            Text(
                style=border_top | border_left | pad_x(1),
                content="top and left\nsides",
            ),
            Text(
                style=border_top | border_left | border_contract(2) | pad_x(1),
                content="top and left\nsides\nborder_contract(2)",
            ),
        ),
    )

│ sides            sides

docs.title: Splitting Space
docs.text:
Each split on this page can be built two ways. With flexbox, each child carries its own share. With grid, the parent lists the shares as track sizes, and children fill the tracks in order. Both give the same screenshot.

The flexbox versions use the constraint utilities, named after the constraints ratatui splits an area with:

Utility The child takes length(n) n cells percentage(p) p percent of the parent ratio(a, b) a / b of the parent fill(n) n shares of the space the others leave

Each acts along its parent's main axis, so the same utility works in a row and in a col, and none of them lets content push a child past its share. They are ordinary Styles, so you can override one part and keep the rest: length(20) | grow(1) takes 20 cells and then a share of whatever is left, and fill(1) | min_width(15) fills but never gets narrower than 15 cells.

The grid versions list the same constraints as track sizes: a plain int is that many cells, and fr(n) is n shares of the space the others leave.

            Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="fill(1)"),

docs.title: Nested splits
docs.text:
With flexbox, a split inside a split is a container inside a container: here a col that fills the rest of the row, split in turn between two children. fill works on the column's vertical axis just as it does on the row's horizontal one. With grid, one parent can hold both axes, and a child spans tracks to cover the space a nested container would have.

docs.title: Content wider than its share
docs.text:
A bare waxy.Fraction track has the same floor as a flex item: it is never narrower than its content's minimum size. In the top grid below, two lines of unwrapped text push their columns past the grid's edge. fr(1) is CSS's minmax(0, 1fr), which lowers the floor to zero, so in the middle grid the columns split the space. Each line is still wider than its column, so it overflows the column, as text does in CSS, over the next column and the grid's border. In the bottom grid, overflow_hidden on each Text clips its line at its own padding box.

@component
def overflow_grid() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(waxy.Fraction(1), waxy.Fraction(1)) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=border, content=LONG),
                    Text(style=border, content=LONG),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(fr(1), fr(1)) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=border, content=LONG),
                    Text(style=border, content=LONG),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(fr(1), fr(1)) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=border | overflow_hidden, content=LONG),
                    Text(style=border | overflow_hidden, content=LONG),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Percentages and gaps
docs.text:
A percentage is a share of the parent's whole content box, and gaps aren't subtracted first, so two halves and a gap don't fit. percentage doesn't shrink, so in the bottom row the halves keep their size and overflow the row by the width of the gap. With shrink(1), as in the top row, each half gives up one cell to the gap instead. To split a row with gaps into equal shares, use fill as in Equal shares.

@component
def percent_gap() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | gap(2) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=percentage(50) | shrink(1) | border, content="percentage(50) | shrink(1)"),
                    Text(style=percentage(50) | shrink(1) | border, content="percentage(50) | shrink(1)"),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | gap(2) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=percentage(50) | border, content="percentage(50)"),
                    Text(style=percentage(50) | border, content="percentage(50)"),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Text in Layout
docs.text: A Text is sized by measuring its content: unwrapped, it is as wide as its longest line; with a wrap mode, its height is the number of lines its content wraps to at the width it gets. Content that doesn't fit overflows the Text's box and is drawn past it, as text is in CSS, unless the Text or one of its ancestors clips it. Text wrapping compares the wrap modes themselves.

docs.title: Wrapping inside a pane
docs.text:
A wrapping Text in a column is stretched to the column's width, and wraps to fit it, taking as many rows as it needs.

@component
def wrap_in_pane() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=(
            Text(style=length(16) | border, content="length(16)"),
            Div(
                style=col | fill(1) | border | pad_x(1),
                children=(Text(style=text_wrap_stable, content=PARAGRAPH),),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.text:

    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2) | border | border_heavy,
        children=(
            Text(style=text_wrap_stable | border, content=PARAGRAPH),
            Text(style=text_wrap_stable | border, content=PARAGRAPH),

docs.title: Justification needs room
docs.text:
text_justify_center and text_justify_right align each line within the Text's own width. A Text stretched across its parent has room to move its lines, but one sized to its content, like the align_self_start one below, has none. With a wrap mode, each line is aligned separately.

    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(style=text_justify_center | border, content="text_justify_center, stretched"),
            Text(
                style=text_justify_center | align_self_start | border,
                content="text_justify_center | align_self_start",
            ),
            Text(
                style=text_justify_center | text_wrap_balance | border,
                content="text_justify_center | text_wrap_balance centers each line of a paragraph "
                "within the width of the box",
            ),

docs.title: Long unwrapped text in a narrow pane
docs.text:
In the top panes below, a line too long for its pane overflows it, as unwrapped text does in CSS, drawing over the pane's border and past it. In a col, the Text is stretched to the column's width, however long its content, so its box fits the column and only its line overflows. In a row, a Text can't shrink below its content's width, so its whole box overflows the row (see Content sets a minimum size).

In the bottom panes, overflow_hidden on the Text fixes both: it clips the line at the Text's own padding box, and, as for any box that hides its overflow, lowers its minimum width to zero, so it shrinks to fit the row. A wrap mode breaks the lines to fit instead. overflow_hidden on the pane clips the Text at the pane's padding box (see Clipping), which in a row cuts off the Text's own right border with its line. overflow_x_scroll on the pane makes it a scroll container the reader can scroll along the line, in a col or a row alike.

@component
def narrow_panes(text_style: Style) -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(8),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col | width(20) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(Text(style=text_style, content="unwrapped text in a col"),),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | width(20) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(Text(style=text_style, content="unwrapped text in a row"),),
            ),
        ),
    )


@component
def narrow() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(narrow_panes(border), narrow_panes(border | overflow_hidden)),
    )

docs.title: Hyperlinks
docs.text:
Any text can be a hyperlink that the terminal opens when it's clicked: set link on a CellStyle. On a Chunk's style, that makes the chunk a link; on a Text's text_style, it makes all of its text one.

LINK = CellStyle(underline=True) | text_color("sky", 300).text_style


@component
def root() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | gap(1) | pad_x(1),
        children=(
            Text(
                content=(
                    Chunk(content="Counterweight is on "),
                    Chunk(content="GitHub", style=LINK | CellStyle(link="https://github.com/JoshKarpel/counterweight")),
                    Chunk(content=", and its docs are at "),
                    Chunk(content="counterweight.dev", style=LINK | CellStyle(link="https://www.counterweight.dev")),
                    Chunk(content="."),
                ),
                style=text_wrap_pretty,
            ),
            Text(
                content="This whole Text is one link.",
                style=pad_x(1)
                | border
                | border_lightrounded
                | Style(text_style=CellStyle(link="https://pygments.org")),
            ),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText

 counterweight.dev.                               

 ╭──────────────────────────────────────────────╮ 
 │ This whole Text is one link.                 │ 
 ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────╯

A link changes how nothing looks, so style it to look like one, as the example does with an underline and a color. It merges like any other field, so a Chunk inside a linked Text can link elsewhere, or set link=None to not be a link at all.

docs.title: How terminals handle them
docs.text:
Counterweight writes links as OSC 8 escape sequences, which most modern terminals support, including iTerm2, kitty, WezTerm, Ghostty, foot, GNOME Terminal and Windows Terminal. A terminal that doesn't ignores them, and shows the text as if it weren't a link.

Clicking a link is handled by the terminal, not the app, and the app never sees the click. Counterweight turns on mouse reporting, so some terminals only open a link with a modifier held, such as Shift, Ctrl or Cmd, depending on the terminal.

A link's URI must be printable ASCII, so CellStyle raises ValueError for anything else: a control character could end the escape sequence and start another. Percent-encode anything outside ASCII, as urllib.parse.quote does.

docs.title: Markdown
docs.text:
markdown_document renders a Markdown document as a component, which goes anywhere a component does. It handles GitHub Flavored Markdown, and YAML front matter at the top of a document.

README = """\
# Peaks

The *fourteen* peaks above **8000 m** are all in Asia;
see [the list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousander).

> Because it's there.

- Himalayas
  - Everest
  - Kangchenjunga
- Karakoram
  - K2

| Peak | Height (m) |
|:-----|-----------:|
| Everest | 8849 |
| K2 | 8611 |

```python
tallest = max(peaks, key=lambda p: p.height)
```
"""


@component
def root() -> Div:
    return Div(style=col | pad_x(1), children=(markdown_document(README),))

  tallest = max(peaks, key=lambda p: p.height)
  • Links, bare URLs, and images are hyperlinks to their destinations. An image is shown as its alt text, since a terminal can't show the image.
  • Fenced code blocks are highlighted as the language their info string names, or shown as written if it names none, or one Pygments doesn't know. Code blocks and tables too wide for the space they're given scroll sideways.
  • Math, between $s within a line or $$s on lines of their own, is shown as written, since a terminal can't typeset it. A dollar sign starts math only by Pandoc's rule, with no space just inside it and no digit right after the closing one, so $5 and $10 stays text.
  • Raw HTML is shown as written.

GitHub's extensions to CommonMark draw like this:

EXPEDITION = """\
---
peak: K2
---

- [x] Reach base camp
- [ ] Summit, weather permitting[^window]

> [!WARNING]
> Bottlenecks form above camp four.

Forecasts are at www.mountain-forecast.com.

[^window]: Usually in late July.
"""


@component
def github() -> Div:
    return Div(style=col | pad_x(1), children=(markdown_document(EXPEDITION),))

  • Front matter is shown dimmed and highlighted as YAML. Pass MarkdownStyles(front_matter=display_none) to hide it.
  • A task list item's box takes the place of its bullet, or follows its number.
  • An alert is a block quote with a title, colored by its kind.
  • Footnotes are numbered in the order they're referenced, and their definitions follow the rest of the document.

docs.title: Parsing
docs.text:
markdown_document is a memo component, so it parses its document again only when its arguments change, and keeps what it rendered while it stays mounted, freed when it unmounts. A transcript that renders each message with one parses only the message that changed, however many messages there are, as React apps wrap a Markdown component in React.memo.

The function it calls, markdown, returns the document's Div of elements, and parses the document each time it's called. Call it to put the elements together with others yourself, under use_memo in a component that renders often.

docs.title: Scrolling
docs.text:
A document is as tall as its content, so one longer than the space it's given runs past the bottom of it. Put it in a scroll container, as a browser puts a page in a scrolling viewport, with scroll_on_keys and scroll_on_wheel to scroll it:

@component
def scrolling() -> Div:
    # Focused, so the keys reach scroll_on_keys.
    use_focus(auto_focus=True)
    return Div(
        style=col | full | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1) | overflow_y_scroll,
        on_input=first(scroll_on_keys(), scroll_on_wheel()),
        children=(markdown_document(README),),
    )

docs.title: Wide code and tables
docs.text:
A code block with lines wider than the space it's given scrolls sideways rather than wrapping them, as GitHub's styles give a pre overflow: auto. markdown puts it in a box with overflow_x_scroll and scroll_on_wheel, so the wheel scrolls it under the pointer:

INSTALL = """\
Install it with:

```bash
uv add counterweight markdown-it-py mdit-py-plugins pygments
```
"""


@component
def wide() -> Div:
    return Div(style=col | pad_x(1), children=(markdown_document(INSTALL),))
BeforeAfter four wheel notches to the right ScreenshotText 

 Install it with:                       

  uv add counterweight markdown-it-py m
ScreenshotText 

 Install it with:                       

 terweight markdown-it-py mdit-py-plugi

A table scrolls the same way once its cells have wrapped as narrow as their words allow, as GitHub's styles make a table a block with overflow: auto. Only a sideways wheel scrolls them, such as a tilting wheel or a trackpad's sideways swipe, or the wheel with Shift held, as in a browser. An up or down notch without Shift over one passes on to the scroll container around the document, so the document scrolls as it does anywhere else. Some terminals keep Shift with the wheel for their own scrollback and never report it, so there only a sideways wheel scrolls them.

Browsers also let Tab focus a scroll container with nothing focusable inside, and the arrow keys scroll it. A code block here isn't focusable, since markdown returns elements, not components that could call use_focus, so only the wheel scrolls it.

To wrap long lines instead, pass MarkdownStyles(code_block_text=text_wrap_stable).

docs.title: Line breaks
docs.text: CommonMark joins the lines of a paragraph with a space, so a document's source can wrap wherever its author likes. What people type into a chat is different: GitHub's comments and chat apps keep each line break they type. Pass keeps_line_breaks=True to break the line wherever the source does, as the chat example does for your messages.

docs.title: Styles
docs.text:
MarkdownStyles holds a Style for each kind of block and a CellStyle for each kind of inline span. A code block and a table are each a box around what they show: code_block and table style the box, which scrolls, and code_block_text and table_grid what's inside it. Pass the fields you want to change, and the rest keep their defaults:

markdown_document(source, MarkdownStyles(heading_1=text_color("amber", 300), code_theme="monokai", block_gap=0))

docs.title: counterweight.markdown.markdown_document
docs.text:
markdown_document(
    source: str,
    styles: MarkdownStyles = MarkdownStyles(),
    keeps_line_breaks: bool = False,
) -> Div

source, a Markdown document, rendered as markdown renders it, by a component that keeps what it rendered while it stays mounted, and parses the document again only when its arguments change, as a memo component does.

What it keeps is one document per mounted component, freed when the component unmounts, so a transcript of many messages, or one streaming in, parses only the message that changed.

docs.title: counterweight.markdown.markdown
docs.text:
markdown(
    source: str,
    styles: MarkdownStyles = MarkdownStyles(),
    keeps_line_breaks: bool = False,
) -> Div

source, a Markdown document, as a Div of its blocks, drawn with styles.

Links, bare URLs, and images are hyperlinks to their destinations. Fenced code blocks are highlighted as the language their info string names, or shown as written if it names none or one Pygments doesn't know. Code blocks and tables wider than the space they're given scroll sideways with the wheel. Math and raw HTML are shown as written, too.

It parses source each time it's called. In a component that renders often, use markdown_document, or call it under use_memo.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION keeps_line_breaks

Whether a line break inside a paragraph breaks the line where it's drawn, as GitHub's comments and chat apps draw what people type, rather than joining the lines with a space, as CommonMark does.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

docs.title: Syntax Highlighting
docs.text:
code_block highlights source code with Pygments, in any of the languages it knows, and draws it on its theme's background.

SOURCE = '''\
@component
def greeting(name: str) -> Text:
    """Say hello."""
    return Text(content=f"Hello, {name}!")
'''


@component
def root() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | gap(1),
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=col,
                children=(
                    Text(content=f" {theme} ", style=text_color("slate", 400)),
                    code_block(SOURCE.rstrip("\n"), "python", theme=theme, style=pad(1)),
                ),
            )
            for theme in ("github-dark", "monokai", "solarized-light")
        ),
    )

A theme is the name of any Pygments style, or a pygments.style.Style subclass, which is how to define your own.

code_block is as wide as its longest line, as an HTML pre is. To scroll lines wider than the space it's given, put it in a scroll container with overflow_x_scroll and scroll_on_wheel, as markdown does, so a sideways wheel, or the wheel with Shift held, scrolls it:

Div(style=overflow_x_scroll, on_input=scroll_on_wheel(), children=(code_block(source, "python"),))

To lay the code out yourself, highlight returns its chunks, to put in a Text with whatever else you like, and code_style the background and text color to draw them on.

Highlighting is cached by its arguments, so a component can highlight the same code on every render without lexing it again. Tabs are expanded, to four columns unless tab_size says otherwise.

highlight(
    code: str,
    language: str,
    theme: CodeTheme = DEFAULT_CODE_THEME,
    tab_size: int = 4,
) -> tuple[Chunk, ...]

code as chunks styled by the tokens a Pygments lexer finds in it.

language is any name or alias of a Pygments lexer, such as python, py, or toml; theme is a Pygments style, by name (any of pygments.styles.get_all_styles()) or as a pygments.style.Style subclass, which is how to define your own. An unknown language or theme raises pygments.util.ClassNotFound. Tabs are expanded to tab_size columns.

The theme's colors are set only where it sets them, so the rest come from the Text's text_style: put the chunks in a Text styled by code_style to draw them on the theme's background.

docs.title: Merging
docs.text:
Styles are merged using the | operator: left | right. Every field starts out unset (the counterweight.styles.UNSET sentinel), and the result takes right's value for every field right sets, and left's value otherwise.

A field set to its default value is still set, so it overrides left. CellStyle(bold=True) | CellStyle(bold=False) is CellStyle(bold=False), border | border_none draws no border, and text_justify_center | text_justify_left justifies left. Utilities set only the fields they are about, so they layer without clearing each other: text_color("red", 500) | text_bg("slate", 900) is red text on a slate background.

merge does the same for any number of Styles: merge(a, b, c) is a | b | c. It skips None wherever it appears, so a style that only sometimes applies can be passed inline, as in merge(base, hover_style if hovered else None), and merge() is an empty Style().

Nested styles merge field by field too: Style(text_style=CellStyle(bold=True)) | Style(text_style=CellStyle(italic=True)) is both bold and italic. layout follows the same rule, field by field.

When an element is drawn, any field still unset takes its default from STYLE_DEFAULTS and CELL_STYLE_DEFAULTS.

docs.title: counterweight.styles.Style dataclass
docs.text:
Style(
    *,
    layout: Style = Style(),
    z: int | UNSET = UNSET,
    clip_to: ClipTo | UNSET = UNSET,
    overflow_anchor: OverflowAnchor | UNSET = UNSET,
    stick_to_end_x: bool | UNSET = UNSET,
    stick_to_end_y: bool | UNSET = UNSET,
    margin_color: AnyColor | UNSET = UNSET,
    padding_color: AnyColor | UNSET = UNSET,
    content_color: AnyColor | UNSET = UNSET,
    border_kind: BorderKind | UNSET | None = UNSET,
    border_style: CellStyle = _DEFAULT_CELL_STYLE,
    border_contract: int | UNSET = UNSET,
    text_style: CellStyle = _DEFAULT_CELL_STYLE,
    text_justify: TextJustify | UNSET = UNSET,
    text_wrap: TextWrap | UNSET = UNSET,
)

How an element is laid out and drawn.

Every field except layout starts UNSET, and the nested border_style and text_style start as empty CellStyles. Merging with | takes the right side's value wherever it is set, including when it is set to the default, so border | border_none has no border. layout merges the same way, field by field. Unset fields resolve to the defaults in STYLE_DEFAULTS.

A border side is drawn where its width in layout (border_top, ...) is 1, and border_kind chooses the characters it's drawn with. A border_kind of None removes the border, along with the space reserved for it. Each side is one cell, so a Style whose layout sets a border width other than Length(0) or Length(1) raises ValueError.

clip_to chooses what clips the element. With "padding", the default, or "border", it's its parent's padding or border box, on each axis where the parent's overflow is Hidden, Clip or Scroll, and every clip above the parent clips the element too; "border" lets a title be drawn on its parent's border. With "screen", the element is unclipped: no ancestor clips it, so a popup can reach past them, though its own overflow still clips its descendants.

overflow_anchor and stick_to_end_x and stick_to_end_y choose how a scroll container's offset follows its content when the content changes. With overflow_anchor "auto", the default, a scroll container keeps the content in view where it was, as CSS's overflow-anchor does; with "none", a scroll container keeps its offset, and nothing inside an element that sets it is an anchor for the scroll container around it. A scroll container that sticks to its end on an axis and is scrolled to its end there stays scrolled to its end when its content grows.

IndexedColor(index: int)

Entry index, from 0 to 255, of the terminal's palette, whose color the terminal decides, as the SGR sequences 38;5;n and 48;5;n name it.

Entries 0 to 7 are black, red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan and white, and 8 to 15 their bright forms, all of which the user's theme sets; 16 to 231 are a 6x6x6 color cube and 232 to 255 a gray ramp, which terminals define as xterm does. How to draw a cell's character: its colors and attributes.

Every field starts UNSET. Merging with | takes the right side's value wherever it is set, including when it is set to the default, so CellStyle(bold=False) turns bold off. Unset fields resolve to the defaults in CELL_STYLE_DEFAULTS.

docs.title: Text Wrapping
docs.text: By default, Text elements render their content on a single line. When the content is wider than the available space, it overflows rather than wrapping. Use the text_wrap_* style utilities to control how long text is broken across lines.

docs.title: Wrap Modes
docs.text:
Counterweight supports four wrap modes, illustrated below with the same paragraph of Markdown, whose paragraphs wrap with the paragraph style of MarkdownStyles:

SAMPLE = """\
It was the *best of times*, it was the *worst of times*,
it was the age of **wisdom**, it was the age of **foolishness**.
"""

WRAP_STYLE: dict[TextWrap, Style] = {
    "none": text_wrap_none | overflow_hidden,
    "stable": text_wrap_stable,
    "pretty": text_wrap_pretty,
    "balance": text_wrap_balance,
}


@component
def wrap_pane(mode: TextWrap) -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=fill(1) | col | border | pad_x(1),
        children=(
            Text(
                content=f" {mode} ",
                style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border,
            ),
            markdown_document(SAMPLE, MarkdownStyles(paragraph=WRAP_STYLE[mode])),
        ),
    )


@component
def root() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | fill(1),
                children=tuple(wrap_pane(mode) for mode in WRAP_STYLE),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: text_wrap_none (default)
docs.text: No wrapping. The text renders as a single line regardless of the available width. A line wider than its box overflows it and is drawn past it, as text is in CSS, unless the Text or one of its ancestors clips it. The comparison above gives the none paragraph overflow_hidden, which clips its line at the paragraph's own padding box.

docs.title: text_wrap_stable
docs.text: Greedy line-breaking — fills each line as much as possible before starting the next. This is the fastest algorithm and produces consistent, deterministic output. Use it when performance matters or when you want predictable line breaks.

docs.title: text_wrap_balance
docs.text: Attempts to make all lines roughly equal in length by binary-searching for the narrowest target width that doesn't increase the total line count. Useful for headings and short paragraphs where visual balance is more important than filling lines to the edge.

docs.title: text_wrap_pretty
docs.text: Dynamic-programming line-breaking (Knuth–Plass style) that minimises the sum of squared slack on non-final lines. This produces typographically "nicer" output than greedy wrapping — shorter lines near the end of a paragraph are avoided — at the cost of slightly higher CPU usage for very long texts.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: A wrapping Text wraps to the width layout gives it. In a column that width comes from the column, since children stretch across it by default. Side by side in a row, wrapping Texts shrink to share it, down to the width of their widest word. Text in layout shows both cases.

docs.title: Long Words and Hyphenation
docs.text: Words longer than the available width are broken with a hyphen (-) inserted at the break point. This applies to all three wrapping modes. Words are measured in terminal cells and broken between grapheme clusters, never inside one, so a line of wide characters may end a cell short.

docs.title: Multi-paragraph Text
docs.text: Newline characters (\n) in the content string are treated as paragraph separators. Each paragraph is wrapped independently, so explicit line breaks in your content are always preserved.

docs.title: Utilities
docs.text:
To avoid the tedium of writing out styles explicitly over and over, Counterweight provides a variety of Tailwind-inspired "utility styles". These utilities are pre-defined styles that can be combined to form more complex styles.

The utilities can be imported from the counterweight.styles.utilities module. We recommend a * import for ease of use:

from counterweight.styles.utilities import *

Each utility is a Style that sets just a small set of properties. Some are constants (e.g., border_heavy, justify_children_center), and the rest are functions that return one (e.g., gap(n), margin_x(n), pad(n)). Color utilities take a color name and shade as arguments. For example, border_color("rose", 200) returns a Style that sets the border color to rose-200: 

from counterweight.styles import Style, CellStyle, Color

border_color("rose", 200) == Style(border_style=CellStyle(foreground=Color.from_hex("#fecdd3")))

Since they are normal Styles, they can be combined to form more complex styles using the | operator. Here we make a new Style for a rose_200-colored heavy border on the top and bottom sides:

from counterweight.styles.utilities import *

border_heavy_top_bottom_rose_200 = border_y | border_heavy | border_color("rose", 200)

Actually giving a name to the new style is optional. We can also use the expression directly in our component:

from counterweight.styles.utilities import *
from counterweight.components import component
from counterweight.elements import Text


@component
def my_component() -> Text:
    return Text(
        content="Hello, world!",
        style=border_y | border_heavy | border_color("rose", 200),
    )

Performance Considerations

If you have an expression like border_y | border_heavy | border_color("rose", 200) in your component, it will be evaluated every time the component is rendered. Merging styles with | does take some time, though it is aggressively cached inside the framework. If you find that this is causing performance issues, you should create the style just once, ideally outside your component (i.e., at module scope), so that it runs only once.

docs.text:
Each table below is built from the utilities module when the docs are built. The constants' tables list every field each one sets. Fields not listed are left unset, so merging the utility into another style leaves them alone (see Merging). The functions' tables give their signatures, since what they set depends on their arguments.

docs.title: Terminal colors
docs.text:
A Color looks the same in every terminal. The terminal's own colors follow the user's theme instead, as the colors of a program run in it do: an IndexedColor is an entry of the terminal's 256-color palette, whose first 16 are the black, red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan and white that themes set, then their bright forms, and TERMINAL_DEFAULT is the terminal's default foreground where it colors text, and its default background where it fills one. These utilities set them in each place the color utilities above do, the *_indexed ones taking a palette index from 0 to 255. Screenshots draw them in DEFAULT_PALETTE, and the defaults as white on black.

docs.title: One-Shot Commands
docs.text:
A one-shot command runs a program that's expected to exit, though not necessarily to succeed, and shows everything it printed, colors and all, as a terminal would have shown it. A slide can run an example command when it's shown, and an editor can run the code in a text area and show what it printed.

This page covers running a command, how its output is sized, the terminal it runs on, cancelling and timing out a run, and showing output recorded ahead of time.

docs.title: Running a command
docs.text:
use_command runs a program when its run is called, and returns the latest run, a CommandRun value holding the program's argv, everything it printed so far as output, and its outcome. command_output shows a run: its output in a scroll_area that sticks to its end, so it follows the output while the program runs, with a line beneath that says how the run is going, or how it ended.

A slide that runs its command when it's shown calls run from an effect:

@component
def slide(title: str, argv: tuple[str, ...]) -> Div:
    # The box the output is shown in, which sets how wide the program's terminal is.
    viewport, _ = use_state(ElementHandle)
    command = use_command(columns=use_rects(viewport).content.width)

    async def start() -> None:
        command.run(argv)

    # Runs the command when the slide is shown, and again if it's shown with another one.
    use_effect(start, deps=(argv,))

    return Div(
        style=col | full | gap(1) | pad(1),
        children=(
            Text(content=title, style=text_color("sky", 300)),
            command_output(command.latest, viewport, style=fill(1)),
        ),
    )

A code runner runs its code on a key press instead:

@component
def code_runner() -> Div:
    code, set_code = use_state('for n in range(3):\n    print(f"{n} squared is {n * n}")')
    viewport, _ = use_state(ElementHandle)
    command = use_command(columns=use_rects(viewport).content.width, timeout=timedelta(seconds=10))

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.F5):
                command.run((sys.executable, "-c", code))
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Escape):
                command.cancel()
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | full,
        on_input=first(on_input, tab_focus),
        children=(
            text_area(code, set_code, enter_inserts_newline=True, auto_focus=True, style=max_height(10)),
            command_output(command.latest, viewport, style=fill(1)),
            Text(content="F5 runs the code, Escape stops it, Tab moves to the output", style=text_color("slate", 500)),
        ),
    )

This follows React Query's hooks for a fetch. useMutation runs on an event, through its mutate(), and exposes the latest run's status and result, which is run and latest here, and useQuery runs when its component mounts and again when its key changes, which is the slide's effect. A run differs from a fetch in two ways: its output streams, so latest shows what the program has printed so far while it runs, updating at most once a frame, and a program that exits with a failing status is a result like any other, not an error.

A run is a value that outlives its program, so a component can keep finished runs in state, show one again, or show it beside the next. Calling run again starts another run, even with the same argv, and hangs up the run in progress.

docs.title: How a run is sized
docs.text:
A run has two sizes, and only the first comes from its box.

  • The terminal's size is what the program formats its output for (wrapping, tables, progress bars). Its width is use_command's columns, which the slide and the runner read from the box their output is shown in, by passing command_output the same viewport handle they measure with use_rects(viewport). It's read when the run starts, and a run waits to start until it's positive, since use_rects reports zero on the first render. A later change doesn't rewrap a run's output: columns past the box's edge are cut off, and running again at the new width is up to the caller. Its height is rows, 24 by default, as a fresh xterm's is, which a program drawing a live display sizes it to. It doesn't come from the box, since the box scrolls rather than being the program's screen.
  • The output's size is how much the program printed: the run's columns wide, and as tall as the lines it printed, which grow while it runs. Its canvas takes that height, and the scroll area shows as many lines as fit.

Size the box from its parent

The output's width is the run's columns, which comes from the box, so the box has to take its width from its parent, by stretching, fill, or a styled width. A box sized by its content stays zero wide, and its run never starts.

docs.title: The terminal it runs on
docs.text:
A run gets a pseudo-terminal rather than pipes, so it prints what it would in a terminal:

  • Colors. Most programs color their output only when their output is a terminal.
  • Cursor movement. A progress bar that rewrites its line with \r, or a live display that moves the cursor up and redraws, leaves its last frame in the output, rather than every frame run together.

Its standard output and standard error arrive together, as they do in a terminal. A program that has to tell them apart is better run with asyncio's subprocess functions, which need no terminal.

The program sees a terminal, so it acts as it would on one:

  • Its standard input is /dev/null, so a program that reads input gets end of file rather than waiting for keys. A program that has to talk to its terminal can still open /dev/tty.
  • PAGER and GIT_PAGER are cat, so git log and other commands that start a pager print instead. Other tools read their own variables, such as MANPAGER, which env can set.
  • A program that asks its terminal something, such as where its cursor is, gets an answer from the emulator.
  • Its environment is the app's, under the terminal's variables (TERM=xterm-256color, COLORTERM=truecolor) and the pager defaults, under env, as for run_pty. clear_env=True leaves out the app's, which keeps a run's output from depending on who runs it.

docs.title: Cancelling and timing out
docs.text:
cancel hangs up the run in progress and makes its outcome Cancelled, keeping what it printed. Starting another run and unmounting the component hang it up too. Hanging up sends the program's process group SIGHUP, as closing a terminal window does, and SIGTERM and then SIGKILL to whatever is still running a second apart, so nothing a run started outlives it. That goes on in the background, so a program slow to exit doesn't hold up the app, which waits for it when it stops (see Hanging up in the background).

A program never gets the keys the app reads, so it can't be interrupted with Ctrl+C: bind a key to cancel, as the runner does with Escape. Ctrl+C reaches the app as a key press, so an app can bind it to cancel, as a shell does, rather than leaving it to quit the app. timeout bounds a run: a program still running when it runs out is hung up, and its outcome is TimedOut. Only the program's own run counts against it: one that exits in time has exited, even if a background job it left keeps its terminal open past the timeout.

A run keeps the last max_lines lines of its output, 10,000 by default, dropping the oldest, so a program that never stops printing can't grow it without bound.

docs.title: Recorded output
docs.text:
Transcript.of turns output recorded ahead of time, such as with script, into the same output a run has, with no program run, so a slide can show a command's output without running it. That's how the screenshots on this page were drawn:

BUILD = (
    b"\x1b[1mBuilding\x1b[0m web v4.2.0\r\n"
    b"[####......] 40%\r[##########] 100%\r\n"
    b"\x1b[32m\xe2\x9c\x93\x1b[0m compiled 42 modules\r\n"
    b"\x1b[33m!\x1b[0m 2 warnings in \x1b[4msrc/app.ts\x1b[0m\r\n"
    b"\x1b[32m\xe2\x9c\x93\x1b[0m wrote \x1b[36mdist/web.js\x1b[0m (184 kB)\r\n"
)


@component
def recorded_build() -> Div:
    viewport, _ = use_state(ElementHandle)
    # Recorded at the width of the box's content: 40 columns, less its border and padding.
    run = CommandRun(argv=("./build.sh",), output=Transcript.of(BUILD, columns=36), outcome=Exited(status=0))
    return Div(children=(command_output(run, viewport, style=size(40, 8)),))

A Transcript is a Canvas painter, so a canvas can show it without command_output.

docs.title: counterweight.commands.use_command
docs.text:
use_command(
    columns: int,
    rows: int = 24,
    env: Mapping[str, str] = frozendict(),
    clear_env: bool = False,
    timeout: timedelta | None = None,
    max_lines: int = MAX_LINES,
    hangup_grace: timedelta = HANGUP_GRACE,
) -> Command

Runs a program, when its run is called, on a pseudo-terminal columns by rows, with its standard input on /dev/null, so a program that reads input gets end of file rather than waiting, and returns the latest run, with everything it printed so far, which updates at most once a frame while it runs. Starting another run, cancelling, and unmounting the component each hang the program up (see run_pty) in the background, so a program slow to exit doesn't hold up the app's rendering, and an app that stops waits for it.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION columns

How wide the program's terminal is, which it formats its output for, such as the content width that use_rects reports for the box the output is shown in. It's read when the run starts, and a run waits to start until it's positive, since use_rects reports zero on the first render. A later change doesn't rewrap a run's output: running it again at the new width does.

TYPE: int

rows

How tall the program's terminal is, which a program that draws a live display sizes it to. It doesn't bound the output, which grows with what the program prints.

TYPE: int DEFAULT: 24

env

Variables to set in the program's environment. It gets PAGER=cat and GIT_PAGER=cat, so a command such as git log prints rather than paging, over the environment run_pty gives it, and env over those.

TYPE: Mapping[str, str] DEFAULT: frozendict()

clear_env

Leave out the app's environment (see run_pty).

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

timeout

How long the program may run before it's hung up and its outcome is TimedOut, or None for no limit (see run_pty).

TYPE: timedelta | None DEFAULT: None

max_lines

How many lines of output a run keeps, dropping the oldest, at most MAX_SCROLLBACK.

TYPE: int DEFAULT: MAX_LINES

hangup_grace

How long the program has to exit after each signal that hangs it up (see run_pty).

TYPE: timedelta DEFAULT: HANGUP_GRACE

docs.title: Embedded Terminals
docs.text:
An embedded terminal runs an interactive program, such as a shell, an editor or htop, in a box, shows its screen as the program draws it, and sends it the keys, pastes and mouse events the box receives, as a terminal window or a multiplexer's pane does. It's enough to build a terminal multiplexer: the multiplexer example runs shells side by side, with a tmux-style prefix key.

This page covers the widget, the hook it's built on, how input reaches the program, and how the terminal is sized. For a program that's expected to exit, whose output is read rather than used, see One-Shot Commands. Pseudo-terminals need Linux or macOS.

docs.title: A terminal widget
docs.text:
terminal is a bordered box that runs a program in a terminal the size of its content:

SHELL = (os.environ.get("SHELL", "/bin/sh"),)


def quit_on_ctrl_q(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    match event:
        case KeyPressed(key=Key.ControlQ):
            return Quit()
        case _:
            return None


@component
def shell() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | full,
        children=(
            terminal(SHELL, style=fill(1), intercept=quit_on_ctrl_q, auto_focus=True),
            Text(content="Ctrl+Q quits", style=text_color("slate", 500)),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

╭──────────────────────────────────────╮
│~/project $ ls --color                │
│docs  src  tests  README.md  build.sh │
│~/project $ git status --short        │
│ M src/app.py                         │
│A  tests/test_app.py                  │
│~/project $                           │
╰──────────────────────────────────────╯

The box takes no size from the program, since the program draws whatever fits the terminal it's given, so size the box with style, as fill(1) does here. The program starts once the box has room, and its terminal resizes with the box.

While the box is focused, the program gets every key, Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z included, so an app that embeds a terminal needs some other way out. intercept is a handler that sees each event before the terminal does, and keeps it from the program by claiming it, as quit_on_ctrl_q does for Ctrl+Q.

docs.title: The hook
docs.text:
use_terminal runs the program, emulates its terminal, and makes the calling component focusable, leaving how it's drawn to the component, which returns a Canvas with the hook's view and on_input. This pane puts a prefix handler before the terminal's, as the multiplexer does:

@component
def pane(argv: tuple[str, ...], prefix: InputHandler) -> Canvas:
    # The terminal is the canvas's content box, so it resizes with the pane.
    content = use_rects().content
    embedded = use_terminal(argv, content.width, content.height, auto_focus=True)

    return Canvas(
        painter=embedded.view,
        style=fill(1) | border | border_heavy | (border_color("amber", 400) if embedded.focus.is_focused else default),
        on_input=first(prefix, embedded.on_input),
    )

The hook returns the program's Screen as of the last snapshot, with its title and the modes it set, and its status: starting, running, exited with its status, or the reason it failed to start. The component's view is a ScreenView that draws the cursor while the component is focused.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
Keys, pastes and mouse events reach the program re-encoded, as tmux sends them, rather than passed through, since the app has already parsed the bytes its terminal sent into events. Each is encoded as xterm sends it, since the program is told TERM=xterm-256color, and for the modes the program set:

  • Keys go to the program while the component is focused and the program is running, and are claimed, so they don't bubble. Cursor keys switch to their application form (ESC O A) for a program that set DECCKM, as vim does.
  • Pastes are wrapped in bracketed paste's markers for a program that set ?2004, with any end marker in the text removed, so a paste can't end itself early.
  • Mouse events on the program's screen go to it only if it asked for them, at the level it asked for: presses, releases and the wheel, motion while a button is held, or all motion. A press focuses the component wherever it lands, and one on the border or padding only focuses it. Once the terminal has claimed a press, the drag and release that follow come to it wherever the pointer goes, and are clamped to the screen's edges. A wheel the program didn't ask for passes on, so a scroll container around the terminal still scrolls.
  • Focus events, ESC [ I and ESC [ O, go to a program that set ?1004 as the component gains and loses focus.

Once the program has exited, keys and pastes pass on, so the app's own keys work again.

docs.title: Keys before the program
docs.text: A handler put before the terminal's with first sees each key first, as a multiplexer's prefix key does: it claims the keys it binds, and passes on the rest to the program. The DOM would intercept with a capture-phase listener on an ancestor, but composing handlers on the terminal's own element does the same. A prefix and its key often arrive in one read, so keep whether the prefix is waiting in a ref, as the Prefix Keys cookbook page does.

docs.title: Queries
docs.text: Programs ask their terminal things, such as where the cursor is or what kind of terminal it is, and wait for the answer. The emulator answers from its own state, as tmux does, and the answer goes to the program as its input.

docs.title: Output and size
docs.text:
The emulator is fed as the program writes, and snapshotted at most once a frame, so a program that writes as fast as it can (cat of a large file) costs one snapshot a frame. When the app falls behind, the pseudo-terminal's buffer fills and the program waits, which is the backpressure a terminal gives.

A component that sizes the terminal from its own box, with use_rects().content, resizes the program's terminal along with it, which sends the program SIGWINCH. use_rects reports the box as of the last frame, so for one frame after a resize the old screen shows, cropped or padded, until the program redraws, as in tmux.

A program's colors reach the app's terminal as the program chose them (see Colors).

docs.title: Emulators and Pseudo-Terminals
docs.text:
One-shot commands and embedded terminals are built from two lower layers, which this page covers for code that needs them directly: a pseudo-terminal, which runs a program as a terminal window does and hands back the bytes it writes, and a terminal emulator, which turns those bytes into what the terminal shows. Neither knows about the other, so output recorded ahead of time can be fed to an emulator with no program run, and a program's output can go somewhere other than an emulator.

Pseudo-terminals need Linux or macOS.

docs.title: Pseudo-terminals
docs.text:
run_pty runs a program on a new pseudo-terminal until it exits, in its own session with the terminal as its controlling terminal, calling on_output with what the program writes, standard output and standard error together. It returns how the program exited (Exited), why it couldn't start (FailedToStart), or that it outran its timeout (TimedOut), and hands out a PtyConnection that writes to the program without blocking and resizes its terminal. Cancelling it hangs the program up, as closing a terminal window does.

use_pty runs a program while its component is mounted, as a terminal window or a multiplexer's pane does: it starts once its size is positive, resizes the terminal as its size changes, and starts the program again when its argv or environment change. It hangs the program up in the background, so a program slow to exit doesn't hold up the app's rendering.

docs.title: Hanging up in the background
docs.text:
The render loop waits for a cancelled effect to finish before it renders again, and hanging up a program that ignores SIGHUP takes up to two hangup_graces. So use_pty, and use_command for each run, call run_pty in a task of the app's task group and await that task through asyncio.shield, which keeps their effect's cancellation from waiting for it:

sequenceDiagram
    participant L as Render loop
    participant E as Effect
    participant R as run_pty, in the app's task group

    L->>E: Start the effect
    E->>R: Start run_pty and await it through shield
    alt The program exits, or outruns its timeout
        R->>R: Hang up whatever it left running
        R-->>E: Exited or TimedOut
        E->>E: Set the status, or report the run's outcome
    else Cancelled, by cancel, another run or argv, or unmounting
        L->>E: Cancel, then wait for it to finish
        E->>R: Cancel
        E-->>L: Finished at once
        Note over L: Renders again
        R->>R: Hang up the program, for up to two hangup_graces
        R-->>R: Ends cancelled, with no outcome to return
    end
    Note over L,R: An app that stops waits for every hangup still going

A program that ends by itself returns its outcome through the effect as usual, but only once run_pty has hung up what it left running. Only that effect waits for it, not the render loop, but a program that exits leaving a background job that ignores SIGHUP reads as running until that job is gone. A cancelled run has no outcome to return: cancel has already made it Cancelled, and another run or argv reports its own.

docs.title: Emulators
docs.text:
An Emulator is fed the bytes a program writes, answers the program's queries through on_reply, and snapshot turns what its terminal shows into an immutable Screen. A snapshot of a terminal that didn't change is the same Screen as before, and rows that didn't change are shared between snapshots, so a canvas drawing one redraws only when it changed. scrolled_off returns the rows that scrolled off the top of the screen since it was last called, for an emulator given a scrollback.

ScreenView is the Canvas painter that draws a Screen, with its cursor when asked, and Transcript the one that draws everything a program printed.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text:
A program's colors reach the app's terminal as the program chose them, so they follow the user's theme as they would had the program run there: a palette color (ESC [ 31 m, or ESC [ 38 ; 5 ; n m) stays an IndexedColor, and an RGB color a Color. A palette entry the program changed (with OSC 4) is the RGB color it changed it to, since the user's terminal doesn't know it.

A cell in the program's default colors leaves them unset, so it follows the text_style of the canvas showing it. To have those follow the user's theme too, give the canvas the terminal's default colors, as text_terminal_default | text_bg_terminal_default | content_terminal_default (see Terminal colors). A cell whose colors the program swapped (inverse video) or hid (invisible text) has to name its default colors, so it takes the emulator's foreground and background instead, which are white and black unless the program changes them (with OSC 10 and 11). set_default_colors changes them on a running emulator, as the user changing their terminal's theme does, though a color the program set stays what it set.

    on_output: Callable[[bytes], None],

        [PtyConnection], None
    ] = lambda connection: None,
